lessons.title: What a Distributed System Is
lessons.content:
Open bKash or Nagad, send 500 taka to your cousin in Rajshahi, and in about two seconds both phones show the new balance. It feels like you talked to one big computer. In reality, your tap probably touched a load balancer, an app server, an authentication service, a database with several copies, a fraud-checking service and an SMS gateway, running on many machines, maybe in more than one building. None of those machines shares memory with the others. None of them has exactly the same clock. Any one of them can crash in the middle of your transfer. Yet the system as a whole is expected to behave like one honest, reliable cashier. How that illusion is built, and where it breaks, is what this whole course is about.

What a distributed system is: The classic textbook definition (Tanenbaum and van Steen) says a distributed system is a collection of independent computers that appears to its users as a single coherent system. Two parts matter. "Independent computers" means each machine, called a node, has its own CPU, its own memory and its own operating system, and they cooperate only by sending messages over a network. "Appears as a single coherent system" means the user, and often the programmer, should not have to care which machine did what. Coulouris and colleagues give a second, more mechanical definition: a system in which components located on networked computers communicate and coordinate their actions only by passing messages. Keep both in mind: one is the goal, the other is the method.

Three facts that change everything: First, there is no shared memory. In the Operating Systems course (deep-cse-4-1) two threads could share a variable and protect it with a mutex. Here, if node A wants node B to know something, A must put it in a message, and the message takes time, may be delayed, duplicated or lost. Second, there is no global clock. Each node has its own quartz clock that drifts, so "which event happened first?" has no free answer (lessons 08 to 10). Third, failures are independent and partial. On one laptop, if the machine dies, everything stops together. In a distributed system one node can crash while the rest keep running, and the others often cannot tell whether it crashed, is just slow, or is cut off by the network.

Leslie Lamport's joke: Turing Award winner Leslie Lamport once described a distributed system as "one in which the failure of a computer you didn't even know existed can render your own computer unusable." It is funny because it is true. Your app hangs because some small configuration server in another building stopped answering. Much of this course is about making sure one hidden failure does not take everything down.

Distributed vs parallel vs networked: These words get mixed up. A parallel system (the subject of deep-cse-7-5) usually has many processors working on one big computation, often with shared memory or a very fast interconnect, and the main goal is speed. A computer network (deep-cse-4-3) is the plumbing: links, routers and protocols that move packets. A distributed system sits on top of the network and tries to make many machines act as one service; the main goals are sharing, scale and staying available when parts fail. A group of laptops that just browse the web are networked, but not a distributed system, because they are not cooperating on a shared task.

Why build one at all, reason 1, sharing resources: Data and devices live in different places. A hospital in Sylhet and a lab in Dhaka may need the same patient record. A university library catalogue must be searchable from every campus. Sharing is the oldest reason distributed systems exist.

Reason 2, scale: One machine has limits: a few hundred gigabytes of RAM, a fixed number of cores, one network card. If an e-commerce site like Daraz has a sale and millions of people search at once, no single server is big enough, and even if it were, it would be very expensive. Adding many ordinary machines, called scaling out or horizontal scaling, is usually cheaper than buying one giant machine, called scaling up or vertical scaling.

Reason 3, availability and fault tolerance: Machines fail. Disks die, power goes, someone trips over a cable. With several copies of a service on different machines, one can fail and users never notice. This is why banks keep a backup data center in a different city.

Reason 4, geography and latency: Light is fast but not instant. If all your servers sit in the USA, a user in Khulna waits for every request to cross half the planet. Putting copies of data and services near users, in a regional data center or at the edge of a CDN, makes apps feel faster.

A small worked example, why failures are normal: Suppose each machine is up 99.9 percent of the time, and failures are independent. If a request needs all of 100 machines to be up at once, the chance is 0.999 to the power 100, which is about 0.905, so roughly 1 request in 10 would fail. With 1000 machines it drops to about 0.368. Another way to see it: if a typical server fails about once every three years, a cluster of 1000 servers sees about 1000 / (3 x 365) = 0.91 failures per day, close to one every day. At scale, failure is not an accident; it is the weather. That is why distributed systems must be designed so that a request does not need every machine, but only enough of them.

The price you pay: Distribution brings new problems that a single program never had. Messages can be lost, so you need retries and timeouts (lesson 04). Retries can cause duplicates, so you need idempotency (lesson 05). Copies of data can disagree, so you need replication and consistency models (lessons 14 to 16). Nodes must sometimes agree on one value, such as who the leader is, which is surprisingly hard (lessons 13, 18, 19). And a transaction that touches two machines needs special protocols (lesson 21). Every benefit of distribution has a matching cost.

What a node and a message really are: A node is just a process running on some machine, with an address such as an IP and port (recap of deep-cse-4-3). A message is a sequence of bytes sent over TCP or UDP. Everything fancy you will see later, from remote procedure calls to consensus, is built from these two humble pieces. When you feel lost in a protocol, ask: which node sends which message to whom, and what happens if that message never arrives?

Modelling the world: To reason about algorithms we make assumptions, called a system model. Timing: in a synchronous model, message delays and processing speeds have known upper bounds; in an asynchronous model there are no bounds at all; real systems are mostly "partially synchronous", usually behaving well but sometimes not. Failures: nodes may crash and stop, or in the worst case behave arbitrarily, even maliciously, which is called Byzantine failure (lesson 20). Network: links may lose, delay, duplicate or reorder messages. The same algorithm can be correct in one model and broken in another, so always ask which model a claim assumes.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet transfer: When Rina in Dhaka sends 500 taka to Karim in Rajshahi, the app sends a request to an API gateway. An authentication service checks her PIN and session. A ledger service debits her account and credits Karim's, ideally in one atomic step even though the accounts may live on different database shards. A notification service puts two SMS messages on a queue. If the SMS service is slow, the money should still move; if the ledger database crashes halfway, the money must not vanish or double. Several lessons in this course zoom into exactly these steps.

Real-life example 2, a ride-sharing app in Chattogram: When you open Pathao or Uber, thousands of drivers send their GPS location every few seconds. The system must split the city into areas so no single machine handles all drivers (partitioning, lesson 22), match you to a nearby driver quickly, and keep working even if one server rack loses power. Your phone, the driver's phone and the servers all have slightly different clocks, so the system cannot blindly trust timestamps to decide who accepted a ride first.

Other everyday examples: Web search engines spread an index of billions of pages across many machines and query them in parallel. Online multiplayer games keep players in Dhaka and Chattogram in the same match. Email, DNS (deep-cse-4-3 lesson 08) and the Web itself are distributed systems. So are blockchains (deep-cse-9-2), which push the idea to nodes that do not trust each other at all.

The course map: Lessons 01 to 03 cover what, why and the main architectures. Lessons 04 to 07 cover communication: message passing, RPC, queues and naming. Lessons 08 to 11 cover time: physical clocks, logical and vector clocks, and global snapshots. Lessons 12 and 13 cover coordination: mutual exclusion and leader election. Lessons 14 to 17 cover replication, consistency models and CAP. Lessons 18 and 19 cover consensus, with Paxos and Raft. Lessons 20 and 21 cover fault tolerance and distributed transactions. Lessons 22 to 25 cover building at scale: sharding, distributed file systems, MapReduce, caching, microservices and observability. Lesson 26 ties everything into a capstone design for a Bangladesh mobile wallet.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often say "a distributed system is just many computers connected by a network". The missing word is cooperation toward one coherent service. Another mistake is thinking distribution makes things automatically faster or more reliable; done badly, it makes them slower and less reliable, because now more parts can fail. Exams typically ask you to define a distributed system, list its characteristics (concurrency, no global clock, independent failures), give advantages and disadvantages, and distinguish distributed from parallel systems. Be ready to explain Lamport's quip in your own words and to compute a simple probability like 0.999 to the power n.

How to think about this course: Almost every topic follows the same pattern. First, a single-machine idea that was easy, such as "read the latest value" or "take a lock". Second, the reason it breaks when machines are separate: delay, no shared clock, partial failure. Third, an algorithm or design that brings back as much of the old guarantee as possible, and the price it charges in messages, latency or availability. If you look for that pattern, the algorithms stop looking like magic tricks and start looking like reasonable answers to clear problems.

Recap: A distributed system is many independent computers, talking only by messages, that try to look like one coherent system. It has no shared memory, no global clock and suffers partial, independent failures. We build them for sharing, scale, availability and closeness to users, and we pay with harder programming. At scale, failures happen every day, so designs must tolerate them. Next lesson looks at the goals such a system aims for, transparency, openness and scalability, and at the eight famous false assumptions that trap new designers.
key_points: A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that appears to its users as a single coherent system.
Nodes cooperate only by passing messages: there is no shared memory and no global clock.
Failures are partial and independent: one node can crash while others run, and others may not know.
We distribute for resource sharing, scale (scaling out), availability and closeness to users.
At scale failure is normal: 0.999^100 is about 0.905, and 1000 servers see roughly one failure a day.
Distributed (cooperating service) differs from parallel (speed on one computation) and from a plain network (the plumbing).
System models fix assumptions about timing (synchronous, asynchronous, partially synchronous) and failures (crash, Byzantine).
lessons.tip: For every system you study, ask three questions: where are the messages, what happens if one is lost, and what happens if one machine dies halfway. These three questions unlock almost every lesson in this course.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily (bKash, Pathao, Facebook or Daraz). On paper, draw the boxes you think sit behind one action, such as sending money or booking a ride, and draw arrows for messages. Mark which box, if it crashed, would hurt the most, and write one idea for keeping the service alive without it.

quiz.q: Which statement best defines a distributed system?
options: Any computer with more than one CPU core
Independent computers, communicating by messages, that appear to users as one coherent system
A single server that handles many users
quiz.explain: The key ideas are independent computers, message passing and the single coherent system seen by users.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a basic characteristic of a distributed system?
options: A single shared memory that all nodes read and write
quiz.explain: Distributed nodes have no shared memory; they cooperate only by sending messages.

quiz.q: Each machine is up 99.9 percent of the time, independently. A request needs all 100 machines up. About how often does it succeed?
quiz.explain: 0.999^100 is about 0.905, so roughly 90 percent; failures multiply across machines.

quiz.q: Adding many ordinary machines instead of buying one bigger machine is called:
quiz.explain: Scaling out means adding more machines; scaling up means making one machine bigger.

quiz.q: In which system model are there NO upper bounds on message delay or processing speed?
quiz.explain: The asynchronous model assumes no timing bounds; synchronous assumes known bounds. Byzantine and fail-stop describe failures, not timing.

lessons.title: Goals of Distributed Systems and the Eight Fallacies
lessons.content:
Think of a good restaurant in Old Dhaka on Eid evening. You order kacchi, and it arrives hot. You never see the six cooks, the two kitchens, the boy who ran to the shop for more onions, or the waiter who covered for a colleague who went home sick. The restaurant hides all of that so that, from your table, it feels like one smooth service. A distributed system tries to do the same trick with computers. In lesson 01 we defined it as independent computers that appear as one coherent system. This lesson asks: what exactly should such a system aim for, how far can the hiding go, and which false beliefs make engineers build systems that collapse on the first bad day?

The four classic goals: Textbooks list four design goals. First, make resources easy to share. Second, hide the fact that resources are spread across machines, called distribution transparency. Third, be open, so that parts from different vendors can work together and the system can grow. Fourth, be scalable, so it keeps working as users, data and distance grow. We will take them one by one, then look at the fallacies.

Goal 1, resource sharing: Resources include storage, printers, data, compute power, and services such as payment or maps. Sharing saves money (one big storage cluster instead of a disk per office) and makes collaboration possible (a shared Google Doc, a shared hospital record). Sharing also brings risks: if everyone can reach a resource, security and access control become important (recap deep-cse-6-2), and many users at once means concurrency control.

Goal 2, distribution transparency: Transparency means hiding something from the user or programmer. The standard list has seven kinds. Access transparency hides differences in how data is represented and accessed, for example whether a file is local or on a server, or whether the machine is little-endian or big-endian. Location transparency hides where a resource physically is; a URL like a bank's website says nothing about which building serves it. Relocation transparency hides that a resource may be moved to another location while it is in use, such as a user's session moving to another server mid-session. Migration transparency hides that a resource may move to another location, for example a virtual machine moving to a different host. Replication transparency hides that several copies exist. Concurrency transparency hides that other users share the same resource at the same time. Failure transparency hides the failure and recovery of a part of the system.

A small table in words: If you ever need to remember them, think "ALRMRCF": Access, Location, Relocation, Migration, Replication, Concurrency, Failure. Exams love asking for the list with one example each, so for each kind, pick an everyday example: access (opening a file on Google Drive like a local file), location (typing a website name, not a server address), relocation (a video call that survives switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data, when the app is designed for it), migration (a cloud VM moved to a new host without you noticing), replication (three copies of your bKash balance, you see one), concurrency (thousands booking train tickets on the same server), failure (a server dies and another takes over before you notice).

Limits of transparency: Full transparency is neither possible nor always wise. You cannot hide the speed of light: a request from Dhaka to a server in the USA takes longer than one to Singapore, no matter what. You cannot fully hide failures either: when a server does not answer, the client cannot tell whether it crashed or is just slow, so it either waits (and seems frozen) or gives up (and maybe the operation actually happened). Sometimes hiding is bad: if your print job is sent to a printer in another building, you want to know where it went. A good designer chooses which details to hide and which to expose, for example by showing "offline mode" honestly in an app.

Goal 3, openness: An open distributed system offers components that can be used by, or integrated into, other systems. The key tool is a well-defined interface: what operations exist, what parameters they take, what they return, often written in an interface definition language (IDL) or a public API specification (lesson 05). Openness brings interoperability (two implementations from different vendors can work together, like any email client talking to any mail server through standard protocols), portability (an app written for one system runs on another that offers the same interface) and extensibility (you can add or replace parts without rewriting everything). A useful principle is to separate policy from mechanism: the system offers a mechanism, such as a cache, and lets you choose the policy, such as how long items stay in it.

Goal 4, scalability: A system is scalable if it keeps meeting its goals as it grows. There are three dimensions. Size scalability: more users and more data. Geographical scalability: users and servers spread far apart, where latency becomes a problem. Administrative scalability: the system spans many organizations with different owners, rules and security policies, such as a payment network linking many banks.

What kills size scalability: Centralized things. A single server that every request must touch becomes a bottleneck: if it can handle 2,000 requests per second, the whole system can never go above 2,000 per second. Centralized data (one database for everything) and centralized algorithms (one node that must know the full state of the network to make a decision) have the same problem. Good distributed algorithms avoid needing complete global information, make decisions on local information, and keep working if one machine fails.

A worked latency example: Dhaka to Singapore is roughly 2,900 km in a straight line. Light in optical fibre travels at about 200,000 km per second, about two thirds of its speed in vacuum. So the one-way trip takes at least 2,900 / 200,000 seconds, about 14.5 ms, and a round trip (RTT) at least about 29 ms. Real cables are longer than straight lines and routers add delay, so actual RTTs are higher, often tens of milliseconds more. Now suppose a page needs 10 calls to a server in Singapore and the real RTT is 50 ms. Made one after another, they cost 10 x 50 = 500 ms, half a second. Made in parallel, the cost is closer to 50 ms. That is the heart of geographical scalability: latency adds up when calls are sequential.

Scaling technique 1, hide communication latency: Do not sit idle waiting for a reply. Use asynchronous communication: send the request, do other useful work, and handle the reply when it arrives. Or move work closer to the client: a web form can check that a phone number has 11 digits in the browser before sending anything, saving a round trip to the server.

Scaling technique 2, partition and distribute: Split data or work into pieces and spread them across machines. DNS (deep-cse-4-3 lesson 08) is the classic example: no single server holds all names; the namespace is split into zones, each managed by different servers. A ride-sharing app can split a city into regions. We study partitioning in detail in lesson 22.

Scaling technique 3, replicate and cache: Make copies of data near where it is needed. This spreads load and cuts latency, and it also improves availability. The price is consistency: copies can disagree, and keeping them in sync costs messages and time. Caching is a special kind of replication decided by the client or a proxy. Lessons 14 to 16 and 25 cover this trade-off.

The eight fallacies of distributed computing: In the 1990s, L. Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems wrote down false assumptions that programmers new to distributed systems tend to make; James Gosling is usually credited with adding the eighth. They are: 1, the network is reliable. 2, latency is zero. 3, bandwidth is infinite. 4, the network is secure. 5, topology does not change. 6, there is one administrator. 7, transport cost is zero. 8, the network is homogeneous. Each one, believed, leads to a real bug.

The fallacies in practice, part 1: "The network is reliable": packets get lost, cables get cut, a router reboots; code must use timeouts and retries. "Latency is zero": a loop that makes one remote call per item works on a laptop and crawls across continents, as our 500 ms example showed. "Bandwidth is infinite": sending 1 MB over a 10 Mbps link takes at least 1,000,000 x 8 / 10,000,000 = 0.8 seconds, so huge responses on mobile data hurt. "The network is secure": anyone on the path may read or change traffic unless you use TLS and authentication (deep-cse-6-2).

The fallacies in practice, part 2: "Topology does not change": servers are added, removed and moved, IP addresses change, so hard-coding addresses breaks things; use names and service discovery (lesson 07). "There is one administrator": different teams and companies run different parts, with different rules and upgrade schedules. "Transport cost is zero": moving data costs CPU time for serialization and real money for bandwidth, especially between cloud regions. "The network is homogeneous": devices, operating systems, link types and protocols differ, from fibre in Dhaka to a weak 3G signal in a char area.

Real-life example 1, a national exam result portal: When results are published, millions of students hit the site in the same hour. A single server falls over immediately (size scalability). A sensible design replicates static pages and caches them close to users (scaling technique 3), splits the lookup by roll number range across servers (technique 2), and sends results by SMS asynchronously so the web servers are not tied up (technique 1). Transparency matters too: students should just type a roll number, not choose a server.

Real-life example 2, an online shop's Eid sale: The shop's checkout calls inventory, payment, coupon and delivery services. A developer who believed "latency is zero" wrote the cart page to call the coupon service once for each item. With 20 items and 40 ms per call, that is 800 ms just for coupons. Batching the call into one request cuts it to about 40 ms. Another developer believed "the network is reliable", so a lost payment reply left orders stuck; adding timeouts, retries and idempotency keys (lesson 05) fixed it.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students mix up relocation and migration transparency; both involve moving, but relocation stresses moving while in use, migration stresses moving at all. Another mistake: thinking transparency should always be maximized; textbooks explicitly discuss the trade-off with performance and honesty about failures. Exams ask you to list and explain the transparency types, define openness and the three scalability dimensions, list scaling techniques with examples, and list the eight fallacies with a consequence for each. Practise the latency calculation, distance divided by about 200,000 km per second, because it shows you understand why geography matters.

Recap: The goals are resource sharing, distribution transparency (access, location, relocation, migration, replication, concurrency, failure), openness through standard interfaces, and scalability in size, geography and administration. The three scaling techniques are hiding latency, partitioning and replicating. Transparency has limits set by physics and failures. The eight fallacies remind you that the network is unreliable, slow, limited, insecure, changing, multi-owner, costly and diverse. Next lesson looks at architectures: the shapes, such as client-server, multi-tier and peer-to-peer, that real systems take to meet these goals.
key_points: Four goals: resource sharing, distribution transparency, openness and scalability.
Seven transparencies: access, location, relocation, migration, replication, concurrency, failure.
Full transparency is impossible and not always wise: latency and partial failures cannot be fully hidden.
Openness comes from well-defined interfaces, giving interoperability, portability and extensibility.
Scalability has three dimensions: size, geographical and administrative; centralization kills size scalability.
Scaling techniques: hide latency (asynchronous calls), partition and distribute, replicate and cache.
Dhaka-Singapore is about 2,900 km: at least about 29 ms RTT in fibre, and sequential calls multiply it.
Eight fallacies: reliable network, zero latency, infinite bandwidth, secure network, fixed topology, one administrator, zero transport cost, homogeneous network.
lessons.tip: Learn the eight fallacies as eight bugs, not eight sentences. For each, remember one concrete failure, such as a hard-coded IP breaking after a server move. Exams reward examples more than lists.
lessons.task: Open any website on your phone with browser developer tools on a computer (or simply time page loads on Wi-Fi and on mobile data). Count roughly how many requests the page makes. Using a 50 ms round trip, estimate the load time if those requests went one after another versus in parallel, and write which fallacy the difference shows.

quiz.q: Which transparency hides that several copies of a resource exist?
quiz.explain: Replication transparency hides that the system keeps multiple copies; the user sees one.

quiz.q: A system spans many organizations with different owners and security policies. Which scalability dimension is this?
quiz.explain: Administrative scalability is about growing across independent administrative domains.

quiz.q: Dhaka to Singapore is about 2,900 km. With light in fibre at about 200,000 km/s, the minimum round-trip time is about:
quiz.explain: One way is 2,900 / 200,000 s, about 14.5 ms, so the round trip is at least about 29 ms.

quiz.q: Splitting the DNS namespace into zones run by different servers is an example of which scaling technique?
quiz.explain: DNS divides the namespace into zones spread over many servers: partitioning and distribution.

quiz.q: A developer hard-codes a server's IP address and the app breaks when the server is moved. Which fallacy was believed?
quiz.explain: Servers get added, removed and moved; assuming a fixed topology leads to hard-coded addresses that break.

lessons.title: Architectures: Client-Server, Multi-Tier, Peer-to-Peer and Middleware
lessons.content:
Think about how a big wedding in Bangladesh gets organized. One way: the bride's father decides everything, and every cook, decorator and driver calls him for every question. He is the server, they are clients, and when his phone battery dies, the wedding stalls. Another way: the work is split into layers, a caterer handles food, a decorator handles stage and lights, and the family only talks to the event manager. A third way: cousins and neighbours help each other directly, with no boss, each bringing chairs, lending cars, passing messages along. These three ways of organizing people map neatly onto the three big families of distributed system architecture: client-server, multi-tier and peer-to-peer. This lesson explains each one, the styles they are built from, and the middleware that glues them together.

Two views of architecture: Textbooks separate the software architecture, how software components are organized and how they interact, from the system architecture, where those components are actually placed on real machines. The first is about styles: layers, objects, resources, events. The second is about placement: is the logic on the user's phone, on one central server, spread across tiers, or shared among equal peers? Keep the two views apart in your head; one style can be deployed in several ways.

Style 1, layered: Components are arranged in layers, and each layer calls only the one below it, getting results back. You met this in networking (the TCP/IP stack, deep-cse-4-3) and it is just as common in applications: an interface layer (what the user sees), a processing layer (the business logic) and a data layer (the database). Layering keeps things understandable and replaceable: you can change the database without touching the screens, as long as the interface between layers stays the same.

Style 2, object-based and service-oriented: Each component is an object, or a service, that wraps its own data and offers operations through an interface. Components call each other's operations, possibly over the network, which is where remote procedure calls (lesson 05) come in. Service-oriented architecture and microservices (lesson 25) grow out of this style: an order service, a payment service, a user service, each owned by one team, each reachable only through its interface.

Style 3, resource-based (REST): The system is seen as a collection of resources, each named by a URL, and every resource is handled through the same small set of operations, the HTTP methods GET, PUT, POST and DELETE (recap deep-cse-4-3 lesson 05 and Web Engineering deep-cse-5-3). For example GET /accounts/123/balance reads a balance, and POST /transfers creates a transfer. REST interactions are meant to be stateless on the server: each request carries everything the server needs, which makes it easy to put many identical servers behind a load balancer.

Style 4, event-based (publish-subscribe): Components do not call each other directly. Instead, a component publishes an event, such as "order placed", and any component that subscribed to that kind of event receives it. Publishers do not know who the subscribers are. This loose coupling is powerful: you can add an SMS sender or an analytics service later without changing the order service. Lesson 06 goes deep into queues and pub-sub.

Style 5, shared data space: Components communicate by writing to and reading from a shared, persistent store, with no direct messages at all. Think of a notice board in a university department: the office pins a notice, students read it whenever they pass by, neither side needs to be present at the same time. In computing, a shared database or a distributed file system used for coordination fits this style. Combining events with a shared data space gives decoupling both in time and in reference.

Client-server: The simplest and most common system architecture. A server process offers a service; a client process sends a request and waits for a reply. Your browser and a web server, a bKash app and its backend, an email client and a mail server: all client-server. The pattern is easy to reason about because the server is the single point of truth. The drawback is that a single server is both a bottleneck and a single point of failure. In practice the "server" is usually a cluster behind a load balancer, which looks like one server from outside, a nice example of replication transparency from lesson 02.

Multi-tier architectures: The three layers of an application (interface, processing, data) can be split across machines in different ways. In a two-tier setup, the client runs the interface and maybe some logic, and talks directly to a database server; old desktop banking software often worked this way. In the classic three-tier setup, the client (browser or app) shows the interface, an application server runs the business logic, and a separate database server stores the data. The application server is itself a client of the database server, so a server can also be a client. Larger systems add more tiers, such as a cache tier, a search tier or a separate authentication service.

Thin and fat clients: How much work should the client do? A thin client only displays and collects input, and every decision goes to the server, like a basic web page or a bank teller terminal. A fat (thick) client does a lot locally: validates input, caches data, maybe runs whole features offline, like a modern mobile app that lets you draft messages without a connection. Fat clients reduce load and latency on servers but are harder to update and to secure, since you do not control the user's device. Most real apps sit in the middle.

Peer-to-peer (P2P): In a P2P system there is no special server; every node, called a peer, is both client and server. Peers store data and forward requests for each other. The appeal is that capacity grows with the number of peers: each newcomer brings its own upload bandwidth and storage. The challenge is how to find anything without a central index. Two broad answers exist.

Unstructured P2P, with a worked example: Peers connect to random neighbours, and data can sit anywhere. To find a file you flood the request: ask all neighbours, who ask theirs, and so on, limited by a time-to-live (TTL) counter that drops by one at each hop. Suppose every peer has 4 neighbours and you send a query with TTL 3. Hop 1: your 4 neighbours get it. Hop 2: each forwards it to its 3 other neighbours, 4 x 3 = 12 messages. Hop 3: each of those forwards to 3 more, 12 x 3 = 36 messages. In the worst case, with no overlaps, that is 4 + 12 + 36 = 52 messages for one search, and it still might miss a file that sits four hops away. Flooding is simple and robust, but it is expensive and gives no guarantee.

Structured P2P: Here peers are organized into a fixed logical shape, such as a ring, and each data item is placed on the peer chosen by hashing its key. That is a distributed hash table (DHT). Given a key, a lookup can follow a known route and reach the responsible peer in a small number of hops, roughly proportional to log N for N peers in designs such as Chord. We work through Chord in lesson 07 and the related consistent hashing idea in lesson 22.

Hybrid architectures: Many real systems mix the two. BitTorrent (recap deep-cse-4-3 lesson 09) uses peers to exchange file chunks, but uses a tracker server, or a DHT, to help peers find each other. Content delivery networks (CDNs) are client-server at heart, but place edge servers in many cities, often inside ISPs, so users fetch content from nearby; this is called an edge-server system. Edge computing pushes this further by running some processing near users, for example close to a mobile base station, so latency-sensitive tasks such as video analytics get quick replies. Cloud Computing (deep-cse-7-3) covers this in more depth.

Middleware, the glue: Applications rarely talk to raw sockets. Between the application and the operating system and network sits middleware: a software layer that offers common services so each application does not reinvent them. Typical middleware services include communication (RPC, messaging), naming and discovery, security (authentication, encryption), transactions, replication and logging. Middleware is to a distributed system roughly what an operating system is to one computer: a manager of resources that offers a friendlier, more uniform interface. Message brokers, RPC frameworks and service meshes are all examples of middleware.

Making middleware adaptable: Two common tricks keep middleware flexible. Wrappers (adapters) put a standard interface around an old component, such as wrapping an old banking system with a REST API so new apps can use it. Interceptors are hooks that sit in the normal call path and can add behaviour without the application knowing, such as automatically adding an authentication token to every outgoing request, retrying failed calls, or logging how long each call took. Modern service meshes rely heavily on this interception idea.

Choosing an architecture: There is no single best shape. Client-server and multi-tier win when you need one clear source of truth, simple security and easy updates, which is why almost every bank and wallet uses them. P2P wins when you want capacity to grow with users and want no single owner or single point of failure, as in file sharing or blockchains. Ask four questions: who owns the data, how many users, how far apart they are, and what happens when one box disappears. The answers usually point to a hybrid.

Real-life example 1, a university result system: Students use a browser (thin client). Requests reach a load balancer and then one of several application servers (logic tier), which query a database server (data tier) and a cache tier for popular pages. It is three-tier client-server, with replication in the logic tier. Adding an event, "results published", lets an SMS service and an email service subscribe without the main app calling them directly.

Real-life example 2, sharing class notes in a hall: In a dorm with poor internet, students run a local file-sharing app where each laptop shares notes with others on the same Wi-Fi, with no central server. That is P2P: when more students join, more copies and more upload capacity appear. To find "DS lecture 3", the app might ask every laptop on the network, a form of flooding, which works fine for 40 laptops but would not scale to 40 million.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often say peer-to-peer means "no servers at all, so nothing can fail"; in reality peers churn constantly, joining and leaving, and the system must handle that. Another confusion is thinking that "three-tier" means three physical machines; it means three logical layers, which may run on one machine or on hundreds. Exams ask you to compare client-server and P2P, describe two-tier versus three-tier, list architectural styles with examples, explain the role of middleware, and compute flooding message counts like our 4 + 12 + 36 example.

Recap: Architectural styles describe how components are organized: layered, object or service based, resource based (REST), event based and shared data space. System architectures describe where components run: client-server, multi-tier (two-tier, three-tier and more), peer-to-peer (unstructured with flooding, structured with DHTs), and hybrids such as BitTorrent with trackers and CDN edge servers. Middleware sits between applications and the network, offering communication, naming, security and more, made flexible by wrappers and interceptors. Next lesson starts the communication block: how nodes actually exchange messages.
key_points: Software architecture is how components are organized; system architecture is where they are placed on machines.
Styles: layered, object/service based, resource based (REST), event based (publish-subscribe), shared data space.
Client-server: a server offers a service, clients request it; simple but a potential bottleneck and single point of failure.
Two-tier puts logic on the client next to a database server; three-tier separates interface, application logic and data.
P2P peers are both client and server; capacity grows with peers, but finding data is the hard part.
Unstructured P2P floods queries with a TTL: 4 neighbours, TTL 3 gives up to 4 + 12 + 36 = 52 messages.
Structured P2P (DHTs) place data by hashing keys and find it in about log N hops; hybrids include BitTorrent trackers and CDN edge servers.
Middleware offers common services (communication, naming, security, transactions) and is adapted with wrappers and interceptors.
lessons.tip: When you meet a new system, draw two pictures: one of the logical layers (interface, logic, data), and one of the physical boxes they run on. Many exam answers go wrong because the two pictures were mixed into one.
lessons.task: Choose three apps on your phone (for example a messaging app, a mobile wallet and a file-sharing app). For each, write whether it looks client-server, multi-tier, P2P or hybrid, which architectural style its main interaction resembles, and whether the app is a thin or fat client. Then compute how many messages a flood with 5 neighbours per peer and TTL 3 could send.

quiz.q: In which architectural style do components communicate by publishing events to which other components subscribe, without knowing each other?
quiz.explain: Event-based systems decouple publishers from subscribers; publishers do not know who receives the events.

quiz.q: In a classic three-tier architecture, where does the business logic run?
options: On an application server between the client and the database server
quiz.explain: Three-tier separates the client interface, an application (logic) tier and a data tier.

quiz.q: Every peer has 4 neighbours and a query is flooded with TTL 3, with no overlaps. How many messages at most?
What best describes middleware?
options: A software layer between applications and the OS/network that offers common distributed services
The CPU scheduler of a server

quiz.explain: It mixes P2P data exchange with a server-like component for discovery, so it is hybrid.

lessons.title: Communication and Message Passing
lessons.content:
Before mobile phones, families in Bangladesh kept in touch with relatives abroad by letter. You wrote on paper, folded it, put it in an envelope with an address, and dropped it at the post office. Then you waited. Maybe the reply came in three weeks. Maybe the letter got lost, and you never knew whether your cousin in Dubai was angry or simply never received it. Maybe two letters you sent a week apart arrived in the wrong order. Every one of those problems is still alive inside modern distributed systems, only faster. Nodes have no shared memory, so the only way to cooperate is to send messages. This lesson is about the most basic layer: what a message is, how it is turned into bytes, and the choices you make about waiting, buffering and repeating.

Recap, sockets and transport: From Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3 lessons 10 to 12) you know that a process talks over the network through a socket, identified by an IP address and a port. TCP gives a reliable, ordered byte stream between two sockets after a handshake; UDP sends independent datagrams that may be lost, duplicated or reordered, with no connection. Distributed systems use both: TCP for most request-reply traffic, UDP where speed matters and a lost packet is acceptable or handled by the application. Everything in this lesson sits on top of these two.

Message passing primitives: At the simplest level, distributed programs use two operations: send(destination, message) and receive(source, message). It sounds trivial, but each has hidden choices. Does send return immediately or wait? Does receive wait forever if nothing arrives? Is the message stored somewhere if the receiver is not running? The answers define the communication style, and they matter as much as the algorithm you build on top.

Synchronous vs asynchronous: In synchronous communication the sender waits (blocks) until something happens: at least until the middleware has accepted the message, or until the message has been delivered to the receiver, or, strongest of all, until the receiver has processed it and replied. A phone call is synchronous: you speak and wait for the answer. In asynchronous communication the sender continues right after handing the message over, like dropping a letter in a postbox. Asynchronous sending hides latency (lesson 02) but means the sender must later check, or be told, whether the message succeeded.

Blocking vs non-blocking receive: On the receiving side, a blocking receive waits until a message arrives, which is simple but wastes a thread if nothing comes. A non-blocking receive returns immediately, either with a message or with "nothing yet", and the program polls again later or registers a callback. Modern servers often use event loops with non-blocking sockets so one thread can handle thousands of connections; you met the idea of blocking versus non-blocking message passing in Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1 lesson 06).

Transient vs persistent communication: In transient communication a message is kept by the communication system only while both sender and receiver are running. If the receiver is down, the message is dropped. A raw TCP connection is transient: if the server process is not running, the connection fails. In persistent communication the middleware stores the message until it can be delivered, even if the receiver is offline for hours. Email is persistent: your mail server keeps the message until the recipient logs in. Message queues (lesson 06) give persistent communication to applications.

Buffers, where messages wait: Between send and receive, messages sit in buffers: in the sender's socket, in routers, and in the receiver's socket and middleware. As in the OS course, a buffer can have zero capacity (the sender must wait until the receiver takes the message, a rendezvous), bounded capacity (the sender waits or gets an error when the buffer is full) or, in theory, unbounded capacity. Real buffers are always bounded. If a fast sender keeps pushing into a slow receiver, buffers fill, latency climbs and eventually messages are dropped or the sender is slowed down. Slowing the sender on purpose is called backpressure, and lesson 06 returns to it.

Putting the two axes together: Combine them and you get familiar patterns. Transient and synchronous: a classic remote call, both sides must be up and the caller waits. Persistent and asynchronous: a message queue, the sender drops a message and moves on, the receiver picks it up later. Many real systems mix: the app synchronously calls an API to place an order, and the API asynchronously puts "send confirmation SMS" on a persistent queue.

Marshalling and serialization: A program holds data as in-memory structures: integers, strings, lists, objects with pointers. The network carries only bytes. Turning a structure into a flat sequence of bytes is called marshalling or serialization; turning bytes back into a structure is unmarshalling or deserialization. Both sides must agree on the format, or the receiver will read garbage. Pointers cannot be sent as they are, because a memory address on one machine means nothing on another; the data they point to must be copied into the message instead.

Text formats: JSON and XML are human-readable text formats. A small transfer record such as {"id":12345678,"amount":2500,"currency":"BDT"}, written without spaces, takes 46 bytes in JSON. Text formats are easy to debug and work across languages, which is why most web APIs use JSON. Their costs are size (field names repeated in every message, numbers written as digit characters) and the CPU time needed to parse text.

Binary formats, worked: A binary format fixes the layout instead. If both sides agree that a record is a 4-byte unsigned integer id, then a 4-byte unsigned integer amount, then 3 ASCII bytes for the currency, the same record takes 4 + 4 + 3 = 11 bytes, about a quarter of the JSON size. For a service sending one million such records a day, that is about 46 MB versus 11 MB. Schema-based binary formats, such as Protocol Buffers (used by gRPC) or Avro, describe the layout in a schema file, generate code for many languages, and add rules for evolving the schema, for example adding a new optional field without breaking old clients. The price is that you cannot read the bytes with your eyes.

Byte order, worked: Multi-byte numbers can be stored with the most significant byte first (big-endian) or the least significant byte first (little-endian). The number 0x12345678 is sent as bytes 12 34 56 78 in big-endian and 78 56 34 12 in little-endian. Our amount 2500 is 0x000009C4, so big-endian bytes are 00 00 09 C4 and little-endian bytes are C4 09 00 00. If a little-endian sender writes raw memory and a big-endian receiver reads it as is, 2500 becomes a huge wrong number. The fix is a fixed wire format: Internet protocols traditionally use big-endian, called network byte order, and serialization libraries handle the conversion for you. This is exactly what access transparency (lesson 02) hides.

Framing on TCP: TCP is a byte stream, not a message stream. If you send two messages of 11 bytes each, the receiver may get 22 bytes in one read, or 5 bytes and then 17. The application must mark where each message ends. Two common ways: put a fixed-size length prefix before each message (for example 4 bytes saying "the next 11 bytes are one message"), or use a delimiter such as a newline, as many text protocols do. Forgetting framing is a classic beginner bug that works fine on a laptop and fails under load.

The request-reply protocol: Most interactions are a client sending a request and the server sending back a reply. A minimal protocol has three parts: the client sends request(id, operation, arguments); the server executes and sends reply(id, result); the client waits with a timeout. Every request carries a unique request id so the client can match replies to requests, especially when several are in flight at once.

Timeouts and retries: If no reply arrives before the timeout, the client cannot know why. The request may have been lost, the server may have crashed before or after doing the work, or the reply may have been lost, or everything is just slow. The usual reaction is to retry. Choosing the timeout is a trade-off: if typical round trips take 40 ms, a timeout of 200 ms gives slow replies a fair chance; a timeout of 50 ms would cause many needless retries when the network is briefly busy, while 30 seconds would leave the user staring at a spinner. Lesson 25 adds exponential backoff and jitter so retries do not pile up.

Duplicate filtering: Retries create duplicates. If the reply was lost, the server receives the same request twice. For an operation like "read balance" that is harmless, but for "transfer 500 taka" it is a disaster. The server therefore remembers recent request ids and their replies, a history. When a duplicate arrives, it resends the stored reply instead of executing again. How long to keep the history, and what happens when the server restarts and forgets it, are exactly the questions behind at-most-once and at-least-once semantics in lesson 05.

Real-life example 1, sending money on a weak signal: Rahim in a village near Sunamganj taps "Send" on his wallet app with one bar of signal. The app sends a request with id 7f3a. The server debits his account, but the reply is lost. After the timeout, the app retries with the same id 7f3a. The server finds 7f3a in its history and simply resends "success, new balance 1,250 taka". Rahim sees one transfer, not two. Without the request id and history, he would have lost 500 taka more.

Real-life example 2, a delivery app's location updates: A delivery rider's app sends a GPS position every few seconds over UDP-like, fire-and-forget messages. If one update is lost, nobody retries, because a fresher one is coming in a few seconds anyway. Here transient, asynchronous, unreliable messaging is the right choice. By contrast, the "order delivered" event goes through a persistent queue with acknowledgements, because losing it would mean the shop never gets paid.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students confuse synchronous with blocking; they overlap, but synchronous describes the sender waiting for some confirmation, while blocking describes whether a call returns before it can complete. Another mistake is assuming that TCP's reliability solves everything: TCP only promises delivery while the connection is alive; if the server crashes after receiving the request, TCP cannot tell you whether the work was done. Exams ask you to define and compare transient/persistent and synchronous/asynchronous communication with examples, explain marshalling and why pointers cannot be sent, show big-endian and little-endian byte layouts, and describe a request-reply protocol with timeouts and duplicate filtering.

Recap: Nodes cooperate only by sending messages over sockets built on TCP or UDP. Communication can be synchronous or asynchronous, blocking or non-blocking, transient or persistent, and real systems mix them. Marshalling turns data into bytes using text formats like JSON (46 bytes in our example) or binary formats (11 bytes), with an agreed byte order such as big-endian network order. TCP needs framing. The request-reply protocol uses request ids, timeouts, retries and duplicate filtering. Next lesson builds a friendlier abstraction on top: the remote procedure call.
key_points: Distributed nodes cooperate only through send and receive over sockets built on TCP or UDP.
Synchronous senders wait for some confirmation; asynchronous senders continue immediately.
Transient communication drops messages if the receiver is not running; persistent communication stores them (email, queues).
Marshalling (serialization) turns in-memory data into bytes; pointers must be replaced by the data they point to.
JSON is readable but bigger: the sample record is 46 bytes in JSON versus 11 bytes in a fixed binary layout.
Byte order: 0x12345678 is 12 34 56 78 in big-endian (network order) and 78 56 34 12 in little-endian.
TCP is a byte stream, so applications need framing such as a length prefix.
Request-reply uses request ids, timeouts and retries; servers filter duplicates by keeping a history of replies.
lessons.tip: For every message in a design, label it on paper with three tags: sync or async, transient or persistent, and what happens on a timeout. Doing this once for a real app makes the vocabulary stick far better than memorizing definitions.
lessons.task: In Python, run json.dumps on a small dictionary describing a money transfer and print len() of the result. Then use struct.pack('>I', 2500) and struct.pack('<I', 2500) and print their .hex() values to see big-endian versus little-endian bytes. Write one sentence on which format you would use for a mobile app on slow data and why.

quiz.q: Email, where your server keeps a message until the recipient logs in, is an example of:
quiz.explain: The middleware stores the message until it can be delivered, even if the receiver is offline.

quiz.q: Why can a pointer not be sent as-is inside a message to another machine?
options: A memory address on one machine is meaningless in another machine's memory
quiz.explain: Each machine has its own address space, so the pointed-to data must be copied into the message.

quiz.q: How are the bytes of 0x12345678 ordered in big-endian (network byte order)?
quiz.explain: Big-endian puts the most significant byte first: 12 34 56 78.

quiz.q: A client retries a transfer after a timeout, but the first request had actually executed. What prevents a double transfer?
options: The server keeping a history of request ids and resending the stored reply
quiz.explain: Duplicate filtering by request id lets the server recognize a retry and reply without re-executing.

quiz.q: Two 11-byte messages sent over TCP arrive as one 22-byte read. What does the application need?
options: Message framing, such as a length prefix
quiz.explain: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries, so the application must mark where each message ends.

lessons.title: Remote Procedure Call (RPC)
lessons.content:
Imagine you are writing a ride-sharing app. On your laptop you write fare = calculateFare(pickup, drop) and it just works: the function runs, returns a number, done. Now the business grows, and the fare logic moves to a separate pricing server in a data center in Dhaka, while your app server runs somewhere else. Wouldn't it be lovely if you could still write fare = calculateFare(pickup, drop) and have the call quietly travel over the network, run on the pricing server, and bring the answer back? That wish is exactly what Remote Procedure Call, or RPC, gives you. It was described by Andrew Birrell and Bruce Nelson in a famous 1984 paper, and the idea is still everywhere today.

Where this fits: In lesson 04 we sent raw messages with send and receive over sockets. That works, but every programmer had to pack bytes, pick message formats, wait for replies and handle timeouts by hand. RPC hides that plumbing behind something every programmer already understands: a function call. This lesson explains how the hiding works, and, just as important, where it leaks, because a network is not a local function call, no matter how nicely it is dressed up.

What RPC is: A remote procedure call lets a program on one machine (the client) call a procedure that runs on another machine (the server), with the parameters and results carried in messages. To the caller it looks like an ordinary call. Behind the scenes a small piece of generated code, called a stub, does all the messaging work. The goal is access transparency from lesson 02: local and remote calls should look the same.

The stubs: The client stub is a fake version of the remote function that lives in the client process. It has the same name and parameters as the real function, but instead of computing anything it packs the parameters into a message and sends it. The server stub (sometimes called a skeleton) lives in the server process. It receives the message, unpacks the parameters, calls the real function, packs the result and sends it back. Neither the calling code nor the real function knows that a network sits between them.

The ten steps: Textbooks usually list the steps like this. 1: The client calls the client stub normally. 2: The client stub builds a message (marshalling the parameters) and calls the local operating system. 3: The client OS sends the message to the remote OS. 4: The remote OS hands the message to the server stub. 5: The server stub unpacks the parameters and calls the server procedure. 6: The server does the work and returns the result to its stub. 7: The server stub packs the result into a message and calls its OS. 8: The server OS sends the message to the client OS. 9: The client OS gives the message to the client stub. 10: The client stub unpacks the result and returns it to the caller. Ten steps instead of one, which is why a remote call costs far more time than a local one.

Marshalling recap: Marshalling means turning parameters into a flat sequence of bytes that can travel; unmarshalling is the reverse. Lesson 04 covered the formats (JSON text, compact binary formats such as Protocol Buffers) and byte order. In RPC the stub generator writes this code for you, so integers, strings, lists and records all get packed in an agreed way on both sides.

Parameter passing, the pointer problem: Locally, you can pass a pointer, a memory address that lets the function change your variable. Across machines a pointer is meaningless, because address 0x7ff3 on the client means nothing in the server's memory, which is separate (no shared memory, lesson 01). So RPC systems pass parameters by value: they copy the data. For something like an array that the server should modify, a classic trick is copy/restore: copy the array to the server, let the server change it, copy it back and overwrite the original. It mostly works, but it is not the same as true call-by-reference, for example if the same array is passed twice as two parameters.

Interface Definition Language: How do the client and server agree on the function names, parameter types and result types, especially when one is written in Java and the other in Go? They write the interface once in an Interface Definition Language (IDL). A tiny example in the spirit of Protocol Buffers: service Pricing { rpc CalculateFare(FareRequest) returns (FareReply); }. A compiler reads the IDL and generates client stubs and server stubs in each language. Change the interface carelessly and old clients break, so interfaces are versioned, and new fields are added in a backward-compatible way.

Binding: Before the first call, the client must find the server. This is called binding. In a simple setup the address is in a configuration file. In larger systems the server registers itself with a registry or naming service ("Pricing is at 10.0.3.7 port 50051"), and the client asks the registry. Lesson 07 on naming and service discovery covers this properly.

Where the illusion breaks, the failure cases: A local call either runs or the whole program crashes with it. A remote call has many more ways to go wrong, and the client often cannot tell which one happened. Case 1: the client cannot find the server at all, which is easy to report as an error. Case 2: the request message is lost. Case 3: the server crashes, either before doing the work or after doing it but before replying. Case 4: the reply message is lost. Case 5: the client crashes after sending the request, leaving the server working on a call nobody waits for (an orphan computation). The painful truth is that cases 2, 3 and 4 all look identical to the client: it sent a request and no answer came back before the timeout.

Retrying and its danger: The natural fix is a timeout plus retry. A small calculation shows why retries help. Say each message is lost with probability 0.1. One attempt succeeds only if both the request and the reply arrive: 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81, so it fails 19 percent of the time. With up to three attempts the call fails only if all three fail: 0.19 x 0.19 x 0.19 is about 0.0069, so success is about 99.3 percent. Great, but there is a catch. If the request did arrive and only the reply was lost, the retry makes the server do the work a second time.

Call semantics: So RPC systems promise one of several call semantics. Maybe semantics: send once, no retry; the call may or may not have run. At-least-once semantics: keep retrying until a reply arrives; the procedure runs one or more times. At-most-once semantics: the server remembers request ids it has already handled and filters duplicates, so the procedure runs zero or one time, never twice; if the client gets no reply it still does not know which. Exactly-once is what everyone wants, but with crashes and lost messages, a plain RPC layer cannot guarantee it in general. In practice people get the effect of exactly-once by combining at-least-once retries with operations that are safe to repeat.

Idempotent operations: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. "Set the account's phone number to 01711-000000" is idempotent: run it five times, the number is still the same. "Read the balance" is idempotent. But "add 500 taka to the account" is not: run it twice and you added 1000. If every operation were idempotent, at-least-once would be perfectly safe. Many are not, so we make them safe.

Worked example, the double charge: Rahim pays a shop 500 taka from his mobile wallet. The app calls Pay(from=Rahim, to=Shop, amount=500). The server debits 500, but the reply is lost on a weak 3G link. After a 2 second timeout the app retries. Without protection, the server debits again: Rahim loses 1000 taka for one purchase. Now add an idempotency key. The app creates a unique id for this payment, say pay-7f3a, once, and sends it with every retry. The server keeps a table of keys it has seen and the result it returned. First request: key pay-7f3a is new, so it debits 500, stores (pay-7f3a, "success, txn 9912") and replies. Retry: key pay-7f3a is already in the table, so the server does not debit again; it simply resends the stored reply. Rahim is charged exactly 500 taka once. The key must be stored in the same transaction as the debit, otherwise a crash between the two reopens the hole.

Server crash and orphans: At-most-once also needs care when the server crashes, because the table of seen request ids may be lost unless it is saved to stable storage. Client crashes leave orphans; solutions include having the server stop work when the client is gone, or tagging calls with a client epoch so old work is discarded after the client restarts. You will meet these ideas again under fault tolerance in lesson 20.

Synchronous and asynchronous RPC: Classic RPC is synchronous: the caller blocks until the reply arrives. That is simple but wastes time if the caller has other work. Asynchronous RPC returns immediately with a future or promise, or the server acknowledges at once and finishes later, possibly calling the client back. Most modern libraries offer both styles. For fire-and-forget work that should survive crashes, a message queue (lesson 06) is usually a better fit than RPC.

RPC today, REST and gRPC: Old systems used Sun RPC (used by NFS) and Java RMI. Today the two most common styles are REST over HTTP and gRPC. REST models the server as resources with URLs and uses HTTP methods; HTTP itself defines GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent and POST as not, which is exactly why payment APIs add idempotency keys to POST requests. gRPC, an open-source framework that started at Google, uses Protocol Buffers as its IDL, runs over HTTP/2, generates stubs in many languages and supports streaming calls. Both are RPC in spirit: a request goes out, a reply comes back.

Real-life example 1, a Dhaka food delivery app: When you tap "Place order", the app's backend makes several RPCs: to the restaurant service to check the menu, to the pricing service for the delivery charge, and to the payment service. Each call has a timeout of maybe a second or two. If the pricing service is slow, the order service can retry, because "get price" is idempotent. The payment call is not naturally idempotent, so it carries an order id as the idempotency key. That is why you are not charged twice when the app shows "Something went wrong, retrying".

Real-life example 2, bus ticket booking: A Chattogram-to-Dhaka bus booking site calls ReserveSeat(bus=42, seat=B3). If the reply is lost and the call is retried, the second attempt may come back "seat already taken", by you! A good design makes the second call recognise the same booking id and return the original success. Another trick is to make operations naturally idempotent: "set seat B3 owner to booking 881" can be repeated safely, while "book any free seat" cannot.

Common mistakes: The first mistake is treating a remote call like a local one: no timeout, so one slow server freezes everything (remember the fallacies in lesson 02: the network is not reliable and latency is not zero). The second is retrying non-idempotent calls blindly, which causes double orders and double payments. The third is believing a timeout means the call did not happen; it only means you did not hear back. The fourth is putting a retry loop at every layer, so one failure turns into 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls on the poor server; lesson 25 adds exponential backoff and circuit breakers to tame this.

What exams ask: List and explain the steps of an RPC. What are client and server stubs? Why can't pointers be passed, and what is copy/restore? Compare maybe, at-least-once and at-most-once semantics. Which failures can the client not tell apart? Define idempotency and give one idempotent and one non-idempotent example. How does an idempotency key prevent duplicate charges? A typical numeric question gives a loss probability and asks for the success rate with k retries, exactly like our 0.81 and 99.3 percent example.

Recap: RPC makes a remote function look local by putting stubs on both sides that marshal parameters into messages, send them, and unmarshal results. An IDL defines the interface and generates the stubs; binding finds the server. The illusion breaks under failure: a lost request, a crashed server and a lost reply look the same to the client. Retries give at-least-once semantics, duplicate filtering gives at-most-once, and idempotent operations or idempotency keys give the practical effect of exactly-once. REST and gRPC are today's everyday forms of RPC. Next, lesson 06 looks at a different style of communication, where sender and receiver do not even need to be awake at the same time: message queues and publish-subscribe.
key_points: RPC lets a client call a procedure on a remote server as if it were local; stubs hide the messaging.
The client stub marshals parameters and sends a request; the server stub unmarshals, calls the real procedure and returns the result.
Pointers cannot cross machines, so parameters go by value; copy/restore imitates call-by-reference for simple cases.
An IDL describes the interface once and a compiler generates stubs for each language; binding finds the server.
Lost request, server crash and lost reply all look the same to the client: no reply before the timeout.
Semantics: maybe (no retry), at-least-once (retry, may repeat), at-most-once (filter duplicates); exactly-once is not guaranteed by RPC alone.
Idempotent operations can be repeated safely; idempotency keys make non-idempotent calls like payments safe to retry.
REST over HTTP and gRPC (Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2) are the common modern forms of RPC.
lessons.tip: Every time you see a remote call in code, ask two questions out loud: what is the timeout, and what happens if this runs twice? If you can answer both, you understand RPC better than many working programmers.
lessons.task: On paper, design an RPC interface for a mobile recharge service with three calls: GetBalance, Recharge and SetDefaultNumber. Mark which are idempotent. For the one that is not, write how an idempotency key table would handle a request, a lost reply and a retry, step by step. Then compute the success rate for 1, 2 and 3 attempts if each message is lost with probability 0.2.

quiz.q: What does the client stub do in an RPC?
options: Runs the real procedure on the client machine
Packs the parameters into a message and sends it to the server
Chooses which server is the leader
quiz.explain: The client stub looks like the real function but only marshals the parameters, sends the request and later unmarshals the reply.

quiz.q: A client sends a request and gets no reply before the timeout. What can it conclude?
options: The procedure definitely did not run
Nothing certain: the request, the server or the reply may have failed
quiz.explain: Lost request, server crash and lost reply look identical from the client side, so it cannot know whether the procedure ran.

quiz.q: Which call semantics may execute the procedure more than once?
quiz.explain: At-least-once retries until it gets a reply, so a lost reply can cause the procedure to run again.

quiz.q: Which of these operations is idempotent?
options: Set the account's phone number to a given value
Append a row to an order log
quiz.explain: Setting a value to the same thing again changes nothing, so repeating it is safe; the others repeat their effect.

quiz.q: Why does a payment API ask the client to send an idempotency key with each request?
options: So the server can recognise a retry and return the stored result instead of charging again
To choose the nearest data center
quiz.explain: The server stores each key with its result; a retry with the same key gets the old reply and no second debit.

lessons.title: Message Queues and Publish-Subscribe
lessons.content:
Think about how letters used to reach a village in Bangladesh. You did not need your aunt in Rangpur to be standing at her door when you posted a letter from Dhaka. You dropped it in a post box, the postal system held it, carried it, and the postman delivered it whenever she was home. Sender and receiver never had to be awake at the same moment, and neither had to know where the other was right now. Compare that with a phone call, where both people must pick up at the same time. RPC from lesson 05 is the phone call. Message queues are the post office, and in big distributed systems the post office is often the better choice.

Where this fits: Lesson 04 introduced transient and persistent communication. Transient means the message is lost if the receiver is not running; persistent means the system stores it until it can be delivered. RPC is transient and synchronous: the server must be up, and the caller waits. This lesson covers message-oriented middleware (MOM), the persistent and asynchronous family: message queues and publish-subscribe. You already met queues as data structures and pipes in Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1, lesson 06); here the queue lives on its own servers and survives crashes.

What message-oriented middleware is: MOM is software that sits between applications and moves messages for them. A sender (producer) hands a message to the middleware, which stores it, usually on disk and often replicated, and later delivers it to one or more receivers (consumers). The middleware is usually run as a set of servers called brokers. The application code only needs two verbs: put a message, get a message.

Decoupling in time and space: The big win is decoupling. Decoupled in time means the producer and the consumer do not need to run at the same time: the producer can send at 10:00 while the consumer is restarting, and the consumer reads at 10:05. Decoupled in space means they do not need to know each other's address: both only know the name of a queue or topic. Add a third consumer tomorrow and the producer code does not change at all. This is also why queues absorb bursts: if 10,000 orders arrive in one second but the warehouse service handles 1,000 per second, the queue simply holds the backlog and it drains in about ten seconds.

Point-to-point queues: In the point-to-point model, each message in a queue is delivered to exactly one consumer. Several consumers may read from the same queue, and the broker shares the messages among them, which is called the competing consumers pattern. It is a natural way to spread work: put 600 image-resize jobs in a queue, start three workers, and each gets roughly 200. If one worker dies, the others keep draining the queue.

Publish-subscribe: In pub-sub, a producer (publisher) sends a message to a topic, not to a queue for one reader. Every subscriber of that topic gets its own copy. If an "order-placed" event is published once and three services subscribe, say billing, delivery and SMS notification, the broker makes three deliveries from one publish. The publisher has no idea who is listening, which is the purest form of decoupling. Subscriptions can be by topic name, or, in content-based systems, by a filter such as "city = Sylhet and amount > 5000".

Push and pull: Brokers deliver in one of two ways. In push delivery the broker sends messages to the consumer as soon as they arrive, which gives low latency but can overwhelm a slow consumer. In pull delivery the consumer asks for the next batch when it is ready, which lets it control its own speed. Many log-based systems use pull; many classic queue brokers push with a limit on how many unacknowledged messages a consumer may hold.

Acknowledgements and redelivery: How does the broker know a message was processed? The consumer sends an acknowledgement (ack) after it finishes. If the consumer crashes before acking, or the ack does not arrive within a timeout, the broker delivers the message again, maybe to another consumer. Notice the order of events: process first, then ack. If a consumer processes a message and crashes just before the ack, the message comes back and gets processed twice. If instead it acked first and then crashed while processing, the message would be lost.

Delivery guarantees: This gives the familiar three choices from lesson 05. At-most-once: ack before processing, so a crash may lose a message but never duplicates it, acceptable for things like live location pings. At-least-once: ack after processing, so nothing is lost but duplicates can happen; this is the common default. Exactly-once processing is offered by some systems inside their own boundaries, but end to end it again comes from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers. A consumer is idempotent when it records the message id it has handled (or uses a natural key, like "order 551 status = shipped") so a repeat changes nothing.

Worked example, the duplicate SMS: An "order-placed" message with id m-204 is delivered to the SMS service. The SMS service sends "Your order is confirmed" and then crashes before acking. After the ack timeout, the broker redelivers m-204 to another SMS worker. Without protection, the customer gets two identical SMS. With an idempotent consumer, the worker first checks a small table: has m-204 been handled? The first worker wrote m-204 into that table together with the send, so the second worker sees it and only acks. In practice the SMS gateway call itself is outside your database, so a tiny duplicate window can remain; that is why such systems are usually described as "effectively once", not perfectly once.

Ordering: Does a queue keep messages in order? A single queue with a single consumer keeps first-in first-out order. But as soon as there are several competing consumers, or redelivery after a crash, messages can be processed out of order. Global ordering across a whole busy system is expensive, so most systems guarantee order only within a smaller unit. In log-based systems that unit is a partition: all messages with the same key, for example the same wallet account number, go to the same partition and are read in order. Messages for different accounts may interleave, which usually does not matter.

The append-only log idea: Log-based brokers, with Apache Kafka as the best known example, store each topic partition as an append-only log on disk. A new message is appended at the end and gets the next offset number: 0, 1, 2, and so on. Messages are not deleted when read; they are kept for a configured retention time or size. Each consumer just remembers its own offset, "I have read up to 1,532". This makes it cheap to have many independent readers and even to replay old messages, for example to rebuild a search index after a bug fix.

Consumer groups: To spread load in a log-based system, consumers join a consumer group. Each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, so the group behaves like competing consumers while order inside a partition is kept. Worked example: a topic has 6 partitions and a group has 3 consumers, so each consumer reads 2 partitions. Add a fourth consumer and the partitions are rebalanced, for instance 2, 2, 1, 1. Add a seventh consumer to a 6-partition topic and one consumer sits idle, because a partition is never split between two members of the same group. Different groups, such as billing and analytics, each get the full stream independently, which is pub-sub.

Dead-letter queue: Some messages can never be processed, maybe a malformed JSON body or a reference to a deleted account. If the consumer keeps failing and the broker keeps redelivering, this "poison message" blocks progress forever.
