The usual fix is a retry limit: after, say, 5 failed attempts the message is moved to a separate dead-letter queue, where engineers can inspect it later, and normal traffic flows on.

Backpressure: What if producers are faster than consumers for a long time, not just in a burst? The queue keeps growing, disks fill up and messages get older and older. Backpressure is any mechanism that pushes the slowdown back towards the producers: bounded queues that reject or block new messages, rate limits, or alerts that trigger more consumers. Watching queue length, or consumer lag (how far behind the latest offset a group is), is one of the most important health signals, and lesson 25 on observability returns to it.

Real-life example 1, an SMS and notification fan-out: Imagine a mobile wallet in Bangladesh running a festival cashback campaign. At 8 pm it must notify 100,000 users. The SMS gateway contract allows 500 messages per second. A web server that tried to call the gateway directly for each user would time out. Instead, the campaign service publishes 100,000 "notify" messages to a queue in a few seconds, and a pool of SMS workers drains it at the allowed 500 per second, finishing in 100,000 / 500 = 200 seconds, a little over three minutes. If the gateway goes down for a minute, messages just wait in the queue. Push notifications and email can subscribe to the same event as separate subscribers.

Real-life example 2, an e-commerce order pipeline: When you order a phone on a Bangladeshi shopping site during a big sale, the checkout service saves the order and publishes "order-placed". The inventory service reserves stock, the payment service waits for confirmation, the warehouse in Gazipur gets a pick list and the analytics team counts sales, each as its own subscriber. If the warehouse system is down for maintenance at 2 am, orders still go through; its messages pile up and are processed when it returns. This loose coupling is a big reason microservices (lesson 25) lean on messaging.

Queues versus RPC: Use RPC when the caller needs an answer right now to continue, like "is this PIN correct?". Use a queue when the work can happen a little later, must not be lost, may take long, or has many interested parties, like "send receipt", "update recommendations" or "generate monthly statement". The price of queues is complexity: there is now a broker to run and replicate, eventual rather than immediate results, duplicates to handle, and harder debugging because the flow is no longer one simple call stack.

Common mistakes: Acking before processing and then losing messages on a crash. Assuming exactly-once delivery and writing consumers that double-charge on a duplicate. Expecting global order from a topic with many partitions. Creating more consumers than partitions and wondering why some are idle. Letting a poison message block a queue because there is no retry limit or dead-letter queue. Treating a queue as a database forever, with no retention plan.

What exams ask: Define message-oriented middleware and explain decoupling in time and space. Compare point-to-point queues with publish-subscribe. Explain why at-least-once delivery causes duplicates and how idempotent consumers fix it. What is a dead-letter queue? How does a consumer group spread partitions, and what happens with more consumers than partitions? Numeric questions often ask drain time: backlog divided by (consume rate minus produce rate).

Recap: Message queues and publish-subscribe move messages through brokers that store them, so producers and consumers are decoupled in time and space. Point-to-point queues give each message to one consumer and spread work; pub-sub topics give every subscriber a copy. Acknowledgements and redelivery give at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent. Order is usually kept only per queue or per partition. Append-only logs with offsets and consumer groups allow replay and scaling. Dead-letter queues and backpressure keep the system healthy. Next, lesson 07 asks a question every one of these systems needs answered: how do we name things and find where they live?
key_points: Message-oriented middleware stores and forwards messages through brokers: persistent, asynchronous communication.
Queues decouple producers and consumers in time (not running together) and space (not knowing each other's address).
Point-to-point: each message goes to one of the competing consumers; pub-sub: every subscriber of a topic gets a copy.
Ack after processing gives at-least-once delivery; duplicates are handled with idempotent consumers (store handled message ids).
Order is usually guaranteed only within a queue or partition; messages with the same key go to the same partition.
Log-based brokers keep messages as an append-only log with offsets; consumer groups split partitions among members.
Dead-letter queues hold poison messages after a retry limit; backpressure and consumer lag keep producers and consumers balanced.
Use RPC when you need an answer now; use a queue for later, durable, slow or fan-out work.
lessons.tip: Draw every messaging design as boxes and arrows with three labels on each arrow: who acks, what happens on a duplicate, and what order is guaranteed. If you cannot fill in all three, the design is not finished.
lessons.task: A shop publishes 30,000 'order-placed' messages during a one-hour flash sale (about 8.3 per second) to a topic with 4 partitions. The invoice service can process 5 messages per second per consumer. How many consumers does the invoice group need to keep up, and what is the most that can be useful? Then write, in plain steps, how the invoice consumer avoids sending two invoices for the same order if a message is redelivered.

quiz.q: What does 'decoupled in time' mean for a message queue?
options: Messages are delivered in timestamp order
The producer and consumer do not need to be running at the same moment
Every message expires after a fixed time
quiz.explain: The broker stores messages, so a producer can send while the consumer is down and the consumer reads later.

quiz.q: An event is published once to a topic with three subscribers. How many deliveries happen?
quiz.explain: In publish-subscribe every subscriber gets its own copy, so one publish fans out to three deliveries.

quiz.q: A consumer processes a message and then crashes before sending the ack. With at-least-once delivery, what happens?
options: The producer is asked to resend
The broker redelivers the message, so it may be processed twice
quiz.explain: No ack means the broker assumes failure and redelivers, which is why consumers must be idempotent.

quiz.q: A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group has 7 consumers. What happens?
options: Each consumer reads 6/7 of a partition
Six consumers each read one partition and one sits idle
The broker rejects the seventh consumer's messages
quiz.explain: Within one group a partition is read by only one consumer, so with more consumers than partitions some are idle.

quiz.q: What is a dead-letter queue for?
options: Storing messages for consumers that are offline
Speeding up delivery to fast consumers
Holding messages that keep failing after a retry limit so they stop blocking the queue
quiz.explain: Poison messages are moved aside after repeated failures, so engineers can inspect them while normal traffic continues.

lessons.title: Naming: Names, Identifiers, Addresses and Discovery
lessons.content:
Suppose a friend says, "Meet me at Rafiq's tea stall." That is a name. You do not know where it is, so you ask a rickshaw puller, who says, "Near the Mirpur 10 roundabout, beside the pharmacy." Now you have something closer to an address, a place you can actually go. If Rafiq moves his stall next month, the name stays the same but the address changes, and anyone using the old directions ends up at the wrong corner. Distributed systems have exactly this problem, millions of times per second. Every service, file, user, machine and message needs a name, and the system needs a way to turn that name into a place where the thing really lives. That turning is called name resolution, and this lesson is about how it is done.

Where this fits: In lesson 05, binding asked "where is the pricing server?" and lesson 06's producers only knew the name of a topic. Both quietly relied on naming. You studied DNS in Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3, lesson 08), so here we only recap it and look at the bigger family: flat names, structured names, attribute-based names, and modern service discovery.

Names, addresses and identifiers: Three words matter. A name is any string used to refer to an entity, like "pricing-service" or "photo-4471.jpg". An address is the name of an access point, the place where you can actually reach the entity, like 10.0.3.7 port 50051. An entity can have several access points, and access points can change, so addresses make bad long-term names. An identifier is a special kind of name with three properties: it refers to at most one entity, each entity has at most one identifier, and an identifier is never reused for another entity. Your national ID number is meant to be an identifier; your mobile number is closer to an address, because operators can recycle numbers.

Human-friendly and location independence: Good naming separates the name people use from the address machines use. A location-independent name keeps working when the entity moves. If a web service moves from a server in Dhaka to one in Chattogram, the name api.example.com stays the same and only the mapping changes. This is the migration and relocation transparency from lesson 02, and naming is how it is achieved.

Flat naming: A flat name is just a bit string with no structure, like a random 128-bit id. It says nothing about where the entity is, so we need clever ways to find it. Four classic approaches: broadcasting, forwarding pointers, home-based approaches and distributed hash tables.

Broadcasting: Simply shout to everyone, "Who has id X?", and the one that has it replies. ARP in a local network works this way: "Who has 192.168.1.5? Tell me your MAC address." It is simple and fine in a small LAN, but it does not scale: in a network of 10,000 machines every lookup disturbs all 10,000 of them.

Forwarding pointers: When an entity moves from place A to place B, it leaves behind a pointer at A saying "I moved to B". A client that goes to A is forwarded to B. Moves can chain: A points to B, B to C, C to D. Lookup still works but gets slower with each hop, and if any machine in the chain crashes the chain breaks. Real systems shorten the chain by telling the client the final location so next time it goes straight there.

Home-based approaches: The entity has a fixed home that always knows where it currently is. Mobile IP is the classic example: a phone has a permanent home address; when it roams to another network it gets a temporary care-of address and tells its home agent. Packets sent to the home address reach the home agent, which tunnels them to the current location. The weakness is the home itself: if your home is in Dhaka and you are in Rajshahi talking to someone next door, traffic still detours through Dhaka, and if the home agent fails, nobody can find you.

Distributed hash tables: A DHT spreads the name-to-location table across many peers with no central server. The best-known textbook design is Chord (2001). Node ids and keys are both m-bit numbers placed on a ring from 0 to 2^m - 1. Each key k is stored at its successor, the first node whose id is equal to or follows k on the ring. To avoid walking around the ring one node at a time, each node p keeps a finger table: entry i points to successor(p + 2^(i-1)), for i = 1 to m. The fingers jump 1, 2, 4, 8 places ahead, and so on, so each hop can roughly halve the remaining distance.

Worked example, a Chord finger table: Take m = 4, so ids run from 0 to 15, and nodes at 1, 4, 9, 11 and 14. For node 1 the targets are 1+1 = 2, 1+2 = 3, 1+4 = 5 and 1+8 = 9. Their successors are 4, 4, 9 and 9, so node 1's finger table is [4, 4, 9, 9]. For node 9 the targets are 10, 11, 13 and 1 (17 wraps around to 1), giving [11, 11, 14, 1]. For node 11 the targets are 12, 13, 15 and 3, giving [14, 14, 1, 4].

Worked example, a Chord lookup: Node 1 wants key 12. Key 12 belongs to successor(12) = 14. Node 1 looks in its finger table for the farthest node that is still before 12: that is 9, so it forwards the query to 9. Node 9 looks at its fingers [11, 11, 14, 1]; 14 would overshoot, so the farthest node before 12 is 11, and it forwards to 11. Node 11 sees that 12 lies between itself and its successor 14, so the answer is node 14. The path was 1 to 9 to 11, then node 14 is named as the owner: two forwarding hops on a ring of 16 ids.

Why DHTs scale: With N nodes, a Chord lookup takes O(log N) hops. For a million nodes, log2 of 1,000,000 is about 20, so a lookup needs at most about 20 hops, and the Chord paper reports about half that, around 10, on average. Each node stores only m fingers, not a list of all million nodes. When nodes join or leave, only nearby keys move to a new successor. DHT ideas live on in peer-to-peer networks (lesson 03) and in the consistent hashing used to partition databases, which lesson 22 works through in detail.

Structured naming, the DNS recap: Flat names are hard for humans and hard to delegate. Structured names are built as paths in a name space, a tree. File paths like /home/rina/notes.txt and domain names like www.example.com.bd are both structured: each label is a step down the tree. The big advantage is delegation: the owner of example.com.bd manages everything below it without asking anyone. DNS splits the tree into zones served by authoritative name servers. Iterative resolution: your resolver asks a root server, which refers it to the servers for bd; those refer it, through com.bd, to the authoritative server for example.com.bd, which returns the address. In recursive resolution, each server does the remaining work on your behalf. Caching with a TTL (time to live) keeps load low: a record with TTL 300 can be reused for 5 minutes without asking again.

Why DNS scales: The top of the tree changes rarely and is heavily replicated and cached, so most lookups are answered by a nearby resolver cache without touching the root at all. Lower levels change more often but each zone carries only its own small share of the load. The price is staleness: if you change an address, clients may keep using the old one until cached copies expire. Teams lower the TTL a day before a planned move for exactly this reason.

Attribute-based naming: Sometimes you do not know the name, only what you want: "a printer on the 3rd floor that prints in colour", or "all employees in the Sylhet branch". Attribute-based naming, also called directory services, stores entities as sets of (attribute, value) pairs and lets you search by attributes. LDAP is the classic protocol, and Microsoft's Active Directory is a widely used directory service built around it. Searches are more powerful than plain lookups but more expensive, because they may need to look through many entries.

Service discovery: In modern cloud systems, services start, stop and move every few minutes, so fixed configuration files go stale fast. Service discovery fixes this with a registry. When an instance of the pricing service starts, it registers "pricing at 10.0.3.7:50051". The registry checks each instance with health checks, such as calling a /health endpoint every few seconds, and removes instances that stop answering. Clients ask the registry, or a load balancer in front of it, for a healthy instance. Tools such as Consul, etcd and ZooKeeper are often used for this, and Kubernetes gives each service a stable DNS name that maps to whichever instances are currently healthy. Because the registry itself must not be a single point of failure, these tools keep their data replicated using consensus, which we study in lessons 18 and 19.

Real-life example 1, moving a website between data centers: A Bangladeshi news portal moves its servers from one Dhaka data center to another. A day before, the team lowers the TTL on www from 3,600 seconds to 60 seconds. On moving day they update the A record to the new address. Within about a minute most resolvers have the new answer; a few slow caches may still send readers to the old servers, so those stay up for a while as a forwarding layer. The name never changed; only the mapping did.

Real-life example 2, finding a driver service in a ride-sharing backend: A ride-sharing app runs 40 copies of its "driver-location" service across Dhaka and Chattogram. Copies start and stop as traffic rises at office hours. The trip service never stores IP addresses. It asks the discovery system for "driver-location", gets a healthy instance, and calls it with RPC. When one copy crashes, its health check fails within a few seconds and it disappears from the registry, so new calls avoid it automatically.

Common mistakes: Confusing names, addresses and identifiers, especially using an address such as an IP as if it were a permanent identifier. Forgetting that caches make DNS changes slow to spread. Assuming flat names can be resolved efficiently without extra machinery like a DHT. Thinking a DHT lookup takes one hop; it takes O(log N). Building service discovery with a single registry server, which becomes a single point of failure.

What exams ask: Define name, address and identifier, and list the three properties of an identifier. Explain forwarding pointers and home-based naming with their drawbacks. Build a Chord finger table for a small ring and trace a lookup, just like our m = 4 example. Explain iterative versus recursive name resolution and the role of caching. Compare structured, flat and attribute-based naming.

Recap: Names refer to entities, addresses tell you where to reach them, and identifiers are names that refer to exactly one entity forever. Flat names are resolved by broadcasting, forwarding pointers, home agents or distributed hash tables like Chord, where finger tables give O(log N) lookups. Structured names such as DNS form a tree that allows delegation, and caching with TTLs makes it scale at the cost of staleness. Attribute-based naming searches by properties, and service discovery keeps a health-checked registry of moving service instances. Next, lesson 08 tackles something even trickier than finding things: agreeing on what time it is.
key_points: A name refers to an entity, an address is an access point where it can be reached, and an identifier names exactly one entity and is never reused.
Location-independent names keep working when entities move; only the name-to-address mapping changes.
Flat names are resolved by broadcasting (small LANs), forwarding pointers (chains), home-based schemes (Mobile IP) or DHTs.
Chord stores key k at successor(k); finger i of node p points to successor(p + 2^(i-1)), giving O(log N) lookup hops.
Worked: ring of 16 ids, nodes 1, 4, 9, 11, 14: node 1's fingers are [4, 4, 9, 9] and a lookup for key 12 goes 1 to 9 to 11 and finds owner 14.
DNS is a structured, delegated name tree; iterative or recursive resolution plus TTL caching makes it scale but changes spread slowly.
Attribute-based naming (directory services, LDAP) searches by properties instead of exact names.
Service discovery uses a replicated, health-checked registry so clients find live instances of moving services.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet a new system, ask: what are its names, what are its addresses, and who keeps the mapping between them up to date? That one question explains DNS, DHTs, Mobile IP and service registries all at once.
lessons.task: Draw a Chord ring with m = 4 and nodes at 2, 5, 8, 12 and 15. Write the finger table of every node, then trace lookups for key 10 starting from node 2 and for key 3 starting from node 8. Count the hops. Finally, run nslookup or dig on a website you use and note its TTL.

quiz.q: Which is a property of an identifier?
options: It always contains the entity's location
It can be reused after the entity is deleted
It refers to at most one entity
quiz.explain: An identifier refers to at most one entity, each entity has at most one identifier, and it is never reused.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of forwarding pointers?
options: Long chains slow lookups and break if any machine in the chain fails
quiz.explain: Every move adds a hop, and a crash anywhere in the chain makes the entity unreachable.

quiz.q: In Chord with ids 0 to 15 and nodes 1, 4, 9, 11 and 14, which node stores key 12?
quiz.explain: Key k is stored at successor(k), the first node at or after k on the ring: for 12 that is node 14.

quiz.q: How many hops does a Chord lookup take with N nodes?
quiz.explain: Finger tables let each hop roughly halve the remaining distance, so lookups take O(log N) hops.

quiz.q: Why do teams lower a DNS record's TTL a day before moving a server?
options: To reduce the number of name servers
So cached copies expire quickly and clients pick up the new address fast
quiz.explain: Resolvers may reuse a cached record until its TTL runs out; a short TTL means the new address spreads within minutes.

lessons.title: Physical Clocks and Clock Synchronization
lessons.content:
Picture a cricket match where the two umpires wear watches that disagree by three minutes. One says the drinks break starts now, the other says not yet. In a single room you could just shout across and fix it. Now picture a thousand umpires spread across Dhaka, Chattogram, Singapore and Frankfurt, each with a cheap watch that drifts a little every hour, and the only way to talk is by sending messages that take an unknown time to arrive. That is the clock problem in a distributed system. A single computer has one clock, so "which happened first" is easy. Many computers have many clocks, and they never quite agree.

Where this fits: Lesson 01 listed "no global clock" as one of the three defining features of a distributed system. This lesson and the next two are all about living with that fact. Here we deal with physical clocks, the real time of day, and how to keep many of them close together: Cristian's algorithm, the Berkeley algorithm and NTP. Lesson 09 then shows that for many problems we do not need real time at all, only the order of events, which logical clocks give us.

Why time matters: Many things depend on timestamps. A build tool like make decides whether to recompile a file by comparing the modification time of the source and the compiled output; if two machines disagree on time, it can skip a needed compile. Databases using "last writer wins" keep the update with the latest timestamp, so a fast clock can make an old write beat a newer one. Security certificates and one-time codes have validity windows. Logs from many servers are merged by time to debug an outage. Financial systems record when each trade happened. If clocks are off, all of these break in quiet, confusing ways.

How a computer keeps time: Inside every computer is a quartz crystal that vibrates at a very steady frequency when voltage is applied. A counter counts these vibrations and raises a timer interrupt every so many of them, a "tick", and the operating system adds one tick to its software clock each time. The problem is that no two crystals are exactly alike, and temperature changes their speed slightly. So each clock runs a little fast or a little slow compared to true time.

Drift and skew: Clock drift is the rate at which a clock gains or loses time compared to a perfect clock, usually given in parts per million (ppm). Clock skew is the difference between two clocks' readings at one moment. Drift causes skew to grow. Worked example: a typical quartz clock may drift around 10 ppm, which means 10 microseconds of error for every second. One day has 86,400 seconds, so the error after a day is 86,400 x 10 / 1,000,000 = 0.864 seconds. If one machine runs 10 ppm fast and another 10 ppm slow, they move apart at 20 ppm, so after one day they disagree by 1.728 seconds.

How often to resynchronize: If the maximum drift rate is rho and we never want two clocks to differ by more than delta, we must resynchronize at least every delta / (2 x rho) seconds, because two clocks can drift apart in opposite directions. With rho = 10 ppm (0.00001) and delta = 1 second: 1 / (2 x 0.00001) = 50,000 seconds, about 13.9 hours. If we want them within 1 millisecond instead, it becomes 50 seconds. Tighter agreement means much more frequent synchronization.

Where "true" time comes from: The world's official time is UTC, Coordinated Universal Time, based on many atomic clocks around the world and kept close to the Earth's rotation by occasionally inserting a leap second (a 2022 international decision plans to stop adding leap seconds by 2035). Bangladesh Standard Time is UTC + 6 hours. Computers get UTC from radio time signals, from GPS satellites, which carry atomic clocks and give receivers time accurate to well under a microsecond, or, most often, over the network from time servers. The algorithms below are how that network synchronization works.

Cristian's algorithm: Proposed by Flaviu Cristian in 1989. A client asks a time server for the time. The trouble is the reply takes time to travel, so by the time it arrives the server's answer is already a little old. Cristian's idea: measure the round-trip time (RTT) with your own clock and assume the reply took half of it. Steps: the client records T0 and sends a request; the server replies with its time Ts; the client records T1 when the reply arrives. The client then sets its clock to Ts + (T1 - T0) / 2.

Worked example, Cristian: The client's clock says 10:00:00.000 when it sends the request. The reply arrives when the client's clock says 10:00:00.040, so the RTT is 40 milliseconds. The server's reply says 10:00:05.200. The client sets its clock to 10:00:05.200 + 40 / 2 milliseconds = 10:00:05.220. How wrong can this be? The reply took somewhere between 0 and 40 ms (if we ignore the server's processing time), and we guessed 20, so the error is at most plus or minus 20 ms, half the RTT. If the minimum possible one-way delay is known, the bound shrinks further. Practical tips: repeat the request several times and trust the sample with the smallest RTT, since it has the tightest error bound. The weak point is that one time server is a single point of failure and could even be wrong.

Berkeley algorithm: Developed for Berkeley Unix machines in the late 1980s, this one does not need any machine to know true UTC. Instead, a master (time daemon) polls all machines, works out how far each clock is from its own, averages, and tells everyone how much to adjust so they agree with each other. It cares about internal agreement, not external accuracy. To estimate each reading the master uses Cristian-style RTT correction, and to protect against a broken clock it ignores readings that are too far from the rest.

Worked example, Berkeley: The master's clock reads 3:00. It polls three machines: A reads 2:50, B reads 3:25 and C reads 4:00. Relative to the master the differences are 0, -10, +25 and +60 minutes. The master uses a cutoff: readings more than 30 minutes away are treated as faulty, so C is left out of the average. The average of 0, -10 and +25 is +15 / 3 = +5 minutes, so the agreed time is 3:05. The master then sends each machine the adjustment it needs, not the new time: master +5, A +15, B -20 and C -55. Sending adjustments rather than absolute times avoids errors from the delay of the reply message. Everyone now reads 3:05, even C, whose wrong reading was simply not allowed to drag the average.

NTP, the Network Time Protocol: NTP, designed by David Mills starting in the 1980s, is what nearly every computer and phone uses today. Servers are arranged in strata. Stratum 0 is a reference clock such as an atomic clock or GPS receiver. A stratum 1 server is directly connected to one, a stratum 2 server synchronizes from stratum 1, and so on; a lower stratum number means closer to the source, not necessarily better. Instead of one request, NTP exchanges four timestamps and computes both the offset (how far the client is from the server) and the delay (round-trip network time).

The NTP formulas: The client sends a request at T1 (client clock). The server receives it at T2 and sends the reply at T3 (server clock). The client receives it at T4 (client clock). Then offset theta = ((T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)) / 2 and delay delta = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2). The delay subtracts the time the server spent processing. The offset assumes the two directions of the network take equal time; if they do not, the error is at most delta / 2.

Worked example, NTP: In milliseconds, T1 = 1000, T2 = 1530, T3 = 1532 and T4 = 1062. Then T2 - T1 = 530 and T3 - T4 = 470, so the offset is (530 + 470) / 2 = 500 ms: the client is half a second behind the server. The delay is (1062 - 1000) - (1532 - 1530) = 62 - 2 = 60 ms. You can check it: if the true offset is 500 and each direction takes 30 ms, then T2 = 1000 + 30 + 500 = 1530 and T4 = 1532 - 500 + 30 = 1062, exactly our numbers. NTP repeats this many times and prefers samples with the smallest delay, since those have the smallest error. Over the public Internet NTP typically keeps clocks within tens of milliseconds, and much better on a good local network.

Never jump backwards: Suppose the client finds it is 500 ms ahead. Should it set the clock back by half a second at once? No. Programs assume time only moves forward; a sudden backward jump can make a file look older than its source, make an elapsed-time measurement negative, or produce two log lines in the wrong order. Instead, the system slews the clock: it makes each tick slightly shorter or longer for a while, so the clock gently speeds up or slows down until the error is gone. Large jumps are usually allowed only at boot. For measuring durations, programmers should use the monotonic clock that the operating system provides, which never goes backwards, not the wall-clock time of day.

Beyond NTP: Some systems need far tighter time. The Precision Time Protocol (PTP, IEEE 1588) uses timestamps taken in network hardware and can reach sub-microsecond agreement on a local network, which telecom networks and stock exchanges care about. Google's Spanner database is a famous example of using GPS and atomic clocks in data centers to give each timestamp a known uncertainty interval, and waiting out that uncertainty before committing. You will meet such designs again in Advanced Database Systems & Big Data (deep-cse-7-2).

Real-life example 1, mobile banking OTP: Many authenticator apps generate a time-based one-time password (TOTP) that changes every 30 seconds, computed from a shared secret and the current time (deep-cse-6-2, lesson 20). If a customer's phone clock in Khulna is two minutes wrong because automatic network time is turned off, the code it shows belongs to the wrong 30-second window and the bank's server rejects it. Servers usually accept one window either side to tolerate small skew, but not two minutes. The fix is simply turning automatic time back on, which makes the phone synchronize, typically over NTP or from the mobile network.

Real-life example 2, debugging an outage with logs: A payment company's request fails somewhere between its load balancer in Dhaka, an app server and a database server. Engineers merge the three logs by timestamp. If the database server's clock is 800 ms behind, its "query started" line appears before the app server's "sending query" line, and the story looks impossible. With all machines on NTP and within a few milliseconds, the merged log reads correctly. Even then, for events less than a few milliseconds apart, timestamps cannot be trusted to give the order, which is exactly why the next lesson introduces logical clocks.

Common mistakes: Thinking clock synchronization can make clocks exactly equal; it only keeps skew within a bound. Forgetting to halve the RTT in Cristian's algorithm, or forgetting that the error bound is RTT / 2. In Berkeley, sending new absolute times instead of adjustments, or including an obviously faulty clock in the average. Mixing up NTP's offset and delay formulas. Setting a clock backwards abruptly. Using wall-clock time to measure durations or to order events that happen very close together.

What exams ask: Define clock drift and skew, and compute the drift after a day for a given ppm. Find the resynchronization interval delta / (2 x rho). Apply Cristian's algorithm and state its accuracy. Run the Berkeley algorithm on four given clock values with a fault cutoff. Compute NTP offset and delay from four timestamps. Explain why clocks must not run backwards and what slewing is. Explain strata in NTP.

Recap: Every computer clock is a counter driven by a quartz crystal that drifts, typically by around 10 ppm, almost a second a day. Skew between machines grows unless they resynchronize, and the needed interval is delta / (2 x rho). Cristian's algorithm sets time to Ts + RTT/2 with error up to RTT/2. Berkeley averages all clocks, ignores outliers, and sends adjustments, aiming for internal agreement. NTP uses four timestamps to compute offset and delay, a stratum hierarchy and careful filtering, and corrects by slewing rather than jumping. Physical time is never perfect, so lesson 09 asks a smarter question: if we only need to know what happened before what, can we do without real time altogether?
key_points: Computer clocks count quartz crystal ticks and drift; at 10 ppm a clock gains or loses 0.864 seconds per day.
Skew is the difference between clocks at one moment; to keep skew under delta with drift rho, resynchronize every delta / (2 x rho).
Cristian: set clock to Ts + RTT/2; worked: Ts = 10:00:05.200 and RTT = 40 ms give 10:00:05.220, accurate to plus or minus 20 ms.
Berkeley: a master polls, ignores outliers, averages and sends adjustments; worked: 3:00, 2:50, 3:25 (4:00 ignored) agree on 3:05.
NTP: offset = ((T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)) / 2 and delay = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2); worked: offset 500 ms, delay 60 ms.
NTP servers form strata: stratum 0 reference clocks, stratum 1 servers attached to them, and so on.
Clocks are corrected by slewing, never by jumping backwards; use a monotonic clock to measure durations.
Physical clocks can only be kept within a bound of each other, so ordering close events needs logical clocks (lesson 09).
lessons.tip: Memorise one tiny example for each algorithm instead of the formulas: 40 ms RTT gives plus or minus 20 ms for Cristian, 3:00/2:50/3:25 gives 3:05 for Berkeley, and 1000/1530/1532/1062 gives 500 and 60 for NTP. The formulas fall out of the examples.
lessons.task: Open your phone's date and time settings and note whether automatic time is on. Then do this on paper: an NTP exchange has T1 = 2000, T2 = 2215, T3 = 2217 and T4 = 2050 (milliseconds). Compute the offset, the delay and the maximum error. Finally, run a Berkeley round for a master at 10:00 and machines at 9:58, 10:08 and 10:45 with a 20-minute cutoff, and write each machine's adjustment.

quiz.q: A quartz clock drifts at 10 ppm. About how much error does it build up in one day?
quiz.explain: 10 ppm is 10 microseconds per second; 86,400 seconds x 10 / 1,000,000 = 0.864 seconds.

quiz.q: In Cristian's algorithm, the server replies 10:00:05.200 and the measured RTT is 40 ms. What time does the client set?
quiz.explain: The client adds half the round trip: 5.200 + 0.020 = 10:00:05.220.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of the Berkeley algorithm?
options: Making the machines agree with each other by averaging, without needing true UTC
quiz.explain: Berkeley averages the clocks of the group and sends adjustments, aiming for internal agreement rather than external accuracy.

quiz.q: NTP timestamps are T1 = 1000, T2 = 1530, T3 = 1532, T4 = 1062 ms. What are the offset and delay?
A client discovers its clock is 500 ms ahead. What should it do?
options: Slew the clock, running it slightly slower until the error disappears
Ignore it because 500 ms is harmless
quiz.explain: Jumping backwards breaks programs that assume time moves forward; slewing corrects gradually.

lessons.title: Logical Clocks and the Happened-Before Relation
lessons.content:
Imagine three friends in a class WhatsApp group: Rafi in Dhaka, Mitu in Rajshahi and Sabbir in Chattogram. Rafi asks, "Is the exam postponed?" Mitu replies, "Yes, to Sunday." Sabbir, who saw Mitu's reply, writes, "Great, more time for Distributed Systems!" Now suppose the server stores these three messages on three different machines, each stamping them with its own wall clock, and one of those clocks is half a second fast. When the history is rebuilt, Mitu's "Yes, to Sunday" might appear before Rafi's question. The answer shows up before the question. Nobody cares about the exact time; everybody cares that the order makes sense. That is the problem logical clocks solve.

Where this fits: In lesson 08 we synchronised physical clocks with Cristian, Berkeley and NTP. They help a lot, but they never make clocks perfectly equal: there is always some leftover error, often milliseconds across a network, and that is plenty of time for two events to be stamped in the wrong order. In 1978 Leslie Lamport published a short paper, "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System", with a surprising idea: for many problems we do not need real time at all. We only need to know which event could have influenced which. This lesson is about that idea.

The system model: We have a few processes, P1, P2, P3, running on different machines. They share no memory and no clock. Each process does a sequence of events, one after another, so inside one process the order is clear. There are three kinds of events: a local event (some computation, like updating a variable), a send event (sending a message to another process) and a receive event (getting a message). Draw each process as a horizontal line, events as dots, and messages as arrows between lines. This picture is called a space-time diagram, and exam questions almost always start with one.

Why order, not time: Think about what you actually need. A replicated database must apply updates in the same order everywhere. A debugger reading logs from twenty servers must know that the "payment failed" log line came after the "timeout" line that caused it. A build tool must know whether a source file changed after its object file was made. In every case the question is "which came first, and could one have caused the other?" rather than "what was the exact time?". If we can answer the first question without trusting clocks, we have removed a whole class of bugs.

The happened-before relation: Lamport defined a relation written a -> b, read "a happened before b". It is the smallest relation obeying three rules. Rule 1: if a and b are events in the same process and a comes before b, then a -> b. Rule 2: if a is the sending of a message and b is the receiving of that same message, then a -> b. Rule 3 (transitivity): if a -> b and b -> c, then a -> c. That is all. Happened-before captures potential causality: a -> b means information from a could have reached b, through a chain of steps inside processes and messages between them.

A tiny example of the rules: In the WhatsApp story, Rafi sending the question happened before Mitu receiving it (rule 2). Mitu receiving it happened before Mitu sending "Yes" (rule 1, same process). So by rule 3, Rafi's question happened before Mitu's answer, whatever any clock says. Sabbir's reply comes after he received Mitu's answer, so the whole chain is ordered: question -> answer -> Sabbir's reply.

Concurrent events: If neither a -> b nor b -> a, we say a and b are concurrent and write a || b. Careful: concurrent does not mean "at the same instant". It means there is no chain of messages linking them, so neither could have influenced the other. Suppose Sabbir, before reading anything, posts "Who has the slides?" That message and Rafi's question are concurrent, even if one was typed an hour before the other on the wall clock, because no information flowed between them. Happened-before is therefore a partial order: some pairs are ordered, some are simply not comparable. It is irreflexive (no event happens before itself) and transitive.

The Lamport clock idea: Lamport's trick is to give each process a simple integer counter, C, and attach a number C(e) to every event e, so that the numbers respect happened-before. We want the clock condition: if a -> b then C(a) < C(b). The counter does not measure seconds. It is a logical clock, a number that only ever moves forward and that travels inside messages.

The rules: Every process starts with C = 0. Rule A: before each event (local, send or receive) the process increments its counter, C = C + 1, and the event gets that value. Rule B: when a process sends a message m, it attaches its current counter value as the timestamp ts(m). Rule C: when a process receives m, it first sets C = max(C, ts(m)) and then does the usual increment, so the receive event gets max(C, ts(m)) + 1. In pseudo-code: on local or send: C = C + 1; on send also ts = C; on receive: C = max(C, ts) + 1. The idea: never go backwards, and always end up past whatever the sender knew.

Worked trace, the setup: Three processes. P1 does a1 (local), a2 (send m1 to P2), a3 (local), and later a4 (receive m3 from P3). P2 does b1 (receive m1), b2 (send m2 to P3), b3 (local). P3 does c1 (local), c2 (local), c3 (receive m2), c4 (send m3 to P1). All counters start at 0.

Worked trace, P1 and P2: On P1, a1 gets 1 and a2 gets 2, so m1 carries timestamp 2. Then a3 gets 3. On P2 the first event is receiving m1: max(0, 2) + 1 = 3, so b1 = 3. Then b2 = 4 and m2 carries 4. Then b3 = 5. Notice how P2's clock jumped from 0 straight to 3: receiving the message pulled it forward past everything P1 had done before sending.

Worked trace, P3 and the end: On P3, c1 = 1 and c2 = 2. Then m2 arrives with timestamp 4, so c3 = max(2, 4) + 1 = 5. Then c4 = 6, and m3 carries 6. Back on P1, the counter is 3 when m3 arrives, so a4 = max(3, 6) + 1 = 7. Final values: a1 = 1, a2 = 2, a3 = 3, a4 = 7; b1 = 3, b2 = 4, b3 = 5; c1 = 1, c2 = 2, c3 = 5, c4 = 6.

Checking the clock condition: Take the chain a1 -> a2 -> b1 -> b2 -> c3 -> c4 -> a4. The numbers are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, strictly increasing, exactly as promised. Inside one process the counter only grows, and across a message the receiver jumps past the sender's timestamp. So every step of a happened-before chain increases the clock, and therefore if a -> b then C(a) < C(b).

The converse is false: Now look at c1 = 1 and b1 = 3. We have C(c1) < C(b1), but is c1 -> b1? No. Nothing from P3 reached P2 before b1, so c1 and b1 are concurrent. Also a3 = 3 and b1 = 3 have equal numbers and are concurrent. So a smaller Lamport timestamp does not prove that one event happened before another. What we can say is the contrapositive: if C(a) >= C(b), then a did not happen before b. Lamport clocks give a consistent order, not a full picture of causality. Lesson 10 fixes this with vector clocks.

From partial order to total order: Many algorithms need every pair of events ordered, with every process agreeing on the order. Lamport clocks can give that with one more trick: break ties using the process id. Stamp each event with the pair (C, process number) and compare pairs like dictionary words: first by C, then by process number. In our trace a3 is (3, 1) and b1 is (3, 2), so a3 comes first. Sorting all eleven events gives a1 and c1 both 1, so a1 (1,1) then c1 (1,3); then a2 (2,1), c2 (2,3); then a3 (3,1), b1 (3,2); then b2 (4,2); then b3 (5,2), c3 (5,3); then c4 (6,3); then a4 (7,1). This total order is consistent with happened-before, and every process computing it gets exactly the same list. Arbitrary but agreed is all we need.

Totally ordered multicast: Here is the classic use. A wallet company keeps two replicas of an account, one in Dhaka and one in Chattogram. The balance is 1000 taka. A customer deposits 100 taka at the same moment a batch job adds 1 percent interest. If Dhaka applies deposit first, then interest, it gets (1000 + 100) x 1.01 = 1111. If Chattogram applies interest first, it gets 1000 x 1.01 + 100 = 1110. The replicas now disagree, and nobody did anything "wrong"; they just saw the updates in different orders.

How the multicast works: Each update is multicast to all replicas, including the sender, with a Lamport timestamp. Every replica puts incoming updates in a local queue sorted by (timestamp, process id) and multicasts an acknowledgement. A replica applies the update at the head of its queue only when it has been acknowledged by every replica (or, in some versions, when it has seen a later-stamped message from every replica). Assuming reliable FIFO channels and no crashes, every replica applies updates in the same total order, so both get 1111 or both get 1110. This is the seed of the replicated state machine idea that we will meet again with Raft in lesson 19. Its weakness is also clear: if one replica crashes, nobody can collect all acknowledgements, and everything stalls. Handling crashes needs the consensus machinery of lessons 18 and 19.

Real-life example 1, group chats and comment threads: In a busy Facebook group about the BPL cricket final, people reply to each other's comments from all over Bangladesh. A reply must never appear above the comment it answers. A system can guarantee that by carrying a logical counter with each post and each read: when your phone loads a comment stamped 41 and you reply, your reply is stamped at least 42. Even if the server that stores your reply has a clock a few hundred milliseconds behind, sorting by the logical stamp keeps the reply after its parent. Unrelated comments posted at almost the same moment may appear in either order, and that is fine, because they are concurrent.

Real-life example 2, debugging a payment: An engineer at a Dhaka fintech company is chasing a bug where a transfer was marked "failed" although the money moved. The logs come from the API server, the ledger service and the SMS service, all on different machines. Sorting the log lines by wall-clock time puts the "failed" line before the ledger's "committed" line, which looks like a clear story but is wrong: one server's clock was 80 milliseconds fast. When each request carries a logical counter through every service call, the merged log shows the real causal chain. Many modern systems use hybrid logical clocks, which combine a physical time reading with a Lamport-style counter, so timestamps stay close to real time while still never breaking happened-before.

Common mistakes: First, thinking "concurrent" means "simultaneous". It means causally unrelated. Second, believing C(a) < C(b) implies a -> b. Only the other direction is guaranteed. Third, forgetting to increment after taking the max on receive; then a receive could get the same number as the send, breaking the clock condition. Fourth, forgetting that the tie-break by process id is needed for a total order, since two events in different processes can carry the same counter value. Fifth, thinking Lamport clocks measure time. They measure nothing physical; a quiet process can have a counter of 3 while a busy one is at 3000.

What exams ask: Typical questions give a space-time diagram and ask you to assign Lamport timestamps to every event, list pairs of concurrent events, or explain why equal or smaller timestamps do not imply causality. Others ask you to state the happened-before rules, prove the clock condition in two lines, or explain how totally ordered multicast keeps replicas consistent and what assumptions it needs (reliable FIFO channels, no failures).

Recap: In a distributed system, ordering events matters more than reading exact times. Happened-before (same process order, send before receive, transitivity) captures potential causality; events with no causal chain are concurrent. A Lamport clock is a per-process counter incremented before each event and pulled forward by max(C, ts) + 1 on receive, which guarantees that a -> b implies C(a) < C(b), but not the reverse. Adding the process id as a tie-break turns this into a total order everyone agrees on, which powers totally ordered multicast for replicas. Next lesson, vector clocks will let us read causality straight off the timestamps.
key_points: In distributed systems the order of events usually matters more than exact physical time, and physical clocks are never perfectly in sync.
Happened-before (Lamport, 1978): same-process order, send before its receive, and transitivity; it captures potential causality.
Events with no happened-before chain either way are concurrent (a || b): causally unrelated, not necessarily simultaneous.
Lamport clock rules: increment before every event, attach the counter to each message, and on receive set C = max(C, ts) + 1.
Clock condition: if a -> b then C(a) < C(b); the converse does not hold, so a smaller timestamp does not prove causality.
Breaking ties with the process id, (C, pid), gives a total order that every process computes identically.
Totally ordered multicast uses that total order plus acknowledgements so replicas apply updates in the same order, assuming reliable FIFO channels and no crashes.
lessons.tip: Always draw the space-time diagram first, with one line per process and an arrow per message. Then walk each line left to right saying out loud "plus one" for local and send events and "max, then plus one" for receives. Saying the rule while you write stops the most common slip, forgetting the plus one after the max.
lessons.task: Draw three processes and five messages of your own on paper, assign Lamport timestamps to every event, then list three pairs of concurrent events and check that at least one of those pairs has different timestamps. Finally, sort all events by (timestamp, process id) to get the total order.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes the happened-before relation a -> b?
options: a has an earlier wall-clock time than b
a and b are on different machines
There is a chain of same-process steps and messages from a to b, so a could have influenced b
a and b have equal Lamport timestamps
quiz.explain: Happened-before is potential causality built from process order, send-receive pairs and transitivity, not from wall-clock readings.

quiz.q: P2's clock is 4 when it receives a message with timestamp 9. What timestamp does the receive event get?
quiz.explain: On receive, C = max(4, 9) + 1 = 10.

quiz.q: Events x and y have Lamport timestamps 3 and 8. What can you conclude for sure?
options: y did not happen before x
quiz.explain: If y -> x then C(y) < C(x) would hold, which is false. But x -> y is not guaranteed: they may be concurrent.

quiz.q: Why is the process id used as a tie-breaker in Lamport timestamps?
options: To turn the partial order into a total order all processes agree on
To make the clock measure real time
quiz.explain: Two events on different processes can have the same counter; comparing (C, pid) orders every pair the same way everywhere.

quiz.q: In totally ordered multicast, what makes all replicas apply updates in the same order?
options: Each replica applies messages in arrival order
A central clock server stamps every update
Every replica sends updates only to the leader
Messages are queued by (Lamport timestamp, process id) and applied from the head once acknowledged by all
quiz.explain: Sorting by the same total order and waiting for acknowledgements gives every replica the identical sequence, assuming reliable FIFO channels and no crashes.

lessons.title: Vector Clocks and Causality
lessons.content:
Before Eid, Ammu and Abbu share one shopping list in a family app. Ammu is in Dhaka, Abbu is visiting his village near Cumilla where the mobile signal keeps dropping. Ammu adds "cooking oil". At almost the same time, offline, Abbu adds "dal". When his phone reconnects, the app has two versions of the list. Did Abbu see Ammu's change and then edit, so his version should simply win? Or did they both edit the same old list without seeing each other, so the app must keep both changes? A Lamport clock from lesson 09 cannot answer that question. A vector clock can, and that is the whole point of today's lesson.

Where this fits: Lesson 09 gave us happened-before and Lamport clocks, with one painful limitation: if a -> b then C(a) < C(b), but a smaller timestamp does not prove a -> b. Two concurrent events can have any numbers. What we really want is a timestamp where the comparison works in both directions: V(a) < V(b) exactly when a -> b. Vector clocks give exactly that. They were proposed independently by Colin Fidge and Friedemann Mattern around 1988.

The idea: In a system with N processes, each process Pi keeps not one counter but a vector Vi of N counters, one slot per process. The meaning is simple and worth memorising: Vi[j] is the number of events of process Pj that Pi knows about, either because they happened at Pi itself (when j = i) or because news of them arrived through messages. A vector clock is a summary of "everything I have heard of so far".

The rules: Every process starts with a vector of zeros. Rule 1: before each event, Pi increments its own slot, Vi[i] = Vi[i] + 1. Rule 2: when Pi sends a message, it attaches a copy of its whole vector. Rule 3: when Pi receives a message carrying vector W, it first takes the element-wise maximum, Vi[k] = max(Vi[k], W[k]) for every k, and then increments its own slot as in rule 1. In pseudo-code: on local or send: V[i] += 1; on send also attach copy of V; on receive(W): for k in 1..N: V[k] = max(V[k], W[k]); then V[i] += 1. Compare with Lamport: the single max becomes a max per slot, and each process only ever increments its own slot.

Worked trace, the setup: We reuse the exact trace from lesson 09 so you can compare. P1 does a1 (local), a2 (send m1 to P2), a3 (local), a4 (receive m3). P2 does b1 (receive m1), b2 (send m2 to P3), b3 (local). P3 does c1 (local), c2 (local), c3 (receive m2), c4 (send m3 to P1). Vectors are written [P1, P2, P3] and all start at [0,0,0].

Worked trace, P1 and P2: a1 = [1,0,0], a2 = [2,0,0], and m1 carries [2,0,0]. Then a3 = [3,0,0]. On P2, receiving m1: max of [0,0,0] and [2,0,0] is [2,0,0], then increment P2's slot, so b1 = [2,1,0]. Then b2 = [2,2,0], and m2 carries [2,2,0]. Then b3 = [2,3,0].

Worked trace, P3 and the end: c1 = [0,0,1], c2 = [0,0,2]. Receiving m2: max of [0,0,2] and [2,2,0] is [2,2,2], then increment P3's slot, so c3 = [2,2,3]. Then c4 = [2,2,4], and m3 carries it. Back at P1, which is at [3,0,0]: max with [2,2,4] gives [3,2,4], and incrementing P1's slot gives a4 = [4,2,4]. I checked every vector with a short Python simulation.

Reading a vector: Look at a4 = [4,2,4]. It says: at this moment P1 knows of 4 of its own events, 2 events of P2 and 4 events of P3. Which two events of P2? b1 and b2, because news of them travelled through m2 to P3 and then through m3 to P1. P2's third event, b3, is not in a4's knowledge at all: b3 happened after P2 sent m2, and no message carried it anywhere. So b3 and a4 should be concurrent, and the vectors will confirm that.

Comparing vectors: For two vectors V and W of length N, we say V <= W if V[k] <= W[k] for every k. We say V < W if V <= W and V is not equal to W, meaning at least one slot is strictly smaller. If neither V <= W nor W <= V, the vectors are incomparable, and we write V || W. The key theorem of vector clocks is: a -> b if and only if V(a) < V(b), and a || b if and only if V(a) || V(b). So causality can now be read directly off the timestamps, in both directions.

Comparisons from the trace: a2 = [2,0,0] and c3 = [2,2,3]: every slot of a2 is <= the matching slot of c3, and they differ, so a2 -> c3. True: the chain a2 -> b1 -> b2 -> c3 exists. Now a3 = [3,0,0] and b1 = [2,1,0]: a3 is bigger in slot 1, b1 is bigger in slot 2, so they are concurrent. In lesson 09 both had Lamport time 3 and we could not say anything; now we can. Also c1 = [0,0,1] vs b1 = [2,1,0]: concurrent, even though their Lamport times were 1 and 3. And b3 = [2,3,0] vs c4 = [2,2,4]: b3 wins slot 2, c4 wins slot 3, so concurrent, matching what we reasoned above.

Detecting conflicts in replicated data: The most practical use of this idea is in replicated storage, where the vectors are kept per replica (or per writer) and are usually called version vectors. Each stored value carries a vector saying which updates it already includes. When two versions meet, the system compares the vectors. If one is smaller, the bigger version already contains the smaller one's history, so the old one can be thrown away. If they are concurrent, there was a genuine conflict: two writes happened without knowing about each other, and the system must keep both or merge them.

The shopping cart, worked: Back to the Eid list, stored on two replicas, Dhaka (D) and Chattogram (C), with version vectors written [D, C]. The list starts empty with [0,0]. Ammu adds "rice" through Dhaka: version [1,0], and this syncs to Chattogram, so both hold {rice} at [1,0]. Now the link between the data centres breaks for a while. Ammu adds "oil" through Dhaka: {rice, oil} at [2,0]. Abbu, whose phone talks to Chattogram, adds "dal" to the copy he read, {rice} at [1,0], so Chattogram stores {rice, dal} at [1,1]. When the link heals, the system compares [2,0] and [1,1]: Dhaka wins slot D, Chattogram wins slot C, so they are concurrent. Neither version may silently replace the other.

Resolving the conflict: The system keeps both versions (often called siblings) and either asks the application to merge them or applies a merge rule. For a shopping list a natural merge is the union, {rice, oil, dal}, stamped with the element-wise maximum [2,1]; when Dhaka stores the merged list as a new write it bumps its own slot, giving [3,1]. Compare this with "last writer wins" by wall-clock time: one of oil or dal would simply vanish, chosen by whichever server clock happened to be ahead. Amazon's well-known Dynamo paper (2007) described exactly this cart style of reconciliation with vector clocks, and also noted a side effect: with a plain union merge, an item that one side deleted can reappear. Smarter merge types, called CRDTs, get a brief mention in lesson 14.

Causal ordering of messages: Vector clocks also let us deliver group messages in causal order, so nobody ever sees an answer before its question. In this variant, each process increments its own slot only when it broadcasts a message, and the vector counts messages, not all events. A process Pk that receives message m from Pj with vector W delivers it only when two conditions hold: W[j] = Vk[j] + 1 (m is the very next message from Pj that Pk has not yet seen) and W[i] <= Vk[i] for every other i (Pk has already delivered everything the sender had seen when it sent m). Otherwise m waits in a buffer. On delivery, Pk sets Vk[j] = W[j].

Causal delivery, worked: P1 broadcasts m1 with [1,0,0]. P2 delivers m1 and then broadcasts its reply m2 with [1,1,0]. At P3, with local vector [0,0,0], m2 arrives first because the network delayed m1. Check: W[2] = 1 equals 0 + 1, fine, but W[1] = 1 is greater than P3's 0, so P3 has not yet seen something m2 depends on. m2 is buffered. Then m1 arrives with [1,0,0]: W[1] = 1 = 0 + 1 and the other slots are 0, so m1 is delivered and P3 moves to [1,0,0]. Now m2 passes both tests and is delivered, and P3 ends at [1,1,0]. The user at P3 sees the question, then the answer, exactly as it should be.

The cost: A vector clock has one slot per process, so it grows with N. With 5 database replicas that is 5 small integers per value, which is cheap. With a million mobile clients each writing directly, a vector per client would be enormous. That is why practical systems keep one slot per replica rather than per client, and why refinements such as dotted version vectors exist to stay accurate while staying small. Some systems also prune old entries, which can occasionally make a version look concurrent when it was not; the safe direction is to keep an extra sibling rather than lose data.

Real-life example 1, offline field data: Health workers for an NGO in the haor areas of Sunamganj collect household survey data on tablets that are offline for days. Two workers sometimes update the same household record, one in the morning and one in the afternoon, each on their own tablet. When the tablets sync with the central server in Sylhet, the version vectors tell the server whether the afternoon edit was made on top of the morning one (just keep the newer version) or whether both edited the same old record independently (flag a conflict for a supervisor to review). Without that, the server would have to guess using clocks that may be badly wrong on tablets.

Real-life example 2, a class discussion app: A university in Khulna runs a discussion forum on three servers. A student asks a question, a teacher answers it, and a third student, on another server, comments "thanks, that helped". With causal delivery using vector timestamps, every server shows the question before the answer and the answer before the thanks, even if the network delivers them in a scrambled order. Posts that are unrelated, like two different questions asked at the same time, can appear in different orders on different servers, and nobody minds.

Common mistakes: First, incrementing every slot or the sender's slot on receive; you only ever increment your own slot. Second, forgetting to take the element-wise max before incrementing on receive. Third, calling two vectors "less than" when one slot is smaller and another is bigger; that is concurrent, not ordered. Fourth, thinking concurrent versions mean an error happened; they simply mean two writes did not know about each other, and the application decides how to merge. Fifth, mixing up the event-counting rules used for timestamps with the send-counting rules used for causal delivery.

What exams ask: Expect a space-time diagram where you must fill in vector timestamps for every event, then decide for given pairs whether a -> b, b -> a or a || b. Other favourites: state the comparison rule and the theorem "a -> b iff V(a) < V(b)", explain why Lamport clocks cannot detect concurrency, show how version vectors detect a write conflict in a replicated key-value store, or trace causal broadcast and say which message is buffered.

Recap: A vector clock gives each process N counters, where slot j counts the events of Pj it knows about. Increment your own slot before each event, send the whole vector, and on receive take the element-wise max before incrementing. Then a -> b exactly when V(a) < V(b), and incomparable vectors mean concurrent events. In our trace a4 = [4,2,4], and pairs like a3 and b1 that Lamport clocks could not separate are clearly concurrent. Version vectors use the same comparison to spot real write conflicts, as in the Eid shopping list, and vector timestamps drive causal message delivery. Next, lesson 11 asks how to photograph the whole system's state at once.
key_points: Vector clocks (Fidge and Mattern, around 1988) fix the Lamport limitation: a -> b if and only if V(a) < V(b).
Each process keeps N counters; slot j counts the events of process Pj that this process knows about.
Rules: increment your own slot before each event, attach the vector to each message, and on receive take the element-wise max before incrementing.
V <= W means every slot is <=; V < W also needs one strict difference; if neither V <= W nor W <= V, the events are concurrent.
Worked trace: a4 = [4,2,4], c3 = [2,2,3], and a3 = [3,0,0] vs b1 = [2,1,0] is concurrent.
Version vectors detect real write conflicts in replicated data: [2,0] vs [1,1] are concurrent, so both versions must be kept or merged.
Causal delivery buffers a message until W[j] = V[j] + 1 for the sender and W[i] <= V[i] for all others.
Cost grows with N, so practical systems keep one slot per replica, not per client.
lessons.tip: When comparing two vectors, write them one above the other and mark each slot with <, = or >. If you see both a < and a > in the same row, stop: the events are concurrent. This one habit answers most exam questions on vector clocks in seconds.
lessons.task: Take the space-time diagram you drew for lesson 09 and redo it with vector timestamps. Then pick every pair of events from different processes, decide -> or || from the vectors, and check two of your answers by tracing message arrows by hand.

quiz.q: In a 3-process system, P2's vector is [1,4,2] and it receives a message carrying [3,2,2]. What is P2's vector after the receive event?
quiz.explain: Element-wise max gives [3,4,2], then P2 increments its own slot: [3,5,2].

quiz.q: Which pair of vector timestamps shows concurrent events?
quiz.explain: [3,1,0] is bigger in slot 1 and [2,2,0] is bigger in slot 2, so neither is <= the other.

quiz.q: What does Vi[j] = 5 mean in a vector clock?
options: Process Pi knows about 5 events of process Pj
Process Pj has sent 5 messages to Pi
The real time difference between Pi and Pj is 5 seconds
Pi has done 5 events in total
quiz.explain: Each slot counts the events of that process that Pi has heard of, directly or through messages.

quiz.q: Two replicas hold versions with version vectors [2,0] and [1,1]. What should the system do?
options: Keep [2,0] because its first number is larger
Keep [1,1] because it was written last
Treat them as concurrent and keep both or merge them
quiz.explain: Neither vector is <= the other, so the writes were concurrent; silently dropping one would lose an update.

quiz.q: Why do practical stores keep one vector slot per replica rather than per client?
options: Per-replica slots make vectors exact Lamport clocks
With very many clients the vectors would become huge
quiz.explain: Vector size grows with the number of participants, so millions of client slots would be impractical.

lessons.title: Global State and Distributed Snapshots
lessons.content:
Every winter, thousands of migratory birds arrive at Tanguar Haor in Sunamganj. Suppose a team wants to count them all at one moment, but the haor is far too big for one camera. They place ten photographers around it. Each one takes a picture when they think the moment has come. Some birds fly from one photographer's area into another's between the shots, so they get counted twice; others fly the opposite way and are counted by nobody. Taking a correct picture of a big moving thing, using many separate cameras and no shared clock, is surprisingly hard. In a distributed system this is called recording a global state, or taking a snapshot.

Where this fits: Lessons 08 to 10 showed that there is no global clock, only partly synchronised physical clocks and logical clocks. That makes "everyone write down your state at exactly 12:00" unreliable. In 1985 K. Mani Chandy and Leslie Lamport published "Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems", with an algorithm that records a meaningful global state while the system keeps running. It is one of the most elegant ideas in this course, and it is the basis of checkpointing in many modern systems.

What a global state is: Picture processes connected by one-way channels. The global state has two parts. First, the local state of every process: its variables, balances, counters. Second, the state of every channel: the messages that have been sent on it but not yet received. People often forget the second part. If money is travelling inside a message when you take the picture, and you only record the processes, that money vanishes from your picture.

Why it is hard: You cannot pause every machine at once; pausing would need exactly the global coordination we lack. If each process records its state when its own clock says 12:00, clock skew of a few milliseconds means some messages are sent after the sender recorded but received before the receiver recorded. Then the receiver's recorded state includes the effect of a message whose sending is not in the picture. Effects without causes appear.

An inconsistent snapshot, worked: Two branches of a wallet system, P1 and P2. P1 holds 1000 taka and P2 holds 500, so the total is 1500. P1 sends 200 to P2, and P2 sends 100 to P1. Suppose P1 records its balance as 1000, before it sends the 200, while P2 records its balance as 600, after it has sent its 100 and received the 200. The two recorded balances add up to 1600 taka, 100 more than exists. The 200 taka transfer is in P2's picture as received but not in P1's picture as sent: money from nowhere. An auditor reading this snapshot would raise a false alarm.

Cuts: To talk about this precisely we use cuts. Write down the events of each process in order. A cut picks, for every process, a point on its line; all events before that point are inside the cut, all after are outside. Drawn on a space-time diagram, a cut is a wavy line crossing every process line once. The recorded state of each process is its state at the cut point.

Consistent cuts: A cut is consistent if, for every message whose receive event is inside the cut, its send event is also inside the cut. In other words, the cut never contains an effect without its cause. A message received inside the cut but sent outside it is called an orphan, and one orphan makes the cut inconsistent. The opposite case is fine: a message sent inside the cut but received outside it is simply in transit at the moment of the cut, and its contents must be recorded as channel state. In our bad example, the 200 taka transfer is an orphan, which is exactly why the total looked wrong. Formally, a consistent cut is one that is closed under happened-before: if b is in the cut and a -> b, then a is in the cut too.

Chandy-Lamport, the assumptions: The algorithm assumes channels are reliable and FIFO (messages on one channel arrive in the order sent, none lost), the processes and channels form a strongly connected graph so a marker can reach everyone, and no process fails during the snapshot. Any process can start a snapshot at any time, several can even start at once, and normal messages keep flowing; nobody stops working.

Marker sending rule: The algorithm uses a special control message called a marker. When a process records its local state, it immediately sends a marker on each of its outgoing channels, before sending any other message on those channels. The initiator simply begins by recording its own state and following this rule.

Marker receiving rule: When process Q receives a marker on an incoming channel c, there are two cases. If Q has not yet recorded its state, it records its local state now, records the state of channel c as empty, follows the marker sending rule, and starts recording every other incoming channel, meaning it notes every normal message that arrives on them. If Q has already recorded its state, it stops recording channel c, and the state of c is exactly the list of normal messages that arrived on c between Q's recording and this marker. Because channels are FIFO, the marker separates messages sent before the sender recorded from messages sent after.

Termination: A process is finished when it has received a marker on every incoming channel. The snapshot is complete when every process is finished. The pieces are scattered across processes, so they are usually sent to the initiator or a collector, which assembles the global state. With N processes and a channel in each direction between every pair, exactly one marker travels on each channel, so N(N-1) markers in total; with our 2 processes that is just 2 markers.

Worked snapshot, the setup: Same two branches. Initially P1 = 1000 and P2 = 500. Channel C12 goes from P1 to P2, and C21 from P2 to P1. Events happen in this real order: t1, P1 sends 200 to P2 (P1 = 800, C12 holds 200). t2, P2 sends 100 to P1 (P2 = 400, C21 holds 100). t3, P1 decides to start a snapshot. I checked the whole run with a small Python simulation that plays these steps with FIFO queues.

Worked snapshot, the steps: At t3, P1 records its state, 800, and sends a marker on C12. C12 now holds 200 followed by the marker. P1 starts recording C21. At t4, P1 receives the 100 from C21; its balance becomes 900, and because it is recording C21, it notes 100 as part of C21's state. At t5, P2 receives the 200 from C12; its balance becomes 600. At t6, P2 receives the marker on C12. This is its first marker, so P2 records its state, 600, records C12 as empty, and sends a marker on C21. At t7, P1 receives that marker on C21 and stops recording it. C21's recorded state is the one message of 100 taka.

Worked snapshot, the result: The snapshot says P1 = 800, P2 = 600, C12 empty, C21 holding 100. Total: 800 + 600 + 100 = 1500 taka, exactly right. Notice why it works. The 200 left P1 before P1 recorded, so it is not in P1's 800, and it arrived at P2 before the marker on C12, so it is in P2's 600; counted once. The 100 left P2 before P2 recorded, so it is not in P2's 600, and it arrived at P1 after P1 recorded, so it is caught as in transit on C21; counted once. No money is created or lost.

A subtle point: Look at the real order of events. At no single real instant was the system in exactly the recorded state; at t4 P1 already had 900 before P2 had received its 200. Yet the recorded state is one the system could have been in: if the network had delivered the 200 slightly before the 100, the state P1 = 800, P2 = 600, with 100 in flight would have existed. Chandy and Lamport proved that the recorded state is always reachable from the starting state and the final state is reachable from it. That is good enough for every question about stable properties.

Stable properties and uses: A stable property is one that, once true, stays true forever: the computation has terminated, a set of processes is deadlocked, an object is garbage (no references anywhere and none in transit), a token is lost. If a snapshot shows a stable property is true, it is really true now; if it shows false, it was false at the snapshot. This makes snapshots the standard tool for termination detection, distributed garbage collection and deadlock detection. The other big use is checkpointing: save a consistent snapshot to disk, and after a crash restart everyone from it, without losing or double-counting messages. Stream processing engines use this idea; Apache Flink's checkpointing, for example, is based on a variant of Chandy-Lamport with markers called barriers. Fault Tolerant Systems (deep-cse-7-10) goes deeper into checkpoint and recovery.

Distributed deadlock detection, briefly: You met deadlock and wait-for graphs in Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1, lessons 16 and 17) and in DBMS (deep-cse-4-2, lesson 22). In a distributed database, transaction T1 on the Dhaka server may wait for T2 on the Chattogram server, which waits for T1. No single site sees the cycle. Collecting each site's local graph at different times can show a cycle that never existed, a phantom deadlock, which is exactly the inconsistent-cut problem again. Solutions include building the global wait-for graph from a consistent snapshot, or edge-chasing algorithms such as Chandy-Misra-Haas, where a blocked transaction sends a probe along wait-for edges and declares deadlock if the probe returns to it. Many real databases simply use timeouts instead.

Real-life example 1, end-of-day audit: A mobile wallet runs its ledger on several servers in Dhaka and Chattogram, and transfers between accounts on different servers travel as messages. Every night, finance must confirm that the sum of all balances plus money in transit equals the money held in partner bank accounts. Stopping all transfers for an audit is not acceptable, because people send money at midnight too. A Chandy-Lamport style snapshot lets the auditors record a consistent total while the system keeps serving customers. If the numbers do not match, the mismatch is real, not an artefact of when each server was photographed.

Real-life example 2, a streaming job that survives crashes: A ride-sharing company counts live ride requests per area of Dhaka (Mirpur, Uttara, Dhanmondi) to set surge pricing, using a streaming job spread over many machines. Every few seconds the source injects markers into the streams; each operator saves its counters when markers arrive, which yields a consistent checkpoint. When one machine crashes, the job restarts from the last checkpoint and replays input after it, so each ride request is counted once, not zero or two times.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting channel state; a snapshot of processes alone can lose money in transit. Second, recording a channel as "everything that arrives after the marker" instead of "between my recording and the marker on that channel". Third, forgetting that the algorithm needs FIFO channels; without FIFO the marker no longer separates before from after. Fourth, thinking the snapshot freezes the system; it runs alongside normal work. Fifth, claiming the recorded state actually existed at some instant; it is consistent and reachable, not necessarily historical.

What exams ask: Define consistent and inconsistent cuts and identify them on a diagram; spot orphan messages. State the marker sending and receiving rules and the assumptions. Trace Chandy-Lamport on a two- or three-process example with balances and show the total is preserved. Count markers, N(N-1) for a complete graph. Explain stable properties and why a snapshot can detect deadlock or termination, and what phantom deadlocks are.

Recap: A global state is every process's local state plus every channel's in-transit messages. A cut is consistent when it contains no orphan messages, meaning no receive without its send. Chandy-Lamport records such a state without stopping the system: record, send markers on all outgoing channels, record incoming channels until a marker arrives on each, assuming reliable FIFO channels. In our example the snapshot P1 = 800, P2 = 600, C21 = 100 preserves the 1500 taka total. Snapshots power checkpointing, termination and deadlock detection, and garbage collection. Next, lesson 12 uses messages and clocks to let processes take turns safely: distributed mutual exclusion.
key_points: A global state is the local state of every process plus the messages in transit on every channel.
A cut is consistent if every message received inside it was also sent inside it; a received-but-not-sent message is an orphan.
Chandy-Lamport (1985) records a consistent global state without stopping the system, assuming reliable FIFO channels and no failures.
Marker rules: on recording, send a marker on every outgoing channel; on the first marker, record and mark that channel empty; afterwards record each incoming channel until its marker arrives.
Worked example: P1 = 800, P2 = 600, C12 empty, C21 = 100, total 1500 taka, the same as at the start.
The recorded state may never have existed at one real instant, but it is reachable, which is enough for stable properties.
With N processes fully connected in both directions, a snapshot uses N(N-1) markers.
Uses: checkpointing and recovery, termination detection, deadlock detection without phantom deadlocks, distributed garbage collection.
lessons.tip: Treat every Chandy-Lamport question like bookkeeping: before you start, write the total money (or tokens) in the system, and after your trace add process states plus channel states. If the totals differ, you have recorded a channel wrongly, usually by including a message that arrived after the marker.
