lessons.task: Change the worked example so that P2 sends 300 to P1 instead of 100, and let P2 start the snapshot right after sending it. Trace the markers by hand, write down every process and channel state, and check that the total is still 1500 taka.

quiz.q: Which of these makes a cut inconsistent?
options: A message sent inside the cut and received outside it
Two processes recording at different real times
A process with no events inside the cut
A message received inside the cut whose send is outside the cut
quiz.explain: That is an orphan message: an effect is in the picture but its cause is not.

quiz.q: What is the first thing a process does when it receives its first marker in Chandy-Lamport?
options: Records its local state, marks that channel empty and sends markers on all outgoing channels
Discards all messages in the channel
Waits until all channels are empty
quiz.explain: The first marker triggers recording; the channel it came on is empty because FIFO means everything before the marker was already received.

quiz.q: Which assumption does the Chandy-Lamport algorithm need about channels?
options: Messages may arrive in any order
Channels must be synchronous with bounded delay
There must be only one channel in the system
quiz.explain: FIFO lets the marker separate messages sent before the sender recorded from those sent after.

quiz.q: In a system of 4 processes with a channel in each direction between every pair, how many markers does one snapshot send?
quiz.explain: One marker per directed channel: N(N-1) = 4 x 3 = 12.

quiz.q: Why can a snapshot reliably detect deadlock or termination?
options: They are stable properties, so if true in the recorded state they remain true
quiz.explain: A stable property stays true once true, and the snapshot state is consistent and reachable, so a detected deadlock is real.

lessons.title: Distributed Mutual Exclusion
lessons.content:
Think of the single washroom in a crowded Dhaka office with a broken lock. People hang a key on a hook: whoever holds it goes in. Now imagine the same washroom shared by people sitting in different buildings who can only talk by sending letters that may arrive late. Nobody can see the door. That is the problem of distributed mutual exclusion: making sure that at most one process at a time uses a shared resource when the processes live on different machines and can only communicate by messages.

Where this fits: In Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1, lessons 12 to 14) you met the critical section problem, race conditions, and tools like test-and-set, mutexes and semaphores. All of those rely on one shared variable in RAM. In a distributed system there is no shared memory and no global clock (lessons 01, 08 and 09 of this course), so a lock variable does not exist anywhere that everyone can see. We have to build mutual exclusion out of messages alone. This lesson uses Lamport timestamps from lesson 09, so keep that idea of (timestamp, process id) ordering in mind.

Requirements: Typical critical sections are updating a shared file or running a job that must run exactly once; the code looks like enter(); use the resource; exit(), and we must build enter() and exit() from messages. A correct algorithm must give three things. Safety: at most one process is inside the critical section at any time. Liveness: every request eventually gets in, so there is no deadlock and no starvation. Fairness (ordering): requests are served in the order they were made, usually meaning happened-before order or timestamp order. We also judge algorithms by three numbers: messages needed per entry and exit, synchronization delay (how long the next process waits after one leaves), and what happens when a process or message fails.

The centralized algorithm: The simplest idea copies the office key hook. Choose one process as coordinator. To enter, a process sends REQUEST to the coordinator. If nobody is inside, the coordinator replies GRANT. If someone is inside, the coordinator queues the request and sends nothing yet. When the process leaves, it sends RELEASE, and the coordinator grants the next queued request. One entry costs exactly 3 messages: request, grant, release. The waiting delay after a release is 2 message times (release travels to the coordinator, grant travels to the next process).

Centralized, good and bad: It is safe, fair (first come first served) and cheap. The weakness is the coordinator itself: it is a single point of failure and a possible bottleneck. Worse, a waiting process cannot tell the difference between "the coordinator is busy and has queued me" and "the coordinator is dead", because in both cases it simply hears nothing. The fix is an explicit "queued" reply plus electing a new coordinator (lesson 13) when it dies. In practice, real systems often use this centralized shape, but they make the coordinator itself fault tolerant by replicating it with consensus (lessons 18 and 19).

Lamport's distributed algorithm: Leslie Lamport showed in 1978 how to do mutual exclusion with no coordinator, using his logical clocks. To enter, process Pi sends REQUEST(ts, i) to all other N-1 processes and puts it in its own queue, ordered by (timestamp, id). Every receiver puts it in its queue and sends back a timestamped REPLY. Pi enters when its own request is at the head of its queue and it has received a message with a later timestamp from every other process. On exit, Pi sends RELEASE to all, and everyone removes its request. That is N-1 requests, N-1 replies and N-1 releases, so 3(N-1) messages per entry. It assumes FIFO, reliable channels.

Ricart and Agrawala's improvement: In 1981 Glenn Ricart and Ashok Agrawala noticed that the release message can be merged into the reply. The rule is: a process does not reply to a request until it is happy for the other one to go first. Each process is in one of three states: RELEASED (not interested), WANTED (has asked, waiting) or HELD (inside the critical section).

Ricart-Agrawala rules: To enter, Pi sets state = WANTED, records its request timestamp T = (Lamport time, i), and sends REQUEST(T) to all N-1 other processes. It enters when it has received N-1 OK replies. When Pj receives REQUEST(T) from Pi: if Pj is HELD, it defers the reply (stores it); if Pj is WANTED and its own request timestamp is smaller than T, it defers; otherwise it replies OK immediately. Comparing timestamps uses the pair (time, process id), so ties are broken by the smaller id and there are never two equal requests. On exit, Pj sets state = RELEASED and sends OK to every deferred request.

Worked trace, setup: Four processes P1, P2, P3 and P4. P3 and P4 are idle. At almost the same moment, P1 asks with timestamp (8, 1) and P2 asks with timestamp (12, 2). Each sends REQUEST to the other three, so 3 + 3 = 6 request messages are on the network.

Worked trace, replies: P3 and P4 are RELEASED, so they reply OK to both requests at once: 4 replies. P2 receives P1's request (8, 1). P2 is WANTED, but its own request (12, 2) is larger than (8, 1), so P1 has priority and P2 replies OK at once: 1 more reply. P1 receives P2's request (12, 2). P1 is WANTED with the smaller timestamp (8, 1), so P1 defers its reply to P2. Now P1 has OKs from P2, P3 and P4, which is all N-1 = 3, so P1 enters. P2 has OKs from only P3 and P4 and must wait.

Worked trace, exit: When P1 finishes, it sets its state to RELEASED and sends the deferred OK to P2. Now P2 has its third OK and enters. Count the messages: 6 requests plus 5 immediate replies plus 1 deferred reply = 12. That is two entries at 2(N-1) = 2 x 3 = 6 messages each, exactly as the formula says. P2 could not enter while P1 was inside, because P1 held back P2's last OK.

Why it is safe: Suppose P1 and P2 were both inside at once. Then each must have sent OK to the other while wanting. But the one with the larger timestamp replies, and the one with the smaller timestamp defers, and both compare the same two pairs and agree which is smaller. So one of them must have deferred, a contradiction. The Lamport clocks also give fairness: requests are granted in timestamp order, and a process that has waited long enough always has the smallest timestamp eventually, so there is no starvation.

Ricart-Agrawala, the cost: Message count improves to 2(N-1), and the synchronization delay is only one message time (the deferred OK). But look at failures: the algorithm needs a reply from every single other process. If any one process crashes, nobody can ever get N-1 OKs again. We replaced one point of failure with N points of failure. Also every process must know the full membership and handle the full load. It is mostly important as a teaching model.

The token ring algorithm: Arrange the processes in a logical ring, P1 to P2 to P3 and so on back to P1, regardless of physical location. A special message called the token circulates around the ring. A process may enter the critical section only while holding the token. If it does not want to enter, it simply passes the token to its neighbour. Safety is obvious, because there is only one token. There is no starvation either: the token visits everyone in turn, so each process waits at most one full trip.

Token ring, the cost: If a process wants to enter, it waits between 0 message times (it already has the token) and N-1 message times (the token just left). The message count per entry ranges from 1 to unbounded, because the token keeps circulating even when nobody wants it, which wastes messages in a quiet system. The failure problems are different: if the token is lost (the holder crashes or a message disappears), someone must detect the loss and create a new token without accidentally creating two. If any process crashes, the ring breaks and must be repaired by skipping the dead process, which requires every process to know the ring order.

Quorum-based voting, Maekawa's idea: Do we really need permission from everyone? Mamoru Maekawa (1985) observed that it is enough to get votes from a voting set, as long as any two voting sets overlap. A process that has given its vote cannot vote for anyone else until the vote comes back, so the shared member acts as a referee. A neat construction puts N = 16 processes in a 4 x 4 grid; the voting set of a process is its whole row plus its whole column, which is 4 + 4 - 1 = 7 processes. Any row-and-column set crosses any other, so every two sets share at least one process. Each process talks to about 2 sqrt(N) others instead of N-1. The basic version can deadlock and needs extra messages to fix that, so treat it as an idea here. The same "two sets must intersect" trick returns in quorum replication (lesson 15) and in Raft majorities (lesson 19).

Comparing the algorithms: Centralized: 3 messages per entry, delay 2 message times, fails if the coordinator crashes. Lamport: 3(N-1) messages, needs FIFO channels, fails if any process crashes. Ricart-Agrawala: 2(N-1) messages, delay 1 message time, fails if any process crashes. Token ring: 1 to unbounded messages, delay 0 to N-1, fails on lost token or broken ring. Surprisingly, centralized is cheapest, and distributed is not automatically more robust.

Real-world practice, lock services and leases: Production systems usually take the centralized idea and make the coordinator highly available, as a lock service built on consensus (ZooKeeper, etcd and Consul are well-known examples). A lock there is usually a lease: it is granted for a limited time, say 10 seconds, and the holder must renew it. If the holder crashes, the lease simply expires and someone else can take it, so a dead holder cannot block the system forever. There is a danger: a holder that pauses (for example during a long garbage collection) may still believe it holds the lock after its lease has expired. The usual fix is a fencing token: every grant carries an increasing number, and the storage server rejects any write that carries a number older than one it has already seen.

Real-life example 1, the daily settlement job: A mobile-wallet company in Dhaka runs three identical servers so that one can die without trouble. Every night at 00:30 a job must calculate the day's agent commissions exactly once. If all three servers run it, agents get paid three times. So each server tries to acquire a lease named "settlement-job" from the lock service. One wins, gets lease with fencing token 41, and runs the job; the others see the lock is taken and skip. If the winner crashes halfway, the lease expires, another server takes the lock with token 42, and the job (written to be safe to rerun) continues. Any late write from the old holder carrying token 41 is rejected.

Real-life example 2, the shared design file: Students of a BUET club keep a poster file on a shared storage server and edit it from different laptops. If two people edit at once, one person's changes overwrite the other's. A simple centralized lock fits well: the storage server is the coordinator, clicking "edit" sends a request, the server grants or queues it, and saving and closing releases it. Nobody needs Ricart-Agrawala here; one trusted server is simpler and good enough.

Common mistakes: Students often say "Ricart-Agrawala is more fault tolerant because it has no coordinator". It is the opposite: it needs replies from all N-1 processes, so any crash blocks it. Another mistake is comparing only Lamport times and forgetting the process-id tie-break; then two requests with equal timestamps would both defer forever or both go ahead. A third is forgetting that a lock held by a crashed process must be released somehow, which is why leases exist. Finally, mutual exclusion (who goes next) is not consensus (lesson 18: agreeing on one value), though lock services are built on consensus.

What exams ask: The three requirements, a Ricart-Agrawala trace with message count, why the token ring has no starvation, and the comparison table of messages, delay and failure problems.

Recap: Distributed mutual exclusion builds a lock out of messages because there is no shared memory. The centralized coordinator costs 3 messages and is simple but a single point of failure. Lamport's algorithm uses 3(N-1) messages, Ricart-Agrawala reduces it to 2(N-1) by deferring replies and breaking ties with (timestamp, id). Token ring passes a single token, so it is safe and starvation-free, but lost tokens and broken rings are trouble. Quorums need only overlapping voting sets. In real systems, a replicated lock service with leases and fencing tokens does the job. Next lesson: when the coordinator dies, how do the survivors pick a new one?
key_points: Distributed mutual exclusion must give safety (one at a time), liveness (no deadlock or starvation) and fair ordering, using messages only.
Centralized coordinator: request, grant, release = 3 messages per entry, but the coordinator is a single point of failure.
Lamport's algorithm uses timestamped requests to everyone, replies and releases: 3(N-1) messages, needs FIFO channels.
Ricart-Agrawala defers replies when it has a smaller (timestamp, id) or is inside: 2(N-1) messages per entry.
Worked: N = 4 with two concurrent requests (8,1) and (12,2) uses 6 + 5 + 1 = 12 messages; P1 goes first.
Token ring: only the token holder may enter; delay 0 to N-1, but lost tokens and crashed members break it.
Maekawa-style voting sets only need to overlap; a 4 x 4 grid gives sets of 7 instead of asking all 15 others.
In practice: a consensus-backed lock service with leases and increasing fencing tokens.
lessons.tip: Draw four circles for P1 to P4 on paper and act out Ricart-Agrawala with coins as messages. Write each request as a pair like (8, 1) and ask at every arrival: am I inside, or do I want it with a smaller pair? If yes, defer; if no, reply. After two rounds the algorithm becomes obvious, and the exam trace becomes easy.
lessons.task: Take N = 5 processes. P2 requests with (5, 2), P4 requests with (5, 4) and P5 requests with (7, 5) at about the same time. Using Ricart-Agrawala, write who defers whom, the order in which the three enter, and count the total messages (it should be 3 x 2(N-1) = 24). Then repeat the counting for the centralized algorithm and compare.

quiz.q: How many messages does the centralized mutual exclusion algorithm need per critical-section entry and exit?
quiz.explain: Request to the coordinator, grant back, release to the coordinator: 3 messages regardless of N.

quiz.q: In Ricart-Agrawala, Pj is WANTED with request (12, 2) and receives a request (8, 1). What does Pj do?
options: Defers the reply until it exits
Replies OK immediately because (8, 1) is smaller
quiz.explain: The request with the smaller (timestamp, id) has priority, so Pj replies at once and keeps waiting itself.

quiz.q: Why is Ricart-Agrawala NOT more fault tolerant than the centralized algorithm?
options: It needs replies from all N-1 processes, so any single crash can block everyone
It only works with a token
quiz.explain: Removing the coordinator spreads the risk: now every process is a point of failure.

quiz.q: In the token ring algorithm, how long can a process wait before it gets the token (in message times)?
quiz.explain: It may already hold the token (0), or the token may have just left, needing N-1 hops to come back.

quiz.q: What problem does a fencing token solve in a lease-based lock service?
options: It stops a paused old lock holder from writing after its lease has expired
It replaces the need for a lock service
quiz.explain: Each grant gets a larger number, so the storage rejects writes carrying an older token.

lessons.title: Election Algorithms
lessons.content:
In a class in Rajshahi, the class captain takes attendance, collects assignments and talks to the teacher. One morning the captain is absent. Within minutes someone has to take over, otherwise the attendance sheet goes nowhere. The students do not hold a long debate; they use a quick rule everyone already accepts, such as "the student with the highest roll number present becomes captain for today". Distributed systems face the same situation all the time. Many algorithms in this course use one special process, a coordinator or leader: the lock coordinator from lesson 12, the time master of the Berkeley algorithm (lesson 08), the primary replica (lesson 14), or the coordinator of two-phase commit (lesson 21). When that process crashes, the others must agree on a replacement. The algorithms that do this are called election algorithms.

What an election must achieve: At the end of an election, exactly one process is the coordinator, and every working process knows who it is. Formally we want safety (all processes that finish the election agree on the same leader, normally the live process with the largest identifier) and liveness (the election eventually finishes, as long as some processes are alive). It does not matter much which process wins; what matters is that everyone agrees.

The usual assumptions: Classic election algorithms assume that every process has a unique identifier, such as a number, and that processes know the identifiers of the others. The winner is normally the live process with the highest identifier, because that is a simple rule everyone can check. Failures are crash failures: a process either works correctly or stops completely; it does not lie (lying is Byzantine failure, lesson 20). Messages are reliable, and a process can detect a crash by a timeout, which quietly assumes we know an upper bound on message delay. Keep that last assumption in mind; it is where real trouble starts.

The bully algorithm: Hector Garcia-Molina described the bully algorithm in 1982. The name comes from its behaviour: the biggest process always wins and pushes smaller ones aside. There are three message types: ELECTION (I am starting an election), OK (also called ANSWER; I am alive and bigger than you, I will take over) and COORDINATOR (I am the new leader). When a process P notices that the coordinator is not responding, it starts an election.

Bully rules: Process P sends ELECTION to every process with a higher identifier. If nobody answers within the timeout, P wins: it sends COORDINATOR to all processes with lower identifiers. If some higher process answers OK, P's job is done; it simply waits for a COORDINATOR message (and restarts the election if none arrives in time). Any process that receives ELECTION from a smaller process replies OK and then starts its own election, if it has not already. In this way the election climbs up through the identifiers until it reaches the highest live process.

Bully, worked example: Six processes with identifiers 1 to 6. Process 6 was coordinator and has crashed. Process 3 notices first. Step 1: 3 sends ELECTION to 4, 5 and 6: 3 messages. Step 2: 4 and 5 are alive, so they reply OK: 2 messages. Process 3 stops; it will wait. Step 3: 4 starts its own election and sends ELECTION to 5 and 6: 2 messages. 5 replies OK: 1 message. Step 4: 5 starts its election and sends ELECTION to 6: 1 message. Nobody answers, because 6 is dead. Step 5: after the timeout, 5 announces itself by sending COORDINATOR to 1, 2, 3 and 4: 4 messages. Total: 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 13 messages, and process 5, the highest live identifier, is the new coordinator.

Bully, best and worst case: The best case is when the process just below the dead coordinator notices first. In our example that is process 5: one ELECTION to 6, a timeout, and 4 COORDINATOR messages, 5 messages in total; if it already knows 6 is the dead one it can skip the probe and send just N-2 = 4. The worst case is when the lowest process notices first: then every process starts an election towards everyone above it. With identifiers 1 to 6 and 6 dead, starting from process 1 gives 29 messages in our count, and in general the number grows with N squared, written O(N^2). For a few dozen machines this is fine; for thousands it is heavy.

Bully, when a process recovers: If a process with a high identifier comes back after a crash, it immediately starts an election. Since it is the biggest, nobody answers, and it sends COORDINATOR to everyone, taking the job from the current leader. That is the "bully" part. It keeps the rule simple (highest live identifier always leads), but it also causes extra leadership changes, which are expensive in real systems. Many modern systems avoid this by keeping a working leader instead of always handing over to the biggest.

The ring algorithm: Now arrange the processes in a logical ring, where each process knows its successor (and can skip a dead successor by trying the next one). In the version taught by Tanenbaum and van Steen, a process that notices the coordinator is dead creates an ELECTION message containing its own identifier and sends it to its successor. Each live process adds its own identifier to the list and passes it on. When the message comes back to the starter (it sees its own identifier in the list), the list contains every live process. The starter picks the highest identifier and sends a COORDINATOR message around the ring carrying the winner and the member list. When that message has gone around once, everyone knows the new leader.

Ring, worked example: Six live processes sit in this ring order: 3, 7, 2, 9, 5, 4, and then back to 3. The old coordinator (say 11) crashed and was skipped. Process 2 notices. It sends ELECTION [2] to 9; 9 makes it [2, 9] and sends to 5; then [2, 9, 5] to 4; then [2, 9, 5, 4] to 3; then [2, 9, 5, 4, 3] to 7; then [2, 9, 5, 4, 3, 7] back to 2. That is 6 messages. Process 2 sees the maximum is 9 and sends COORDINATOR(9) around the ring: 6 more messages. Total 12, which is 2N for N = 6. If two processes start elections at the same time, two messages circulate, both produce the same list, and both announce the same winner; extra messages, same result.

Chang and Roberts, a cheaper ring: Ernest Chang and Rosemary Roberts (1979) improved the ring idea. Instead of carrying a full list, the message carries only one number, the largest identifier seen so far. A process forwards the message if the number is larger than its own identifier, replaces it with its own identifier if its own is larger, and drops it if it has already sent a larger one. When a process receives its own identifier back, it knows it is the maximum and announces itself. In our ring with process 2 starting: 2 sends 2 to 9, 9 replaces it with 9, and the 9 travels through 5, 4, 3, 7 and 2 back to 9: 7 election messages, then 6 elected messages, 13 in total. With one starter, the cost lies between 2N and 3N - 1 messages, depending on where the maximum sits. If everyone starts at once and identifiers are arranged badly, it can reach O(N^2), but for random arrangements the average is O(N log N). A later bidirectional algorithm by Hirschberg and Sinclair guarantees O(N log N) even in the worst case.

Comparing bully and ring: Bully needs every process to know every identifier and to talk to all of them directly, but it finishes in a few message rounds. Ring only needs each process to know its neighbours, its message count is linear for a single starter, but its time is also linear, because the message must travel around the whole ring, twice. Both assume crash failures, reliable messages and timeouts that are accurate.

Elections in wireless and large systems: In a network of battery-powered sensors or phones, links come and go and there is no neat ring or full membership. Algorithms here typically build a spanning tree by flooding an election message outwards and collecting the best candidate back towards the starter, where "best" may mean most battery or best connection rather than biggest identifier. In very large peer-to-peer systems, elections usually pick several super peers rather than one leader. We only mention these ideas; Fault Tolerant Systems (deep-cse-7-10) goes further.

The big danger, split brain: The algorithms above trust timeouts. But in a real network a slow process and a dead process look the same: both are silent. Suppose the network between two data centers breaks. Each side times out the other, and each side elects its own leader. Now there are two leaders, both accepting writes, and their data drifts apart. This is called split brain, and it can corrupt data badly. Bully and ring, as stated, do nothing to stop it, because they assume the timeout is never wrong.

How real systems avoid split brain: Three ideas help. First, majority quorums: a leader must be voted in by more than half of all processes, and since two majorities always overlap (the same "sets must intersect" idea as lesson 12), there cannot be two leaders chosen in the same round. Second, leader leases: a leader only acts while its lease from a majority is valid, and the old leader stops before a new one can start. Third, terms or epochs with fencing: every new leader gets a higher term number, and other nodes reject commands from an older term. Raft (lesson 19) combines these with randomized timeouts, and that is how etcd- or Consul-style systems elect leaders today.

Real-life example 1, dispatch servers: Imagine a ride-sharing company in Dhaka with five dispatch servers in one data center. One of them is leader and batches trip requests into driver assignments every two seconds; the others stand by. The leader's power supply fails. Within a few seconds the followers notice missing heartbeats and run an election. With a simple bully rule, the highest identifier wins and starts matching drivers again. Customers in Gulshan might see a few seconds of delay, not hours. If the company also replicates the trip state with a consensus protocol, the new leader continues exactly where the old one stopped.

Real-life example 2, sensors in a garment factory: A garment factory in Gazipur installs battery-powered temperature sensors across its floors. One sensor acts as the gateway that collects readings and sends them to the internet. When that gateway's battery dies, the others run a wireless election, flooding a message and choosing the sensor with the most battery left and a good link, and that sensor becomes the new gateway. Here the "best" candidate is chosen by a measured value, not by the largest identifier.

Common mistakes: In bully, students often forget that a process receiving OK stops and waits; it does not keep sending messages. They also forget that ELECTION goes only to higher identifiers and COORDINATOR only to lower ones. In the ring algorithm, students forget the second trip around the ring for the COORDINATOR message. Another mistake is saying the bully algorithm is safe in any network; it is only safe when timeouts are reliable, which is not true across real networks with partitions. Finally, remember that "highest identifier" is a convention, not a law.

What exams ask: Trace the bully algorithm for a given set of identifiers and count messages, explain best and worst cases, trace the ring algorithm and count 2N messages, compare the two, and explain why timeouts can cause two leaders and how majority voting prevents it.

Recap: Elections pick one coordinator that everyone agrees on, usually the highest live identifier. Bully sends ELECTION upwards, OK back down and COORDINATOR to everyone smaller; our example cost 13 messages, with O(N^2) in the worst case. The ring algorithm collects identifiers in one round trip and announces the winner in a second, 2N messages; Chang-Roberts carries only the maximum. All of these rely on accurate timeouts, so real systems add majorities, leases and terms to prevent split brain, which leads us to Raft in lesson 19.
key_points: An election picks exactly one coordinator that all live processes agree on, usually the highest live identifier.
Classic assumptions: unique ids, known membership, crash failures only, reliable messages and accurate timeouts.
Bully: ELECTION to higher ids, OK replies from live higher ids, winner sends COORDINATOR to lower ids.
Worked bully with ids 1 to 6, 6 dead and 3 starting: 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 13 messages, 5 wins; worst case O(N^2).
Ring: ELECTION collects ids around the ring, then COORDINATOR goes around again: 2N messages (12 for N = 6).
Chang-Roberts carries only the maximum id; one starter costs between 2N and 3N - 1 messages.
Timeouts cannot tell slow from dead, so partitions can create two leaders (split brain).
Majority votes, leases and increasing terms prevent split brain; Raft uses them (lesson 19).
lessons.tip: Practice with your friends: give each person a roll number, make the 'captain' leave the room, and run the bully algorithm out loud, counting every message on the board. Then sit in a circle and run the ring version passing a paper list. Physically doing it makes message counting in exams almost automatic.
lessons.task: Take processes with identifiers 1 to 8, where 8 has crashed. Count the bully messages if process 6 starts the election, and again if process 2 starts it. Then place the same seven live processes in a ring in the order 4, 1, 7, 3, 6, 2, 5 and count the messages for the Tanenbaum ring algorithm started by process 3. Check your counts with a short Python loop.

quiz.q: In the bully algorithm, to whom does a process send its ELECTION message?
options: Only to processes with higher identifiers
quiz.explain: It asks bigger processes if they are alive; if none answers, it becomes coordinator itself.

quiz.q: Ids 1 to 6, process 6 dead, process 3 starts a bully election. How many messages in total, using the count from the lesson?
quiz.explain: 3 ELECTION from 3, 2 OK, 2 ELECTION from 4, 1 OK, 1 ELECTION from 5, then 4 COORDINATOR: 13.

quiz.q: In the Tanenbaum ring algorithm with N live processes and one starter, how many messages are sent?
quiz.explain: N messages to collect the list around the ring, and N more to circulate the COORDINATOR message.

quiz.q: What is split brain?
options: Two processes both believe they are leader, usually after a network partition
A ring with two tokens in mutual exclusion only
A leader with a broken disk
quiz.explain: Each side of a partition times out the other and elects its own leader, so writes diverge.

quiz.q: Which idea prevents two leaders in the same term?
options: Requiring votes from a majority, since two majorities always overlap
quiz.explain: A voter votes once per term, and any two majorities share a voter, so only one leader can get a majority.

lessons.title: Replication I: Why Replicate, Primary-Backup and Multi-Leader
lessons.content:
Every Bangladeshi student knows this habit: before submitting the original certificate for admission, you make photocopies, keep one at home, one in your bag and one with your father. If one copy is lost, the others save you. But the habit has a cost. If you later correct a spelling mistake on the original, every copy must be corrected too, or you will have papers that disagree. Distributed systems keep copies of data for the same reasons and face exactly the same cost. Keeping copies of the same data on several machines is called replication, and the copies are called replicas.

Where this fits: You have met copies before: caches in Computer Architecture, RAID 1 mirroring in Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1, lesson 23), and replication as a NoSQL feature in DBMS (deep-cse-4-2, lesson 24). Here we study replication properly across machines connected by an unreliable network. This lesson covers why we replicate and the two designs where writes go through leaders: single leader (primary-backup) and multi-leader. Lesson 15 covers leaderless replication and quorums, lesson 16 the consistency models that describe what readers can see, and lessons 18 and 19 the consensus protocols used to replicate safely.

Reason 1, availability: If one machine is up 99 percent of the time, it is down 1 percent, which is about 87.6 hours per year (0.01 x 8,760 hours). Put the same data on three machines that fail independently, and the data is unavailable only when all three are down at once: 0.01 x 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.000001. So the availability for reads becomes 1 - 0.01^3 = 0.999999, "six nines", about 31.5 seconds of total outage per year. Two replicas give 1 - 0.01^2 = 0.9999. That is the power of replication.

The catch in the availability math: That calculation has two hidden assumptions. First, failures must really be independent. Three replicas in the same rack share one power strip and one switch; three replicas in one building share one flood. That is why replicas are placed in different racks, and important data in different data centers, for example one in Dhaka and one in Chattogram. Second, it only counts operations that need just one replica. If a write must reach all three replicas before it succeeds, the write needs all three up at once: 0.99 x 0.99 x 0.99 = 0.970299, so writes become less available than a single machine. Replication helps availability only when operations need some of the replicas, not all of them. Keep this in mind for quorums in lesson 15.

Reason 2, performance: Replicas let you spread load. If one database server can answer 5,000 reads per second and you have four read replicas, you can serve around 20,000 reads per second, because reads can go to any copy. Replicas also reduce distance: a user in Chattogram can read from a Chattogram copy instead of waiting for a round trip to Dhaka. This is the same idea as a CDN (lesson 25).

The cost, consistency: As soon as there are copies, a write must reach every copy, and while it is travelling some copies are new and some are old. A reader may see the old value. Every replication design is a choice about when copies are updated and what readers are allowed to see in between. Faster usually means less consistent, and more consistent usually means slower or less available. That trade-off runs through lessons 14 to 17.

Replica placement: Tanenbaum and van Steen describe three kinds of replicas. Permanent replicas are the planned copies, such as three database servers in different racks. Server-initiated replicas are created dynamically when a region becomes busy, such as copying a popular video to an edge server. Client-initiated replicas are caches kept by or near the client, such as your browser cache. Deciding where to place servers is itself an optimization problem: put copies close to where users are and where failures are unlikely to coincide.

Primary-backup, the idea: The most common design is single-leader replication, also called primary-backup, master-slave in older texts, or leader-follower. One replica is the primary (leader). All writes go to it. The primary applies each write locally, records it in a replication log, and sends the log to the backups (followers), which apply the same changes in the same order. Reads may go to the primary, or to any follower if slightly old data is acceptable. Because only one node orders the writes, there are never two conflicting versions of the same record; the order the primary chooses is the order everyone follows.

Synchronous replication: In synchronous mode the primary waits until a follower confirms it has stored the write before telling the client "done". Worked example: the primary is in Dhaka, and a synchronous follower is in Chattogram. Suppose the local write takes 2 ms and the Dhaka-Chattogram round trip is 8 ms (an assumed figure for the example). A synchronous write then takes about 2 + 8 = 10 ms. The benefit: if the primary dies right after replying, the follower definitely has the write, so nothing confirmed is ever lost. The problem: if the follower is down or the link is slow, every write waits or fails.

Asynchronous replication: In asynchronous mode the primary replies "done" right after its local write (about 2 ms in our example) and ships the change to followers in the background. Writes are fast and keep working even when followers are down. The risk: if the primary dies before a write has reached any follower, that write is lost even though the client was told it succeeded. For a photo like on a social app, that might be acceptable; for a money transfer, it is not.

Semi-synchronous replication: A common middle path is to make one follower synchronous and the rest asynchronous. Every confirmed write is on at least two machines, but a slow asynchronous follower does not slow down writes. If the synchronous follower fails, one of the asynchronous followers is promoted to be synchronous. Many relational databases offer options along these lines; the names differ by product.

Replication lag and its anomalies: With asynchronous followers, a follower may be behind the primary by milliseconds normally, or by seconds or minutes when overloaded. This delay is replication lag, and it causes visible oddities. Read-your-writes failure: you update your profile photo, the app then reads from a lagging follower, and your old photo comes back, so you think the update failed. Monotonic reads failure: you refresh twice, the first refresh hits an up-to-date follower and shows a new comment, the second hits a lagging follower and the comment vanishes. Lesson 16 gives these guarantees names and shows how to provide them, for example by reading your own data from the primary for a short time after you write it.

Failover: When the primary dies, the system must make a follower the new primary. That involves three steps: detect the failure, usually by timeout (lesson 20); choose the new primary, ideally the follower with the most up-to-date log, by an election (lesson 13) or by consensus (lesson 19); and reconfigure clients and other followers to send writes to the new primary. Each step can go wrong. With asynchronous replication, writes the old primary had not yet shipped are lost. A timeout that is too short causes unnecessary failovers during a brief slowdown. And if the old primary was only slow, not dead, it may come back still believing it is the primary.

Fencing the old primary: Two primaries accepting writes is split brain (lesson 13), and it can corrupt data. Systems prevent it by fencing: the new primary gets a higher epoch or term number and storage rejects writes with an older number, or the old node is forcibly cut off from storage or power. The blunt version has the memorable name STONITH, "shoot the other node in the head". The cleaner version is to let a consensus protocol decide who the primary is, which is why consensus (lessons 18 and 19) sits underneath many replicated databases.

How the log is shipped: There are three common ways. Statement-based replication sends the SQL statements themselves, but statements like NOW() or RAND() would produce different values on each replica, so they must be replaced with fixed values first. Write-ahead log shipping sends the low-level log the database already writes for crash recovery (deep-cse-4-2, lesson 23); it is exact but tied to the storage format, so primary and followers usually need the same software version. Logical (row-based) logs describe changes per row, such as "row with id 42 now has balance 900"; they are independent of storage internals and can also feed other systems, which is the idea behind change data capture.

Multi-leader replication: Single leader means every write in the country must travel to one place. If the primary is in Dhaka, writes from Chattogram always pay the round trip, and if the Dhaka-Chattogram link breaks, Chattogram cannot write at all. Multi-leader replication puts a leader in each data center. Each leader accepts local writes quickly and replicates them asynchronously to the other leaders. Writes stay fast and keep working during a link failure. Mobile apps that work offline, like a notes app that syncs later, are also multi-leader systems in disguise: each phone is a leader for its own local copy.

The price, write conflicts: Now two leaders can accept conflicting writes to the same record. A small online shop sets the price of a sari to 500 taka through the Dhaka leader, and at the same moment a manager in Chattogram sets it to 520 through the Chattogram leader. Both succeed locally. When the leaders exchange changes, each sees a different value. A conflict exists, and it must be resolved so that both data centers converge to the same value.

Resolving conflicts: Last-writer-wins (LWW) attaches a timestamp to each write and keeps the one with the larger timestamp. It is simple and converges, but it silently throws away the other write, and with clock skew (lesson 08) the "later" write may actually be the earlier one. Merging keeps both: for a shopping cart, take the union of items. Vector clocks (lesson 10) tell us when two writes are concurrent and therefore need merging. Application-defined resolution stores both versions and asks the user or custom code to decide, like a "conflicting copy" file in a sync folder. Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) are data structures designed so that concurrent updates always merge automatically. The simplest is a grow-only counter: each replica keeps its own count, the value is the sum, and merging takes the maximum per replica. If the Dhaka replica has counted 5 likes and Chattogram 3, the merged counter is {Dhaka: 5, Chattogram: 3}, value 8, and merging again changes nothing.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet ledger: A wallet service in Bangladesh keeps its account ledger on a primary database in a Dhaka data center, with a synchronous follower in a second Dhaka facility and an asynchronous follower in Chattogram. A transfer is confirmed only when two machines have it, so a single crash loses nothing. Balance-check screens can read from followers, while the transfer itself reads from the primary. If the primary fails, the most up-to-date follower is promoted by the consensus-backed control system and the old primary is fenced. Money never lives on a multi-leader design here, because conflicts in balances are not acceptable.

Real-life example 2, a news portal on election night: A Bangla news website has one primary for editors and many read replicas for readers. On election result night, traffic jumps many times. The portal adds more read replicas to absorb it, and asynchronous lag of a second or two is fine, because a reader seeing an update one second late hurts nobody. Editors always read from the primary so they see their own changes immediately.

Common mistakes: Multiplying availabilities without checking independence. Forgetting that requiring all replicas for writes reduces write availability. Saying asynchronous replication cannot lose data; it can, at failover. Thinking multi-leader is simply "better" because it is faster; it buys speed with conflicts. Trusting last-writer-wins without realizing it discards data and depends on clocks.

What exams ask: Reasons for replication, availability with k replicas, synchronous vs asynchronous with advantages and disadvantages, replication lag anomalies, failover steps and split brain, statement vs log shipping, multi-leader conflicts and ways to resolve them.

Recap: Replication copies data for availability and performance, but every copy creates a consistency problem. With independent failures, three 99 percent replicas give 99.9999 percent read availability. Primary-backup orders all writes at one leader; synchronous replication protects confirmed writes at the cost of latency, asynchronous is fast but may lose recent writes, and semi-synchronous sits in between. Failover needs detection, a careful choice and fencing. Multi-leader keeps writes local and fast but creates conflicts, resolved by LWW, merging, application logic or CRDTs. Next, lesson 15 removes the leader entirely.
key_points: Replication keeps copies of data on several machines for availability and performance; the cost is keeping copies consistent.
With independent failures, three replicas at 99 percent each give 1 - 0.01^3 = 99.9999 percent read availability.
If a write needs all three replicas, write availability drops to 0.99^3 = 97.03 percent.
Primary-backup: one leader orders all writes and ships a replication log to followers.
Synchronous replication never loses confirmed writes but adds latency; asynchronous is fast but can lose recent writes at failover.
Replication lag causes read-your-writes and monotonic-read anomalies; failover needs detection, choice and fencing against split brain.
Multi-leader keeps writes local and fast but needs conflict resolution: last-writer-wins, merge, application logic or CRDTs.
lessons.tip: When you meet any replication design, ask three questions: who accepts writes, when is the client told 'done', and what happens to a write that is in flight when a machine dies. Those three answers explain almost every trade-off in this lesson and in the next three.
lessons.task: Assume each server is up 98 percent of the time and failures are independent. Calculate the read availability with 1, 2 and 3 replicas, and the write availability if every write must reach all replicas. Convert each result to hours of downtime per year (8,760 hours) and write one sentence on what the numbers teach you.

quiz.q: Three replicas each have 99 percent availability and fail independently. What is the availability for reads that need any one replica?
quiz.explain: Data is unavailable only if all three fail: 0.01^3 = 0.000001, so availability is 1 - 0.000001.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of asynchronous primary-backup replication?
options: Writes the client was told succeeded can be lost if the primary dies before shipping them
Every write must wait for all followers
quiz.explain: The primary replies before followers have the write, so a crash at the wrong moment loses it.

quiz.q: You update your profile photo, refresh, and see the old photo because you read from a lagging follower. Which guarantee is violated?
quiz.explain: Read-your-writes promises a user always sees their own earlier updates.

quiz.q: Why do systems fence the old primary after failover?
options: To stop two primaries from accepting writes at the same time (split brain)
quiz.explain: An old primary that was only slow may return; fencing with a higher term or cutting it off prevents conflicting writes.

quiz.q: What is a drawback of last-writer-wins conflict resolution in multi-leader replication?
options: It silently discards one of the concurrent writes and depends on clocks
It needs a human for every conflict
It only works with one leader
quiz.explain: LWW keeps the larger timestamp; the other write is lost, and clock skew can pick the wrong one.

lessons.title: Replication II: Leaderless Replication and Quorums
lessons.content:
Suppose you want to know whether tomorrow's class test at your university in Sylhet is cancelled. You message three friends. Two reply quickly; the third is asleep. If at least one of the two replies comes from a friend who heard the latest announcement, you will know the truth. Now suppose the class representative, when the test was cancelled, made sure that at least two of those three friends were told. Then whichever two friends you ask, at least one of them knows. That small piece of counting is the whole idea of quorums, and it lets a replicated system work without any leader at all.

Where this fits: Lesson 14 showed single-leader and multi-leader replication, where some leader orders the writes. This lesson removes the leader. In leaderless replication, any replica can accept a write, and clients (or a coordinator node acting for them) talk to several replicas in parallel. The design became widely known through Amazon's Dynamo paper (2007), and several open-source databases, such as Cassandra and Riak, adopted similar ideas. Lesson 16 will name the consistency guarantees involved, and lesson 22 shows how keys are spread over many nodes with consistent hashing; here we look at one key and its N replicas.

The three numbers: Each key is stored on N replicas. A write is sent to all N replicas, and the client considers it successful once W of them acknowledge. A read is sent to the replicas, and the client waits for R replies. Every stored value carries a version number (or a richer version vector, lesson 10), so when the replies differ, the client can tell which one is newer. N, W and R are configuration choices, sometimes even set per request.

The quorum condition: If R + W > N, then every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica. The reason is simple counting: a write touched W replicas and a read touches R; if they had no replica in common, there would have to be at least W + R distinct replicas, but only N exist, and W + R > N. More precisely, they share at least R + W - N replicas. When they overlap, at least one reply in every read carries the latest successful write, and the version number lets the client pick it.

Worked example, N = 3, W = 2, R = 2: Replicas A, B and C all hold the value "Dhanmondi" with version 1. A user updates their delivery address to "Mirpur", version 2. The write is sent to all three; A and B acknowledge, but C is briefly unreachable and misses it. Since W = 2 acks arrived, the write succeeds. Now another request reads with R = 2. The possible read sets are {A, B}, {A, C} and {B, C}. {A, B} gives version 2 twice. {A, C} gives version 2 and version 1. {B, C} gives version 2 and version 1. In every case at least one reply has version 2, so the client returns "Mirpur". Check the formula: R + W = 4 > 3, and the overlap is at least 4 - 3 = 1. We verified all three cases with a tiny script.

Worked counterexample, N = 3, W = 1, R = 1: Now R + W = 2, which is not greater than 3. The write "Mirpur" might be acknowledged only by A. A later read might be answered only by C, which still says "Dhanmondi". The read and write sets do not overlap, and the user gets the old address. This setting is very fast and very available, but it gives no guarantee of seeing the latest write.

What each choice favours: With N = 3, W = 3 and R = 1, reads are fast (one reply is enough) but a write fails if even one replica is down. With W = 1 and R = 3, writes are fast and very available but reads need everyone. The balanced choice uses majorities: W = R = 2 for N = 3, or W = R = 3 for N = 5. A useful rule: writes still succeed when up to N - W replicas are unavailable, and reads when up to N - R are. So N = 3, W = R = 2 tolerates 1 unavailable replica for both; N = 5, W = R = 3 tolerates 2. A setting like N = 5, W = 2, R = 3 gives R + W = 5, not greater than 5, so a read and a write can miss each other completely.

Picking the newest reply: The client needs to know which reply is newer. With a single version counter per key, the larger number wins. But in a leaderless system two clients may write the same key at the same time through different replicas; neither write happened before the other. Version vectors (lesson 10) detect this: if neither vector dominates, the values are concurrent "siblings", and the database either keeps both for the application to merge (like the shopping cart of lesson 14) or applies a rule such as last-writer-wins.

Read repair: When a read notices a stale replica, it can fix it on the spot. In our example, if the read set was {B, C}, the client saw version 2 from B and version 1 from C, so it writes version 2 back to C. Over time, frequently read keys become consistent everywhere. Keys that are rarely read are not repaired this way, which is why a second mechanism is needed.

Anti-entropy with Merkle trees: A background process regularly compares replicas and copies missing data. Comparing every key would mean sending huge amounts of data, so replicas build a Merkle tree: each leaf is a hash of one range of keys, and each parent is a hash of its children (hashes are from Computer Security, deep-cse-6-2, lesson 15). Two replicas first compare their root hashes. If the roots match, everything matches and they are done. If not, they compare the children and descend only into branches whose hashes differ. With 8 key ranges and only one range different, they compare the root, then 2 children, then 2 grandchildren, then 2 leaves, and transfer just that one range instead of all 8.

Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff: Suppose the 3 home replicas of a key are A, B and C, and a network problem makes B and C unreachable from the client, while other nodes D and E are reachable. A strict quorum write with W = 2 would fail. A sloppy quorum accepts the write on A and on D, even though D is not a home replica for that key. D stores it with a hint saying "this belongs to B". When B comes back, D hands the write over, which is called hinted handoff. Sloppy quorums improve write availability, but notice what they break: a later read from B and C may not overlap with A and D at all, so R + W > N no longer guarantees seeing the latest write until the handoff completes.

Last-writer-wins and clock skew: Many leaderless stores resolve concurrent writes with last-writer-wins, using a timestamp from a client or node clock. Clocks drift (lesson 08). Worked example: client 1 writes "Mirpur" at true time 10:00:00 through a node whose clock is 3 seconds fast, so the write is stamped 10:00:03. Client 2 writes "Uttara" two seconds later, at true time 10:00:02, through a node with an accurate clock, stamped 10:00:02. Last-writer-wins keeps "Mirpur", the older write, and silently discards "Uttara". No error is shown to anyone. Data is lost purely because of clock skew.

When quorums still return stale data: R + W > N is necessary but not a complete guarantee. Stale reads can still happen when a sloppy quorum was used; when a write and a read run concurrently, so the write has reached some replicas but not others and different readers may see different results; when a write succeeded on fewer than W replicas and was reported as failed, but was not rolled back on the replicas that did store it, so later reads may or may not see it; when a replica holding the new value fails and is restored from an older copy, so fewer than W replicas now hold it; and when clock-based last-writer-wins drops a write. That is why quorum systems usually offer eventual consistency with good odds rather than linearizability (lesson 16). Getting linearizable behaviour needs extra work, such as consensus (lessons 18 and 19).

Monitoring staleness: In leader-based systems you can measure replication lag directly (how far a follower's log position is behind the leader). In leaderless systems there is no single log, so it is harder; operators often estimate how stale reads tend to be from measurements. If a system promises "eventually", it is still wise to know how long "eventually" usually takes.

Real-life example 1, a flash-sale shopping cart: A Bangladeshi e-commerce site runs a big 11.11-style sale. Millions of "add to cart" clicks arrive, and the company decides it would rather accept every click than reject any because a replica is slow. Carts are stored with N = 3, W = 2, R = 2, plus sloppy quorums during node trouble. If two devices of the same customer add items concurrently, the version vectors show two siblings and the application merges them by taking the union of items. The worst case is that a removed item reappears, which the customer can delete again; that is acceptable for a cart, never for a payment.

Real-life example 2, driver locations in a ride-sharing app: Every driver's phone sends its location every few seconds. The newest location matters, but a slightly old one is not a disaster, and a new update will arrive soon anyway. The company stores locations with N = 3, W = 1, R = 1 for speed: each update just needs one replica, and a read takes the first answer. Occasionally a rider in Banani sees a car icon a few metres behind reality. The trade-off is deliberate: fast and highly available, with weak consistency where it hurts nobody.

Common mistakes: Writing R + W >= N instead of R + W > N; with N = 4, W = 2, R = 2 the sets can be disjoint. Believing that R + W > N alone gives strong consistency; the list above shows why not. Forgetting that W = N makes writes fragile. Mixing up N (replicas per key) with the total number of servers in the cluster; a cluster of 100 servers might still use N = 3 per key. Forgetting that the client needs version numbers or vectors to know which reply is newest.

What exams ask: Prove that R + W > N forces overlap, compute the minimum overlap R + W - N, decide whether given values of N, W and R guarantee overlap, compute how many failures reads and writes tolerate, explain read repair, anti-entropy and Merkle trees, explain sloppy quorums and hinted handoff, and give scenarios where quorums return stale data.

Recap: Leaderless replication sends writes to N replicas and waits for W acks, and reads from replicas waiting for R replies. If R + W > N, every read overlaps every write by at least R + W - N replicas, so with version numbers the latest successful write is visible; N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 is the classic setting. Read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy bring stale replicas up to date. Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff raise availability but weaken the overlap, and last-writer-wins with skewed clocks can silently lose data. Next we give names to all these guarantees: consistency models.
key_points: Leaderless replication: any replica accepts writes; a write needs W acks out of N replicas and a read needs R replies.
If R + W > N, every read set and write set share at least R + W - N replicas.
Worked: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 always overlaps in at least one replica, so a read sees the newest version.
Writes tolerate N - W unavailable replicas and reads N - R; majorities balance both.
Version numbers or version vectors tell which reply is newer and detect concurrent siblings.
Read repair fixes stale replicas during reads; anti-entropy with Merkle trees fixes the rest in the background.
Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff improve availability but break the overlap guarantee until handoff.
Quorums can still return stale data (concurrent writes, failed partial writes, restores, LWW clock skew), so they are not linearizable by default.
lessons.tip: For any quorum question, draw N boxes, shade W of them for the write, and try to place R read boxes so that none is shaded. If you cannot, the quorum overlaps. This picture proves R + W > N faster than any formula and helps you spot tricky counterexamples.
lessons.task: Write a short Python script using itertools.combinations that, for a given N, W and R, checks whether every write set intersects every read set. Run it for (N, W, R) = (3, 2, 2), (4, 2, 2), (4, 3, 2), (5, 3, 3) and (5, 2, 3), and compare the results with the rule R + W > N.

quiz.q: With N = 3 replicas, which setting guarantees that every read overlaps the latest successful write?
quiz.explain: Only W = 2, R = 2 satisfies R + W = 4 > 3; the others sum to 3 or less.

quiz.q: With N = 5, W = 3, R = 3, how many unavailable replicas can a write tolerate?
quiz.explain: A write needs 3 acks out of 5, so up to 5 - 3 = 2 replicas may be down.

quiz.q: What is read repair?
options: When a read sees a stale replica, it writes the newer value back to that replica
Rebuilding a crashed disk from backup
Retrying a read until all N replicas answer
Choosing a new leader after a read fails
quiz.explain: The reader already holds the newest version, so it updates any replica that replied with an older one.

quiz.q: Why can a sloppy quorum return stale data even when R + W > N?
options: The write may have landed on substitute nodes outside the key's home replicas, so a read of the home replicas need not overlap it
quiz.explain: Hinted writes sit on other nodes until handoff, so the counting argument over the same N replicas no longer holds.

quiz.q: A node with a clock 3 seconds fast stamps an earlier write 10:00:03; a later write is stamped 10:00:02. What does last-writer-wins do?
options: Reports a conflict to the user
Keeps the earlier write and silently discards the later one
quiz.explain: LWW compares timestamps only, so the skewed clock makes the older write look newer.

lessons.title: Consistency Models
lessons.content:
Imagine your family has a shared notice board app for the monthly bazar list. Your mother, in Mirpur, adds "2 kg rice". A second later your brother, in Uttara, opens the app and sees no rice on the list. He adds "2 kg rice" too, and now the family buys 4 kg. Nobody's phone was broken. The app simply had several copies of the list on different servers, and your brother read a copy that had not heard about your mother's change yet. Was that a bug or was it allowed? The answer depends on one promise the system makes to you. That promise is called a consistency model, and it is the topic of this lesson.

What a consistency model is: In lessons 14 and 15 we copied data onto several replicas for availability and speed. The moment there is more than one copy, a reader can ask "which value will I see?" A consistency model is a contract between the data store and its users. It says which values a read is allowed to return, given the writes that happened before or during it. A stronger model allows fewer surprising results and is easier to program against. A weaker model allows more surprises but lets replicas answer faster and keep working during network trouble. There is no free lunch: every step towards stronger consistency usually costs latency or availability, which is exactly what lesson 17 on CAP and PACELC will make precise.

Two families of models: Textbooks split models into two groups. Data-centric models describe what all processes together may observe about a shared data item, as if you were looking at the whole system from above. Client-centric models describe what one single client is guaranteed to see as it moves around between replicas, for example a phone that talks to the Dhaka server in the morning and the Chattogram server in the evening. We will start from the strongest data-centric model and walk down, then finish with the client-centric guarantees.

Notation we will use: We write W(x)1 for "write value 1 into item x" and R(x)1 for "a read of x returned 1". Each operation takes some real time: it starts when the client sends the request and ends when the client gets the answer. Two operations overlap if neither finished before the other started. All our examples use one register x that starts at 0.

Strict consistency, the ideal: Under strict consistency every read returns the value of the most recent write in absolute global time. If Rahim writes x = 1 at 10:00:00.000 and Karim reads at 10:00:00.001 on a server in another city, Karim must see 1. This needs a perfect global clock and instant message delivery. Lesson 08 showed that clocks always drift and lesson 02 reminded us that latency is never zero, so strict consistency is impossible to build across machines. We keep it only as the yardstick that real models are measured against.

Linearizability, the realistic strongest model: Linearizability (Herlihy and Wing, 1990) relaxes strictness just enough to be buildable. Each operation is imagined to take effect at one single instant, called its linearization point, somewhere between its start and its end. The system is linearizable if we can pick such points so that the resulting single order is legal (every read returns the latest write before it in that order) and respects real time: if operation A finished before operation B started, A must come first. The effect for the programmer is the single-copy illusion. However many replicas exist, the data behaves as if there were only one copy and every operation hit it atomically.

Worked linearizability check: Client A performs W(x)1 from time 1 to time 4. Client B performs a read from time 2 to time 3. Client C performs a read from time 5 to time 6. B overlaps with A's write, so B may legally return either 0 (its point is before the write's point) or 1 (after). C starts after A's write has finished, so real time forces the write before C, and C must return 1. Now check four histories. B=0, C=1: linearizable. B=1, C=1: linearizable. B=1, C=0: not linearizable, because C started after the write ended, so C has to come after the write. B=0, C=0: also not linearizable for the same reason. The interesting trap is the third one. Once anyone has seen the new value 1, and the write has completed, nobody who starts later may see the old value 0 again. A small Python brute-force checker that tries every ordering of the three operations confirms exactly these four verdicts.

Where linearizability is needed: Locks and leader leases (two nodes must never both believe they hold the lock), unique constraints (two people must not both register the username "rahim"), and account balances where an overdraft is unacceptable. Systems usually build it with a single leader plus consensus (lessons 18 and 19), so every operation is ordered through one log. ZooKeeper and etcd are well-known coordination services used this way; ZooKeeper linearizes writes while letting reads be served by followers, so a plain ZooKeeper read can be slightly stale unless you ask for a sync first.

Sequential consistency: Leslie Lamport defined sequential consistency in 1979. The rule: the result of any execution is the same as if all operations of all processes were executed in some single sequential order, and the operations of each individual process appear in that order in the order its program issued them. Compare with linearizability: both demand one global order that everybody agrees on, but sequential consistency drops the real-time requirement. An operation may "take effect" later than the moment it finished, as long as every process sees the same order and each process's own order is kept.

Worked sequential example: P1 does W(x)a. P2 does W(x)b. P3 reads x twice and gets b then a. P4 reads x twice and also gets b then a. This is sequentially consistent: the global order W(x)b, R3(x)b, R4(x)b, W(x)a, R3(x)a, R4(x)a explains everything. Now change P4 so it reads a then b, while P3 still reads b then a. That is not sequentially consistent. P3 says b's write came before a's; P4 says a's came before b's. No single order can satisfy both, and a brute-force search over all orderings finds none. Notice the rule is about agreement, not about which write "really" happened first in time.

Causal consistency: Sequential consistency still forces everyone to agree on the order of writes that have nothing to do with each other, which needs a lot of coordination. Causal consistency, built on the happened-before relation from lesson 09, asks for less. Writes that are potentially causally related must be seen by every process in the same order. Writes that are concurrent, meaning neither could have influenced the other, may be seen in different orders on different machines. Example: on a class Facebook-style group, Nusrat posts "Exam moved to Sunday?" and Tanvir, after reading it, replies "Yes, confirmed". The reply causally depends on the question, so no member may ever see the reply without the question before it. But if Rafi and Mitu each post an unrelated photo at about the same moment, different members may see those two photos in different orders. Vector clocks (lesson 10) are the classic tool to track these dependencies.

FIFO or PRAM consistency: Weaker still, FIFO consistency (also called PRAM, pipelined RAM) only guarantees that writes done by a single process are seen by everyone in the order that process issued them. Writes from different processes may appear in any order, even if one caused the other. It is cheap: each replica just applies each sender's updates in sequence number order, like processing each sender's messages in a queue.

Eventual consistency: The weakest common model makes only a liveness promise: if no new writes arrive for an item, eventually all replicas will converge to the same value. In the meantime a read can return an old value, and two reads in a row can even go backwards. This is what the leaderless Dynamo-style stores from lesson 15 offer by default, and what DNS caching (lesson 07) gives you: after a record changes, resolvers keep serving the old answer until their TTL runs out, then they catch up. Eventual consistency is very available and fast, but the application must tolerate staleness and resolve conflicts, for example with last-writer-wins or merge rules.

Client-centric models, why they exist: Many apps can live with eventual consistency across users but feel broken when a single user sees nonsense. Picture a bKash-style wallet user who changes their profile picture, then refreshes and sees the old one. The data is not wrong for the world, but it is confusing for that person. Client-centric guarantees fix the single user's view without paying for strong consistency everywhere.

Read-your-writes: If a client has written a value, its later reads will see that write or a newer one. Typical implementation: after a write, route that user's reads to the leader for a while, or remember the version number the write produced and only accept replies from replicas that have reached that version.

Monotonic reads: If a client has read a value, later reads never return an older value. Without this a user might see a comment, refresh, see it vanish (because the request hit a lagging replica), and refresh again to see it come back. A simple fix is to pin each user to one replica, for example by hashing the user id.

Monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads: Monotonic writes says a client's writes are applied everywhere in the order the client issued them, so "set price 100" followed by "set price 120" never ends as 100. Writes-follow-reads says that if a client reads a value and then writes, its write is ordered after the write it read; this is what keeps a reply from appearing before the post it answers. Together these four session guarantees were described in the Bayou project in the 1990s.

Real-life example 1, a train ticket system: Suppose a Bangladesh Railway style booking service sells seat 23 on the Subarna Express. The seat inventory must be linearizable: if two customers in Rajshahi and Sylhet press "book" at the same moment, exactly one may win, and once someone has been told "booked", no later request may see the seat as free. The same company's "popular routes" page, however, can be eventually consistent. If it shows yesterday's ranking for a few minutes, nobody is harmed. One app, two very different consistency needs, so a good design picks the model per feature rather than per company.

Real-life example 2, a ride-sharing chat: In a Pathao-style app the rider writes "I'm at the Farmgate footbridge" and the driver replies "Coming in 2 minutes". Causal consistency guarantees the rider never sees the reply above the message it answers. Read-your-writes guarantees the rider sees their own message immediately after sending it, even if the message is still travelling to other replicas. Full linearizability would be overkill for chat and would make messages slower when the network between data centers is shaky.

Choosing a model: Ask three questions. What is the cost of a stale or out-of-order read for this feature: money lost, a confused user, or nothing? How far apart are the replicas, since stronger models need coordination round trips that grow with distance? And what must happen during a network partition: refuse requests, or answer with possibly old data? Strong models suit money, inventory, locks and configuration. Causal and session guarantees suit social feeds, chat and collaborative editing. Eventual consistency suits counters, caches, analytics and anything that can be repaired later. Many real databases let you choose per request, for example by choosing quorum sizes (lesson 15) or by asking for a linearizable read explicitly.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: First, mixing up linearizable and sequential: both have a single global order, but only linearizability respects real time. Second, thinking eventual consistency means "usually consistent within a second". It promises nothing about when, only that convergence happens if writes stop. Third, confusing the C of ACID (application invariants, from the DBMS course) with the C of CAP and of this lesson (agreement among replicas). Fourth, forgetting that a quorum system with R + W > N can still fail to be linearizable without extra steps such as read repair before returning. Typical exam questions: given a history with time intervals, decide whether it is linearizable; given per-process read sequences, decide whether it is sequentially consistent; order the models from strongest to weakest; and explain one client-centric guarantee with an example.

Recap: A consistency model is the promise about which values reads may return when data has replicas. Strict consistency is an unbuildable ideal. Linearizability gives the single-copy illusion with real-time order; sequential consistency gives one agreed order without real time; causal consistency only orders related writes; FIFO only orders each writer's own writes; eventual consistency only promises convergence. Client-centric guarantees, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads, make one user's experience sane on top of weak models. Next lesson asks the big question: when the network splits, how much of this can you keep?
key_points: A consistency model is a contract saying which values a read may return when data is replicated.
Strict consistency (latest write in absolute time) is an ideal that cannot be built across machines.
Linearizability: every operation takes effect at one instant between its start and end, respecting real-time order; it gives the single-copy illusion.
Sequential consistency: one global order that all processes agree on, keeping each process's program order, but without real-time constraints.
Causal consistency orders only causally related writes; concurrent writes may be seen in different orders.
Eventual consistency only promises that replicas converge once writes stop.
Client-centric guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads) protect one user's view.
Pick the model per feature: strong for money, seats and locks, weaker for feeds, counters and caches.
lessons.tip: Draw every history as horizontal bars on a timeline, one row per client. For linearizability, try to place a dot inside each bar so the dots read left to right as a legal sequence. If you can, it is linearizable. This one picture solves most exam questions.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the three-operation history from the lesson (W(x)1 from 1 to 4, a read from 2 to 3, a read from 5 to 6) and test all four combinations of read results by placing linearization points. Then open any two of your social apps on two devices, post something on one, and note on the other which client-centric guarantee you notice or miss.

quiz.q: Which property does linearizability have that sequential consistency does not?
options: It respects real-time order between non-overlapping operations
It keeps each process's program order
It gives one global order of all operations
It allows concurrent writes to be seen in different orders
quiz.explain: Both models have one agreed global order and keep program order; only linearizability also forces an operation that finished earlier to come first.

quiz.q: W(x)1 runs from time 1 to 4 (x was 0). A read runs from 5 to 6. What may it return?
quiz.explain: The read starts after the write ended, so in any linearization the write comes first and the read must return 1.

quiz.q: P3 reads x as b then a, while P4 reads x as a then b (single writes of a and b by P1 and P2). This history is:
quiz.explain: P3 and P4 disagree about the order of the two writes, so no single global order explains both.

quiz.q: A user changes their profile name, refreshes, and sees the old name. Which guarantee was missing?
quiz.explain: Read-your-writes promises a client always sees its own earlier writes.

quiz.q: What exactly does eventual consistency promise?
options: All reads are fresh within one second
If writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value
Each client sees its own writes
quiz.explain: It is only a convergence promise, with no time bound and no ordering guarantee in the meantime.

lessons.title: CAP and PACELC
lessons.content:
Picture a mobile wallet company with two data centers, one in Dhaka and one in Chattogram, connected by fibre that runs along the highway. One afternoon a road construction crew cuts the fibre. Both data centers are healthy, both are full of customers' requests, but they cannot talk to each other. A customer in Chattogram asks for her balance. The Chattogram servers have a copy of the data, but they know it might be out of date, because Dhaka might have accepted a payment in the last few minutes. What should Chattogram do: answer with the copy it has, or refuse until the link comes back? There is no third option that gives both a guaranteed fresh answer and an answer at all. That uncomfortable fact is the CAP theorem.

Where this fits: Lesson 14 showed replication for availability, lesson 15 showed quorums, and lesson 16 listed consistency models from linearizable down to eventual. This lesson explains why we cannot simply always pick the strongest model: network failures and even plain distance force a trade-off. In the DBMS course (deep-cse-4-2, lesson 24) you met CAP in one paragraph. Here we state it carefully, see why it is true, and then add PACELC, which describes the trade-off you face even when nothing is broken.

The history in one paragraph: Eric Brewer presented the idea as a conjecture in a keynote at the PODC conference in 2000. In 2002 Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch published a formal proof, which turned the conjecture into a theorem under precise definitions.
