In 2012 Brewer himself wrote a follow-up article explaining that the popular slogan "pick two out of three" is misleading. We will see why.

The careful statement: In a distributed system where the network may lose messages between nodes, it is impossible to guarantee both of these for every request at all times: consistency in the sense of linearizability, and availability in the sense that every request received by a non-failed node gets a non-error response. Put more simply: when a network partition happens, each operation must give up either consistency or availability. When there is no partition, the theorem says nothing at all and you can have both.

What C means: The C in CAP is linearizability from lesson 16, the single-copy illusion: once a write has completed, every later read anywhere must see it or something newer. It is not the C of ACID, which means a transaction keeps the application's rules such as "balance never negative". Mixing these two Cs is the most common mistake students make about CAP.

What A means: The A is a strong, specific kind of availability: every request that reaches a node that has not crashed must eventually receive a real answer, not an error and not a timeout. A system that answers 99.99 percent of requests but refuses those that reach the minority side of a partition is not "available" in the CAP sense, even though in everyday language we would call it highly available. Keep the formal and the everyday meanings separate.

What P means: P stands for partition tolerance. A partition is when the network splits the nodes into groups that cannot exchange messages, while each group keeps running. In the proof, the network is allowed to drop any number of messages. Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating correctly by its own definition when this happens. Since real networks do drop messages, because cables get cut, routers fail, configuration mistakes happen, and long garbage-collection pauses look like silence, partition tolerance is not something you choose. It is a fact you must live with.

Why the theorem is true, a two-node proof sketch: Take two replicas, G1 in Dhaka and G2 in Chattogram, both storing x = v0. Cut every message between them. A client writes x = v1 at G1. If the system is available, G1 must acknowledge the write, even though it cannot tell G2. Now another client reads x at G2. If the system is available, G2 must answer, and the only value it knows is v0. Returning v0 after a completed write of v1 breaks linearizability. The only way to stay consistent is for G1 to refuse the write or G2 to refuse the read, or to wait forever, which breaks availability. Nothing cleverer is possible, because no message can cross the cut. That is the whole idea of the Gilbert and Lynch proof.

Why "pick two of three" misleads: The slogan suggests a menu where you can choose "C and A, no P". But you cannot opt out of partitions; they happen to you. A system that claims CA is really saying "we assume the network never splits", which is reasonable only for a single machine or a single rack. Also, the choice is not made once for the whole system. It is made during a partition, and it can differ per operation: a wallet may stay consistent for transfers and available for showing the transaction history. And the choice is not all-or-nothing: a system can stay available for reads while refusing writes, or serve slightly stale data with a warning.

CP systems: A CP system keeps consistency and gives up availability on the side that cannot reach a majority. Consensus-based stores such as ZooKeeper and etcd behave this way: they replicate through a leader and a majority (lessons 18 and 19), so a minority group cut off by a partition will refuse writes. Example with three replicas, two in Dhaka and one in Chattogram: a majority is 2. During the partition Dhaka still has 2 and keeps working; Chattogram has 1 and must refuse. Chattogram users get errors, but nobody ever sees wrong data.

AP systems: An AP system keeps answering on every side and accepts that replicas will disagree for a while. Dynamo-style stores, when configured with small read and write quorums or sloppy quorums (lesson 15), behave this way, and so does DNS. After the partition heals, the replicas must reconcile their differences using last-writer-wins, version vectors (lesson 10), or application-specific merging. Note that many real databases are tunable, so it is more accurate to call a configuration or an operation CP or AP than to stamp a whole product.

Worked example, the joint account: A brother and sister share an account with 1,000 taka. The data is on three replicas, two in Dhaka and one in Chattogram. The fibre is cut. The sister in Dhaka withdraws 700 taka; the brother in Chattogram tries to withdraw 600 taka at the same moment. In an AP design both sides say yes. When the link returns, the merged balance is 1,000 - 700 - 600 = -300 taka, an overdraft the company now has to chase. In a CP design Dhaka holds the majority (2 of 3) and approves the 700 withdrawal, leaving 300 taka; Chattogram has only 1 of 3, cannot form a majority, and refuses the brother's request with "please try again later". Annoying, but correct. For money, most designs pick CP, or AP plus very careful limits and compensation.

Worked example, the like counter: Now take the "likes" on a post in the same app. During the partition, people in Dhaka add 120 likes and people in Chattogram add 45. An AP design keeps counting on both sides, and after healing it adds the increments, showing 165 new likes. Nobody is hurt by a temporarily different number on each side. Counters like this are even designed as CRDTs, data types whose merges always converge. Here AP is the obvious choice. The lesson: CAP choices belong to features, not companies.

PACELC, the trade-off without failures: Partitions are relatively rare. What hurts every single day is latency. Daniel Abadi proposed PACELC (around 2010 to 2012) to capture this: if there is a Partition, choose between Availability and Consistency; Else, when the system runs normally, choose between Latency and Consistency. The "else" half matters because strong consistency needs coordination, and coordination needs round trips between replicas, and round trips take time even on a perfect network.

Worked PACELC numbers: Suppose a local write in Dhaka takes 1 ms, and the round-trip time between Dhaka and Chattogram is 10 ms (an assumed round number for illustration). If every write must be confirmed by the Chattogram replica before replying, each write costs about 1 + 10 = 11 ms. A checkout that performs 5 writes one after another takes about 5 ms with asynchronous replication but about 55 ms with synchronous replication. If the second data center were in Singapore, with a much larger round trip, the gap would grow further. That cost is paid on every request, not just on bad days.

Classifying with PACELC: A system is described by two letters for each half. PC/EC means it chooses consistency both during partitions and in normal operation, paying with availability and latency; fully consensus-replicated stores are typical. PA/EL means it chooses availability during partitions and low latency normally; Dynamo-style stores in their default fast settings are the classic example. Mixed choices also exist. Abadi described Yahoo's PNUTS as PC/EL: it favours latency in normal operation but is careful during partitions. As with CAP, settings can move a system between categories, so classify configurations rather than brand names.

BASE vs ACID recap: The AP side is often summarised as BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. ACID from the DBMS course describes single-database transactions. BASE is not the opposite of every ACID property; it is a design philosophy that accepts temporary disagreement between replicas in exchange for availability and speed. Many modern systems mix both: ACID inside one partition, BASE-like behaviour between regions.

Real-life example 1, ride sharing in a storm: During heavy monsoon rain a ride-sharing company's link between regions flaps. Driver location updates use AP behaviour: each region keeps accepting GPS pings and shows the latest position it knows, because a map that is two seconds old is better than no map. Trip payment and the "trip assigned to exactly one driver" decision use CP behaviour through a consensus-backed store: if the region cannot reach a majority, it pauses new assignments instead of risking two drivers for one rider.

Real-life example 2, an exam result portal: When board exam results are published, millions of students rush to check. Result data is written once and then only read, so the portal can serve cached copies from many servers and CDN edges (AP and EL). If one cache is a few seconds behind at the moment of publication, the student simply refreshes. Writes are rare, reads are huge, staleness is harmless, so availability and latency win.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Saying "CAP lets you pick any two" without noting that partitions are not optional. Confusing CAP's C with ACID's C, or CAP's A with "high availability" in the everyday sense. Forgetting that CAP says nothing when there is no partition, which is exactly the gap PACELC fills. Calling a product permanently "CP" or "AP" when it is tunable. Typical exam questions: state CAP precisely and define each letter; give the two-node proof sketch; decide CP or AP for a list of features and justify; explain PACELC with a latency calculation; and compare BASE with ACID.

Recap: CAP says that during a network partition an operation must choose between linearizable consistency and availability; partitions are not optional, so "CA" is not a real choice for a distributed system. Brewer stated it in 2000, Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002. CP systems refuse on the minority side; AP systems answer everywhere and reconcile later. PACELC adds that even without partitions you trade latency for consistency, because coordination costs round trips. Choose per feature. Next we study consensus, the machinery that makes CP systems possible.
key_points: CAP: when the network partitions, an operation cannot have both linearizable consistency and availability.
Brewer conjectured it in 2000; Gilbert and Lynch proved it formally in 2002.
C means linearizability (not ACID's C); A means every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response.
Partitions are not optional, so "pick two of three" misleads; the real choice is C or A during a partition.
CP systems refuse on the minority side; AP systems answer everywhere and reconcile after healing.
PACELC: if Partition choose A or C, Else choose Latency or Consistency, because coordination costs round trips.
Worked: 5 sequential writes cost about 5 ms locally vs about 55 ms if each waits for a 10 ms remote round trip.
Choose per feature: money and assignments lean CP, counters, locations and read-heavy data lean AP.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see CAP in a question, first write the two-node picture: G1, G2, a cut between them, a write on one side and a read on the other. Every CAP answer falls out of that drawing.
lessons.task: List five features of an app you use daily (for example balance, chat, likes, ride assignment, notifications). For each, decide whether you would make it CP or AP during a partition and write one line of reasoning. Then estimate the extra latency if each feature's write had to wait for a 10 ms remote round trip.

quiz.q: What does CAP actually say?
options: Every system can have only two of C, A and P at all times
During a network partition an operation must give up either consistency or availability
Partition tolerance can be switched off for speed
Consistency always costs exactly one round trip
quiz.explain: CAP only constrains behaviour during a partition; when there is no partition both C and A are possible.

quiz.q: The C in CAP means:
quiz.explain: CAP's consistency is linearizability; ACID's C is about application invariants.

quiz.q: Three replicas: two in Dhaka, one in Chattogram; the link is cut. In a CP majority-based system, what happens?
quiz.explain: Majority is 2 of 3; Dhaka has 2 and can proceed, Chattogram's single replica cannot.

quiz.q: What does the "ELC" part of PACELC describe?
options: Else, the trade-off between latency and consistency in normal operation
Election of a leader after a crash
Encryption of links between data centers
quiz.explain: When there is no partition, stronger consistency still costs latency because replicas must coordinate.

quiz.q: Why is the slogan "pick two of three" misleading?
options: Because partitions are not optional, so the real choice is between C and A when one happens
quiz.explain: A distributed system cannot opt out of network failures; CA only fits a single machine.

lessons.title: Consensus I: the Problem, FLP and Paxos
lessons.content:
Five friends in a WhatsApp group want to pick one place for iftar: Dhanmondi or Old Dhaka. Messages sometimes arrive late, one friend's phone may die at any moment, and nobody is in charge. Still, they must all end up going to the same place, it must be a place someone actually suggested, and they must decide before the sun sets. That is the consensus problem in miniature. It sounds like a group chat squabble, but it sits at the heart of almost every reliable distributed system: electing a leader, agreeing on the next entry of a replicated log, deciding who holds a lock, or agreeing on the current list of servers.

What consensus is: A group of processes each propose a value, and all of them must decide on a single value. A correct consensus algorithm satisfies three properties. Agreement: no two non-faulty processes decide different values. Validity: the decided value was proposed by some process, so the algorithm cannot invent "Gulshan" when nobody suggested it. Termination: every non-faulty process eventually decides. Usually we also require integrity: a process decides at most once and never changes its mind. Agreement and validity are safety properties (nothing bad ever happens); termination is a liveness property (something good eventually happens). Keep this split in mind, because the famous impossibility result below is exactly about the liveness half.

Why it is hard: On one computer, agreeing is trivial: one variable, one write. In a distributed system there is no shared memory, messages can be delayed or lost (lesson 02's fallacies), and processes can crash. A process waiting for a reply cannot tell whether the other side has crashed, is just slow, or the network dropped the message. Lesson 13's election algorithms and lesson 12's coordinator-based mutual exclusion quietly assumed reliable timeouts. Consensus algorithms are designed to stay correct even when those timeouts lie.

Where consensus is used: A replicated state machine keeps several servers identical by having them apply the same commands in the same order; agreeing on "command number 57 is transfer 500 taka from A to B" is one consensus instance per log slot. Leader election in a CP store is consensus on "who is leader for term 4". Configuration services agree on which servers are members. Atomic commit (lesson 21) is a close relative: all participants must agree to commit or abort. The CP systems from lesson 17 are built on top of consensus.

System models: How hard consensus is depends on what we assume about time. In a synchronous model, message delays and processing speeds have known upper bounds, so a missing reply after the bound means a crash. In an asynchronous model there are no bounds at all: a message may take one millisecond or one hour, and a slow process is indistinguishable from a dead one. The partially synchronous model (Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer, 1988) sits in between: the system may behave asynchronously for a while, but eventually bounds hold. Real networks look like partial synchrony: usually fast, occasionally terrible.

The FLP impossibility result: In 1985 Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch and Michael Paterson proved that in a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination if even one process may crash. Stated carefully: you cannot have agreement, validity and guaranteed termination together in that model. The intuition is the slow-versus-dead problem. If the algorithm waits for a process, that process may have crashed and the algorithm waits forever. If it moves on without it, the "crashed" process may have been merely slow and may be holding information that changes the outcome. FLP shows that an adversarial schedule of message delays can always keep the algorithm undecided.

What FLP does not say: It does not say consensus is impossible in practice. Real algorithms such as Paxos and Raft never violate safety, in any timing, and they terminate whenever the network behaves well enough for long enough, which partial synchrony gives us. Other escapes are randomisation (Ben-Or's algorithm terminates with probability 1) and failure detectors that are eventually accurate. So the honest summary is: in an asynchronous world you can always be safe, but you can only be guaranteed live when timing cooperates.

Majorities and 2f + 1: Most crash-tolerant consensus algorithms use majority quorums. With N processes, a majority is floor(N/2) + 1. Any two majorities share at least one process, because two groups each larger than half must overlap. That overlap is how information from an earlier decision survives into a later one. To tolerate f crashed processes, the remaining N - f must still form a majority, which gives N = 2f + 1. Worked: N = 3 has majority 2 and tolerates 1 crash; N = 5 has majority 3 and tolerates 2; N = 7 has majority 4 and tolerates 3. N = 4 has majority 3 and still tolerates only 1 crash, so even-sized clusters add cost without adding fault tolerance. A Python check over all pairs of majorities for N = 3, 4, 5 and 7 confirms that every pair overlaps. Byzantine (lying) processes need more, 3f + 1, which is lesson 20.

Paxos, the roles: Leslie Lamport's Paxos (written up as "The Part-Time Parliament", published in 1998, and re-explained in "Paxos Made Simple", 2001) is the classic crash-tolerant consensus algorithm. It has three roles, which a single server often plays at once. Proposers suggest values. Acceptors vote and remember what they have promised and accepted. Learners find out which value was chosen. A value is chosen when a majority of acceptors accept the same proposal.

Proposal numbers: Every proposal carries a number, and numbers must be unique and totally ordered. A common trick is a pair (round, server id), compared round first, so server 2's round 1 is (1, 2) and server 1's round 2 is (2, 1), and no two servers ever use the same number. Higher numbers win. The numbers are what let a newer proposer safely take over from an older one.

Phase 1, prepare and promise: A proposer picks a number n and sends Prepare(n) to the acceptors. An acceptor that has not already promised a higher number replies Promise(n), and attaches the highest-numbered proposal it has already accepted, if any. By promising, it agrees never again to accept any proposal numbered less than n.

Phase 2, accept and accepted: If the proposer collects promises from a majority, it sends Accept(n, v). The crucial rule: v must be the value of the highest-numbered proposal reported in those promises; only if none of them had accepted anything may the proposer use its own value. An acceptor accepts Accept(n, v) unless it has since promised a number higher than n. When a majority have accepted, the value is chosen and learners can be told.

Walk-through with three acceptors: Acceptors A1, A2 and A3, majority 2. Proposer P1 wants "Dhanmondi" and uses number 1. It sends Prepare(1) to A1 and A2; both promise and report nothing accepted. P1 sends Accept(1, Dhanmondi) to A1 and A2; both accept. Two of three have accepted, so Dhanmondi is chosen, even though P1 then crashes before telling anyone. Now proposer P2, who wanted "Old Dhaka", starts with number 2 and sends Prepare(2) to A2 and A3. A3 has accepted nothing, but A2 replies with its promise plus "I accepted (1, Dhanmondi)". The rule forces P2 to propose Dhanmondi, not its own wish. It sends Accept(2, Dhanmondi); A2 and A3 accept. The decision did not change. If a delayed Accept(1, Dhanmondi) from P1 now reaches A3, A3 rejects it because it promised 2; harmless either way. A short Python simulation of these acceptor rules reproduces every step.

Why the rule works: P2's prepare majority {A2, A3} and P1's accept majority {A1, A2} must overlap, here in A2. So any later proposer is guaranteed to hear about a value that might already have been chosen, and it will carry that value forward instead of overwriting it. That is the entire safety argument in one sentence: majorities intersect, and newer proposers adopt what they hear.

Duelling proposers and FLP in action: Suppose P1 sends Prepare(1) and gets promises, then P2 sends Prepare(2) to everyone before P1's accepts land. P1's Accept(1) is rejected, so P1 retries with Prepare(3), which in turn makes P2's Accept(2) fail, and so on. Safety is never broken, but nobody decides: this is a livelock, and it is precisely the kind of endless schedule FLP warns about. The practical fix is to elect a single distinguished proposer, a leader, and to add random back-off, so that in calm periods one proposer runs uncontested.

Multi-Paxos: Real systems need not one decision but a whole log of them. Multi-Paxos runs one Paxos instance per log slot, but once a stable leader has completed phase 1 for all future slots, it can skip straight to phase 2 for each new command. In the normal case that costs one round trip to a majority per command. Paxos is famously hard to understand and harder to implement fully; that difficulty is what motivated Raft, the subject of the next lesson.

Real-life example 1, a lock service: Google described Chubby, a lock and small-file service whose replicas use Paxos to agree on state. Other systems rely on a coordination service for leader election and configuration, for example ZooKeeper (which uses its own protocol called Zab) or etcd (which uses Raft). When a mobile-wallet backend in Dhaka needs exactly one active "settlement job runner", it asks such a service for a lock; the consensus underneath guarantees that two runners never both believe they hold it, as long as a majority of the coordination servers are up.

Real-life example 2, a replicated ledger: Imagine a five-server ledger for a cooperative society's savings in Rajshahi, three servers in one building and two in another. Every deposit becomes one log slot decided by consensus. If one building loses power, the three-server side still forms a majority and keeps accepting deposits. If the two-server side is cut off, it stops accepting writes rather than inventing a different history. When power returns, the minority catches up by learning the chosen values. Nobody ever sees two different balances for the same account.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Saying FLP proves consensus is impossible; it only rules out guaranteed termination for deterministic algorithms in a fully asynchronous model with one crash. Forgetting the "adopt the highest accepted value" rule in phase 2, which is what keeps Paxos safe. Thinking a value is chosen when one acceptor accepts it; it needs a majority. Choosing 4 servers to "tolerate more failures" than 3. Confusing crash tolerance (2f + 1) with Byzantine tolerance (3f + 1). Typical exam questions: define the three properties of consensus; state FLP precisely; compute N for f failures; trace Paxos with two proposers; and explain why proposal numbers and majority intersection guarantee safety.

Recap: Consensus makes processes agree on one proposed value, with agreement and validity as safety and termination as liveness. FLP (1985) says no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash, yet practical algorithms stay safe always and finish when timing behaves. Majorities of N = 2f + 1 always overlap, which carries decisions forward. Paxos uses numbered proposals, a prepare-promise phase and an accept phase, and forces newer proposers to adopt previously accepted values. Multi-Paxos with a stable leader makes a replicated log practical. Next, Raft shows the same ideas in a design built for understandability.
key_points: Consensus: processes propose values and must decide one, with agreement, validity and termination.
Agreement and validity are safety; termination is liveness.
FLP (1985): in a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination if even one process may crash.
Practical algorithms are always safe and terminate when the network behaves (partial synchrony), or use randomisation.
Majority quorums overlap; tolerating f crashes needs N = 2f + 1 (N = 5 tolerates 2).
Paxos phase 1: Prepare(n) and Promise with any previously accepted proposal; phase 2: Accept(n, v) and Accepted.
A newer proposer must adopt the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal it hears about; this keeps decisions safe.
Duelling proposers can livelock; a stable leader (Multi-Paxos) fixes this and needs one round trip per command.
lessons.tip: Practise Paxos with three coins as acceptors on your desk. Write each acceptor's promised number and accepted value on sticky notes and move two proposers through prepare and accept by hand. After two traces the adopt-the-highest-value rule feels obvious.
lessons.task: With five acceptors, write your own Paxos trace: P1 gets Accept(1, X) to only two acceptors and crashes; then P2 runs Prepare(2) to three acceptors. Work out whether X could already have been chosen, which value P2 must propose in each case, and check that every majority of 5 overlaps every other.

quiz.q: Which consensus property is a liveness property?
quiz.explain: Termination says something good eventually happens; agreement, validity and integrity forbid bad outcomes, so they are safety properties.

quiz.q: What does the FLP result state?
options: In a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination if even one process may crash
Consensus is impossible in every real network
Paxos can violate agreement during partitions
quiz.explain: FLP is about guaranteed termination in the asynchronous model; safety can still always be kept.

quiz.q: How many servers are needed to tolerate 2 crash failures with majority quorums?
quiz.explain: N = 2f + 1 = 5; the majority of 3 is still reachable after 2 crashes.

quiz.q: In Paxos phase 2, which value must a proposer send?
options: The value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported in the promises, or its own if none
quiz.explain: Adopting the highest accepted value is what carries a possibly-chosen value forward safely.

quiz.q: Two proposers keep pre-empting each other with higher numbers and nothing is decided. This is:
options: A livelock that leaves safety intact
quiz.explain: Duelling proposers can stall progress without ever choosing two values; a stable leader with back-off avoids it.

lessons.title: Consensus II: Raft
lessons.content:
Think of a class of five students keeping one shared attendance register for a whole semester. One student is the class captain and writes every entry; the others copy each new line into their own notebooks. If the captain falls sick, the class must quickly pick a new captain, and the new captain must not lose or rewrite any line that was already agreed. Old lines that only one student copied may be fixed, but lines that most of the class already copied are sacred. That classroom routine is almost exactly Raft, the consensus algorithm that today sits under many coordination services and databases.

Where this fits: Lesson 18 explained the consensus problem, the FLP limit and Paxos. Paxos is correct but notoriously hard to understand and to turn into a complete system. In 2014 Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout published Raft in a paper titled "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm". Raft gives the same guarantees as Multi-Paxos for crash failures, but splits the problem into clear pieces: leader election, log replication and safety. It is the version of consensus most engineers meet first.

The replicated state machine: Every server holds a log, a numbered list of commands such as "set x = 5" or "transfer 500 taka from Rahim to Karim". Each server also runs the same deterministic state machine, for example a key-value store. If all servers apply the same commands in the same order, they all end up in the same state. Raft's job is to keep the logs identical. A command is committed once it is safely stored on a majority; only committed commands are applied to the state machine and answered to the client.

Server states: At any moment a server is a follower, a candidate or a leader. Followers are passive: they only answer requests from leaders and candidates. A leader handles all client requests and sends log entries to the followers. A candidate is a server trying to become leader. In normal operation there is exactly one leader and all others are followers. With five servers, Raft tolerates two crashes, because a majority of three is still available (N = 2f + 1 from lesson 18).

Terms: Raft divides time into terms numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. Each term starts with an election, and at most one leader can win in a term. Some terms end with no winner, in which case a new term starts soon. Every message carries the sender's current term. If a server sees a higher term than its own, it updates its term and, if it was a leader or candidate, immediately becomes a follower. If it receives a message with an older term, it rejects it. Terms act like the logical clocks of lesson 09: they let servers detect stale leaders without trusting physical time.

Heartbeats and election timeouts: The leader sends periodic AppendEntries messages, empty ones acting as heartbeats, to all followers. Each follower runs an election timeout. If it hears nothing from a leader before the timeout expires, it assumes the leader is gone and starts an election. The timeouts are randomised, for example a fresh random value between 150 and 300 milliseconds, the range used as an example in the Raft paper. Randomness makes it likely that one server times out clearly before the others, wins, and sends heartbeats before anyone else even starts. That is how Raft sidesteps the duelling-proposer livelock from Paxos in practice; FLP still means termination is not guaranteed in the worst case, but split votes become rare and short.

RequestVote and the up-to-date rule: To start an election, a follower increments its term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote(term, candidate id, last log index, last log term) to all others. A server grants its vote if the term is not older than its own, it has not already voted for someone else in this term (one vote per term, first come first served), and the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own. Up-to-date is decided by comparing the term of the last entry first: the higher last term wins. If the last terms are equal, the longer log wins. Example: a candidate whose log ends with (term 1, index 3) is less up-to-date than a voter whose log ends with (term 2, index 2), because 2 > 1, even though the candidate's log is longer. A candidate that collects votes from a majority becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats.

Election walk-through, the setup: Five servers S1 to S5. In term 1, S1 was leader and wrote three entries, all in term 1. Entries 1 and 2 reached everyone. Entry 3 reached S1, S2 and S3, a majority, so it was committed, but S4 and S5 had not received it yet. Then S1 crashes. Now S2 and S3 have logs ending at (term 1, index 3), while S4 and S5 end at (term 1, index 2).

Election walk-through, a failed attempt: Suppose S4's random timeout expires first. S4 moves to term 2, votes for itself and asks the others. S5's log is equally up-to-date, so S5 votes yes. S2 and S3 have a longer log with the same last term, so S4 is less up-to-date and they refuse, though they do update their own term to 2. S1 is dead. S4 has 2 votes out of 5, short of the 3 needed, so term 2 ends with no leader. Notice what just happened: the rule stopped a server that was missing committed entry 3 from becoming leader.

Election walk-through, the winner: Next, S3's timeout expires. S3 moves to term 3 and asks for votes with last entry (term 1, index 3). S2's log is identical, so S2 votes yes. S4 sees the higher term 3, steps down from candidate to follower, has not voted in term 3, and finds S3's log more up-to-date, so it votes yes. S5 does the same. S3 has 4 votes, itself plus three, which is more than the majority of 3. S3 becomes leader of term 3 and immediately sends heartbeats so nobody else starts an election. A small Python simulation of these voting rules gives the same counts: 2 votes for S4 in term 2 and 4 votes for S3 in term 3.

Log replication, the normal case: A client asks S3 to record "transfer 500 taka to Karim". S3 appends it to its own log as index 4, term 3. It then sends AppendEntries to every follower containing the new entry plus two important fields: prevLogIndex = 3 and prevLogTerm = 1, describing the entry just before the new one. A follower accepts only if its own log has an entry at index 3 with term 1. This consistency check is the heart of log replication.

Log replication, repairing lagging followers: S2 has (index 3, term 1), so it accepts and appends index 4. S4 and S5 have only two entries, so the check fails and they reply false. The leader keeps a nextIndex for each follower; on failure it decrements it and retries. For S4 it now sends prevLogIndex = 2, prevLogTerm = 1 and the entries for index 3 and 4. The check passes and S4's log becomes identical to the leader's. If a follower had conflicting uncommitted entries from an older leader, they would be deleted and overwritten in the same way; the leader's log always wins.

Log replication, committing: Entry 4 is now stored on S3, S2 and S4, three of five servers, a majority. The leader marks index 4 committed, applies "transfer 500 taka to Karim" to its state machine, and replies success to the client. In later AppendEntries messages it sends its commit index, so followers learn that index 4 is committed and apply it too. S5 will be repaired by the same nextIndex process. A subtle rule from the paper: a leader only decides commitment by counting replicas for entries from its own current term; older entries become committed indirectly when a newer entry after them commits. Raft leaders therefore commonly append a no-op entry at the start of their term so that earlier entries get committed promptly.

Why it is safe: Two properties do the work. The Log Matching property: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical up to that index, which the prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm check guarantees by induction. The Leader Completeness property: a committed entry is stored on a majority, a winning candidate needs votes from a majority, the two majorities overlap, and the up-to-date rule means no voter in the overlap will vote for a candidate missing that entry. So every future leader already has every committed entry, exactly as the S4 attempt showed.

When the old leader returns: S1 restarts, still believing it is leader of term 1, and sends AppendEntries with term 1. Followers reply with their term, 3, and S1 immediately steps down to follower and lets S3 repair its log. Because commits need a majority and every majority now knows term 3, the stale leader cannot commit anything. One extra care point: for linearizable reads (lesson 16), a leader should confirm it is still leader, for example by exchanging a heartbeat with a majority, before answering, otherwise a deposed leader could serve a stale read.

Cluster membership changes: Adding or removing servers is itself risky, because during the switch an old majority and a new majority might not overlap. The Raft paper uses joint consensus, where decisions temporarily need majorities of both the old and new configurations; later work describes a simpler approach of changing one server at a time. You do not need the details now, only the reason: majorities must always intersect.

Real-life example 1, Kubernetes and etcd: Kubernetes stores its cluster state in etcd, a key-value store replicated with Raft. A Dhaka e-commerce company running a three- or five-node etcd cluster can lose one or two etcd nodes respectively and keep scheduling containers, because a Raft majority remains. If too many fail, etcd stops accepting writes rather than letting the cluster state fork, the CP choice from lesson 17. HashiCorp Consul is another widely used tool whose servers replicate their state with Raft.

Real-life example 2, a wallet ledger: Imagine five ledger servers for a mobile wallet, three in a Dhaka data center and two in Chattogram. Every transfer is one Raft log entry. If the Chattogram link fails, the Dhaka three still form a majority and keep committing transfers; the Chattogram two cannot elect a leader and refuse writes. When the link returns, their logs are repaired by the leader's nextIndex process. Customers never see a transfer committed on one side and missing on the other.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Thinking the longest log always wins elections; the last term is compared first. Thinking an entry is committed once the leader writes it; it needs a majority, and a leader counts replicas only for current-term entries. Forgetting that each server votes at most once per term. Assuming randomised timeouts defeat FLP; they make progress very likely, not guaranteed. Typical exam questions: list Raft's three server states and transitions; trace an election with given logs and decide who can win; trace AppendEntries with prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm and show how a lagging follower is repaired; explain why a new leader always has all committed entries; and compare Raft with Paxos.

Recap: Raft keeps a replicated log identical on a majority of servers. Time is split into terms with at most one leader each. Followers that miss heartbeats become candidates after a randomised timeout and ask for votes; a vote goes only to a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date, comparing last term then length. The leader appends client commands, replicates them with AppendEntries and a consistency check, repairs laggards by stepping nextIndex back, and commits once a majority stores an entry from its term. Majority overlap plus the voting rule guarantees that committed entries survive every leader change. Next lesson looks at failures more broadly, including Byzantine faults that consensus like this cannot handle.
key_points: Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014) is a crash-tolerant consensus algorithm designed for understandability, split into election, replication and safety.
Servers are followers, candidates or leaders; time is divided into numbered terms with at most one leader per term.
Randomised election timeouts (e.g. 150-300 ms) make one candidate usually win quickly and avoid repeated split votes.
A vote goes only to a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date: compare the last entry's term first, then log length.
AppendEntries carries prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm; a mismatch makes the leader step nextIndex back and resend.
An entry is committed once stored on a majority; leaders count replicas only for current-term entries.
Majority overlap plus the voting rule guarantee every new leader already holds all committed entries.
etcd (used by Kubernetes) and Consul replicate their state with Raft.
lessons.tip: Draw each server's log as a row of boxes with the term written inside each box, one row per server. Every Raft exam question, election or replication, becomes a matter of comparing the last box and counting rows that match.
lessons.task: Draw five logs: S1 [1,1,2,2], S2 [1,1,2], S3 [1,1,2,2,2], S4 [1,1], S5 [1,1,2,2] (numbers are terms). For each server, decide whether it could win an election if it became a candidate, by checking which others would vote for it. Then visit the interactive Raft visualisation on the official Raft website if you have internet and watch an election happen.

quiz.q: What triggers a Raft follower to start an election?
options: Its election timeout expiring without hearing from a leader
quiz.explain: Missing heartbeats until the randomised timeout runs out makes a follower become a candidate.

quiz.q: Candidate's log ends (term 1, index 3); voter's log ends (term 2, index 2). Will the voter grant its vote?
options: Yes, because the candidate's log is longer
Yes, always in a new term
No, because the voter's last term is higher
quiz.explain: Up-to-date compares the last term first; 2 > 1, so the voter's log is more up-to-date and it refuses.

quiz.q: In a five-server Raft cluster, when is a new entry from the current term committed?
options: When it is stored on at least 3 servers
quiz.explain: A majority of 5 is 3; the leader counts itself plus followers that stored the entry.

quiz.q: What does a follower do when AppendEntries' prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm do not match its log?
options: Rejects it, and the leader retries with an earlier nextIndex
quiz.explain: The consistency check fails; the leader steps nextIndex back until the logs match, then overwrites the rest.

quiz.q: An old leader of term 1 returns after a new leader was elected in term 3. What happens?
options: It sees term 3 in replies and steps down to follower
quiz.explain: Higher terms always win: the stale leader converts to follower and its log gets repaired.

lessons.title: Fault Tolerance and Failure Models
lessons.content:
Think about a wedding in a Bangladeshi village. Something always goes wrong: the power cuts, one cook falls sick, the rice delivery is late. Yet the guests still eat, because the family planned for trouble. There is a backup generator, two extra cooks, and an uncle whose only job is to notice when something stops. A good distributed system is built like that wedding: it assumes things will break, every day, and keeps serving anyway. That ability is called fault tolerance, and it is the reason we bothered building distributed systems in the first place.

Where this fits: In lessons 13, 18 and 19 we already used crashes as the villain: elections replace a dead coordinator, and Raft keeps a log safe while a minority of nodes are down. In lesson 14 we replicated data for availability. This lesson steps back and gives the vocabulary and the basic tools: what exactly a failure is, which kinds of failure exist, how a machine can even tell that another machine has failed, and how much redundancy you need for each kind. The deeper engineering of reliable systems belongs to Fault Tolerant Systems (deep-cse-7-10); here we only build the foundation.

Fault, error, failure: These three words sound alike but mean different things, and exams love them. A fault is the root cause, such as a bug in the code, a cracked memory chip, or a cut fibre cable. An error is the wrong internal state that the fault produces, for example a balance variable that now holds a wrong number. A failure is when the system visibly stops delivering its promised service, for example a customer sees the wrong balance or the app does not respond. A fault can sleep for months without causing an error (a bug in a code path nobody uses). An error can be caught and fixed before it becomes a failure (a checksum detects a flipped bit and the data is re-read). Fault tolerance means: faults will happen, but we stop them from turning into failures that users see.

Kinds of faults by timing: A transient fault appears once and disappears, like a bit flipped by electrical noise or one lost packet; simply retrying usually fixes it. An intermittent fault comes and goes, like a loose connector, and is the hardest to debug. A permanent fault stays until someone repairs it, like a dead disk or a burnt power supply.

Dependability: Engineers split "can I depend on this system" into four properties. Availability is the probability that the system is ready to serve at a random moment. Reliability is how long it runs continuously without failing. Safety means that when it does fail, nothing catastrophic happens. Maintainability means how easily and quickly it can be repaired. These are different. A system that crashes for one millisecond every hour has great availability but poor reliability.

Availability worked: Two numbers describe a component. MTTF, mean time to failure, is how long it runs on average before failing. MTTR, mean time to repair, is how long it takes on average to bring it back. Availability A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR). Suppose a server runs on average 1,000 hours between crashes and takes 2 hours to repair. A = 1000 / 1002 = 0.998, about 99.8 percent. Over a year of 8,760 hours that is roughly 17.5 hours of downtime. Notice the lever: cutting MTTR from 2 hours to 12 minutes helps as much as making the machine ten times more reliable, which is why automatic failover is so valuable.

The nines: People describe availability in nines. "Three nines", 99.9 percent, allows about 8.76 hours of downtime per year. "Four nines", 99.99 percent, allows only about 52.6 minutes per year. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by ten.

Series and parallel: If a request must pass through three components in a row, each 99.9 percent available, the whole chain is only 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.997, about 99.7 percent, worse than any single part. Chains multiply weaknesses. If instead you have two independent replicas and either one can serve, the system fails only when both are down at once. With each replica 99 percent available, the probability both are down is 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 1 - 0.0001 = 99.99 percent. Parallel redundancy multiplies strengths. The big assumption is independence: two replicas in the same rack, on the same power line, running the same buggy software, can fail together, and then the math lies.

Failure models: To design a protocol, we must say exactly how components are allowed to misbehave. This list is called the failure model, and it is the most important assumption in the whole course. A crash failure means a process works correctly and then simply stops; it never sends a wrong message. Fail-stop is the polite version, where other processes can reliably detect that it stopped. An omission failure means the process or channel fails to send or receive some messages, like a full buffer dropping packets. A timing failure means a response comes outside the allowed time window, usually too late, which matters in real-time systems. A response failure means the reply itself is wrong: a wrong value, or a wrong state transition. Finally, an arbitrary or Byzantine failure means the process can do anything at all: send wrong values, send different values to different peers, lie about what it received, or act maliciously because an attacker controls it. The models nest: a protocol that survives Byzantine faults also survives crashes, but not the other way round, and it costs more.

Failure detection with heartbeats: How does node B know that node A has crashed? It cannot look inside A. The usual trick is the heartbeat: A sends a small "I am alive" message every second, and B suspects A if no heartbeat arrives within a timeout, say 3 seconds. Alternatively B can ping A and wait for a reply. Either way the only evidence is silence, and silence is ambiguous: A may have crashed, A may be paused by a long garbage collection, or the network between them may be slow or partitioned. In an asynchronous system there is no way to tell these apart for certain, which is the same root problem behind the FLP result in lesson 18. So real failure detectors are "unreliable": they suspect, they do not know.

The timeout trade-off worked: Suppose heartbeats come every 1 second and normal delay is under 200 ms. With a 3 second timeout, a real crash is noticed within about 3 to 4 seconds, and a false alarm happens only if three heartbeats in a row are lost or delayed, which is rare. With a 0.5 second timeout, crashes are noticed fast, but every small network hiccup triggers a false suspicion, a needless failover, and maybe two leaders fighting. With a 60 second timeout there are almost no false alarms, but a dead payment server stays dead in the eyes of the system for a full minute. There is no perfect value; you weigh false alarms against slow detection.

Redundancy, three kinds: Every fault-tolerance technique adds something extra. Information redundancy adds extra bits, such as parity, checksums, CRC or error-correcting codes (recap from Data Communication), so damaged data can be detected or even repaired. Time redundancy repeats an action, such as resending a lost message or retrying a failed transaction; it is cheap but only fixes transient faults, and the action must be safe to repeat (idempotent, lesson 05). Physical redundancy adds extra hardware or processes, such as replicas, spare disks in RAID, or a second data center. In triple modular redundancy, three units compute the same result and a voter takes the majority.

Process groups: In software, physical redundancy usually means a process group: several identical processes act as one logical service, and a message to the group reaches every member. Groups can be flat, where all members are equal and decide together (more robust, but every decision needs coordination), or hierarchical, with a coordinator and workers (simple, but the coordinator is a weak point until an election replaces it, lesson 13). How many members do you need? It depends on the failure model. To survive f crash failures with majority voting and still make progress, you need 2f + 1 members, because the f + 1 survivors still form a majority. To survive f silent crashes where any single answer is good enough, f + 1 members are sufficient. Byzantine faults need more.

The Byzantine generals: Lamport, Shostak and Pease described this problem in 1982. Several generals of the Byzantine army surround a city and must agree on one plan, attack or retreat, by sending messengers. Some generals are traitors who may send "attack" to one general and "retreat" to another. The loyal generals must all agree on the same plan, and if the commander is loyal, they must follow the commander's order. The famous result: with oral (unsigned) messages, agreement is possible only if there are at least 3f + 1 generals when up to f are traitors. So one traitor needs at least 4 generals, two traitors need 7, and three traitors need 10. With exactly 3 generals and 1 traitor it is impossible: a loyal lieutenant who receives conflicting reports cannot tell whether the commander or the other lieutenant is lying.

Why 3f + 1, intuition: The system must make a decision after hearing from n - f nodes, because f nodes may never answer. Among those n - f answers, up to f may come from liars. For honest answers to outnumber lying ones in that set, we need n - f - f > f, which gives n > 3f, so n is at least 3f + 1. Compare with crashes, where nodes never lie and 2f + 1 is enough. Signed messages (deep-cse-6-2, lesson 17) stop traitors from forging what others said, and the original paper showed that this version needs fewer generals; practical BFT protocols such as PBFT (Castro and Liskov, 1999) still use 3f + 1 replicas. Blockchains face this problem at internet scale; that story belongs to Blockchain (deep-cse-9-2).

Checkpoints and logging: Redundancy keeps the service running, but a crashed process must also recover its state. Checkpointing saves the state to stable storage from time to time, so after a crash the process restarts from the last checkpoint instead of from zero. Independent checkpoints of different processes may not fit together, the consistent-cut problem of lesson 11, so coordinated checkpoints are used. Message logging adds the other half: record the messages received after the checkpoint, and replay them to rebuild the exact state. DBMS write-ahead logging (deep-cse-4-2, lesson 23) is the single-machine version.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet at Eid: Picture a Dhaka wallet service on the evening before Eid. The API runs on 6 identical servers behind a load balancer that sends a health check every 2 seconds and removes a server after 3 failed checks. One server's disk dies (permanent fault). Within about 6 seconds the load balancer stops sending it traffic, and users notice nothing except perhaps one retried request. The ledger database runs as a 5-node Raft group, which tolerates 2 crashed nodes (2f + 1 = 5, f = 2). A lost SMS confirmation (transient omission) is simply retried from a queue.

Real-life example 2, power in an office building: Many offices in Bangladesh run IPS units and a diesel generator because grid power is not perfectly reliable. That is physical redundancy for power, and the transfer switch is a failure detector with a timeout. Too fast, and a tiny voltage dip triggers a needless switchover; too slow, and the computers lose power. Data centers do the same at bigger scale, and they test their backups, because an untested backup is only a hope.

Common mistakes: Students mix up fault, error and failure, so learn one example of each. Many think replicas automatically mean fault tolerance, forgetting correlated failures (same bug, same rack, same bad config). Another mistake is treating a timeout as proof of death; it is only a suspicion, and acting on it carelessly creates split brain. People also confuse availability with reliability. Finally, the bounds: crash tolerance with majority needs 2f + 1, Byzantine tolerance needs 3f + 1, and these are minimums, not recommendations.

What exams ask: Define and distinguish fault, error and failure. List and explain the failure models in order of severity. Compute availability from MTTF and MTTR, or for components in series and parallel. Explain the heartbeat timeout trade-off. State the Byzantine generals result and show why 3 generals cannot handle 1 traitor, or compute the number of replicas for f faults.

Recap: Faults cause errors, and errors may cause failures; fault tolerance stops the chain. Availability is MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR), so fast repair matters as much as rare failure. Failure models range from crash to Byzantine, and the model decides the cost. Failure detectors only suspect, using heartbeats and timeouts that trade speed against false alarms. Redundancy comes as extra information, time or hardware. Crash faults need 2f + 1 replicas for majority decisions; Byzantine faults need 3f + 1.
key_points: A fault is the cause, an error is the wrong internal state, a failure is visible loss of service; fault tolerance stops faults becoming failures.
Faults can be transient, intermittent or permanent; retries fix only the first kind reliably.
Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR): 1000 h and 2 h give about 99.8 percent, roughly 17.5 hours down per year.
Components in series multiply availabilities (worse); independent replicas in parallel multiply unavailabilities (better): two 99 percent replicas give 99.99 percent.
Failure models from mild to severe: crash (fail-stop), omission, timing, response, arbitrary (Byzantine).
Heartbeats and timeouts only suspect failures; short timeouts cause false alarms, long ones slow recovery.
Redundancy comes as information (checksums, ECC), time (retries) and physical (replicas, TMR).
Majority-based crash tolerance needs 2f + 1 nodes; Byzantine agreement with unsigned messages needs at least 3f + 1.
lessons.tip: Make a small table with three columns: failure model, example, replicas needed. Fill it for crash, omission and Byzantine. If you can say why 3 generals cannot beat 1 traitor in two sentences, you have understood the hardest part of this lesson.
lessons.task: Pick any app you use daily (bKash, Pathao, your bank). Write down three things that could fail (a server, a network link, an SMS gateway), label each fault as transient, intermittent or permanent, and suggest which redundancy (information, time or physical) would hide it. Then compute the availability for MTTF = 500 hours and MTTR = 1 hour, and for MTTR = 6 minutes.

quiz.q: A server has MTTF = 1,000 hours and MTTR = 2 hours. What is its availability, approximately?
A bug sits in a rarely used code path and has never been triggered. In fault-error-failure terms, what is it?
quiz.explain: The bug is the root cause, a fault. It becomes an error only when triggered, and a failure only when users see wrong service.

quiz.q: Which failure model allows a node to send different, conflicting values to different peers?
quiz.explain: Only the arbitrary or Byzantine model allows lying and inconsistent messages; crash and omission nodes never send wrong values.

quiz.q: How many nodes are needed to reach agreement with unsigned messages if up to 2 nodes may be Byzantine?
quiz.explain: The bound is n >= 3f + 1, so f = 2 needs at least 7 nodes.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of a very short heartbeat timeout?
options: Slow but alive nodes are wrongly suspected, causing needless failovers
It turns crash failures into Byzantine failures
quiz.explain: A short timeout reacts fast but mistakes delays or GC pauses for crashes, causing false alarms and possible split brain.

lessons.title: Distributed Transactions: 2PC, 3PC and Sagas
lessons.content:
Imagine a family in Rajshahi arranging a wedding. The groom's side and the bride's side must both agree on the date, the venue must be booked, and the caterer must be confirmed. If the venue says yes but the caterer says no, you cannot simply keep the venue and hope; either everything is fixed together, or nothing is. Usually one elder acts as coordinator: she phones everyone, asks "can you do the 14th?", waits for all answers, and only then announces "it is final" or "cancel, we try another date". Distributed transactions work exactly like this, and that elder has a famous name in computing: the two-phase commit coordinator.

Where this fits: In DBMS (deep-cse-4-2, lessons 20 to 23) you learned ACID transactions, locking with two-phase locking, and recovery with a write-ahead log, all inside one database server. Lesson 24 of that course previewed two-phase commit. Here we take the problem seriously: what happens when one transaction must change data on several machines that can crash independently and talk over an unreliable network (lesson 20)? We cover two-phase commit in detail, its blocking problem, the three-phase commit idea, and sagas, the practical alternative used across microservices.

Why one transfer can touch two machines: Suppose a mobile wallet stores accounts sharded by phone number (lesson 22). Rahim's account lives on shard A in one server, and Karim's account lives on shard B in another. Sending 500 taka means: subtract 500 on A, add 500 on B. If A commits and B crashes before committing, 500 taka has vanished. If B commits and A fails, money was created from nothing. Each server alone guarantees ACID for its own part, but we need the whole thing to be atomic: both parts commit or both abort. This is called the atomic commitment problem.

ACID recap in one breath: Atomicity means all or nothing. Consistency means rules such as "total money is constant" hold before and after. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work. Durability means once committed, it survives crashes. In a distributed transaction, atomicity is the hard new part; isolation is usually handled by each participant's own locking, and durability by each participant's own log.

The players: A coordinator (often the server where the transaction started, or a dedicated transaction manager) drives the decision. The participants (also called cohorts or resource managers) are the servers that hold the data, here shard A and shard B. Each participant can run its local part of the transaction and then must answer one question honestly: if asked, can you guarantee to commit?

Two-phase commit, phase 1 (voting): The coordinator writes a "begin commit" record to its log and sends PREPARE to every participant. Each participant checks whether it can commit: are the constraints satisfied, did it get its locks, is there disk space? If yes, it writes all the transaction's changes and a PREPARED record to its own stable log, so it can commit even after a crash, and then replies VOTE-YES. If anything is wrong, it replies VOTE-NO and can abort locally right away. The key promise: after voting yes, a participant has given up its right to decide alone. It must wait for the coordinator.

Two-phase commit, phase 2 (decision): If every participant voted yes, the coordinator writes COMMIT to its log. That log write is the true moment of commit; everything after is just delivering the news. It then sends COMMIT to all participants. If any participant voted no, or did not answer before a timeout, the coordinator writes ABORT and sends ABORT to all. Each participant applies the decision, writes it to its log, releases its locks, and sends an ACK. When all ACKs arrive, the coordinator writes an END record and may forget the transaction.

2PC worked trace: Coordinator C, participants A (Rahim's shard) and B (Karim's shard). Step 1: C logs begin, sends PREPARE to A and B (2 messages). Step 2: A checks that Rahim has at least 500 taka, logs the debit and PREPARED, replies YES. B logs the credit and PREPARED, replies YES (2 messages). Step 3: C logs COMMIT, sends COMMIT to A and B (2 messages). Step 4: A and B apply, log COMMIT, release locks and send ACK (2 messages). Total 8 messages. In general, with N participants, 2PC uses 4N messages in the normal case: N prepares, N votes, N decisions, N acks. With 3 participants that is 12 messages, plus several forced log writes, which is why 2PC is noticeably slower than a local commit.

Abort trace: Now suppose Rahim has only 300 taka. A replies NO. C does not need to wait for B's vote to know the outcome; it logs ABORT and sends ABORT to both. A has already undone its tentative debit; B undoes its tentative credit using its log. Nobody's balance changes. Atomicity is safe.

Recovery rules from the log: Because every decision point is logged, crashes are handled by reading the log on restart. A participant that finds no PREPARED record simply aborts. A participant that finds PREPARED but no decision must ask the coordinator what happened. A coordinator that finds COMMIT or ABORT in its log resends that decision. A coordinator that crashed before writing a decision can safely abort, since nobody could have committed yet. This is the same write-ahead idea as single-machine recovery, just spread across machines.

The blocking problem: Here is the weak spot. Suppose A and B have both voted YES, and then the coordinator crashes before sending the decision. A is now in the uncertain state. It cannot commit on its own, because maybe C decided to abort (perhaps C itself had a problem). It cannot abort on its own, because maybe C logged COMMIT and B already committed. So A must wait, holding Rahim's account locked, until C recovers. If C's disk is being replaced, Rahim's account is frozen for hours. Participants can ask each other: if B already received the decision, it can tell A; if B has not voted yet, both may abort. But if every participant voted yes and none heard the decision, all of them are stuck. That is why 2PC is called a blocking protocol.

Making 2PC less painful: In practice, systems reduce blocking by making the coordinator itself highly available. Instead of one coordinator machine, the coordinator's log is replicated with consensus (Paxos or Raft, lessons 18 and 19), so if one replica dies another takes over and knows the decision. Google's Spanner database, for example, runs 2PC across groups that are each replicated with Paxos. Timeouts and administrators can also step in, though a manual decision risks breaking atomicity if guessed wrong. The XA standard defines a common interface so that different databases and message brokers can take part in one 2PC.

Three-phase commit, the idea: Three-phase commit (3PC) adds a middle phase to avoid blocking. Phase 1, CanCommit: like the vote. Phase 2, PreCommit: if all voted yes, the coordinator tells everyone "we are going to commit" and waits for acknowledgements. Phase 3, DoCommit: the actual commit. The trick is that no participant can be in a state where some others have already committed while it is still uncertain; so if the coordinator dies, the survivors can elect a new coordinator and safely finish the protocol. The cost is an extra round trip, about 6N messages, and a strong assumption: 3PC is non-blocking only if failures are crashes and message delays are bounded, so a timeout really means a crash. In a network partition, the two sides can decide differently, breaking atomicity. Because real networks partition, 3PC is mostly a textbook idea; real systems prefer 2PC with a replicated coordinator.

Isolation across machines: Atomic commit decides whether to commit, but concurrent transactions still need isolation. The usual answer is strict two-phase locking at every participant: each site holds its locks until the global commit or abort arrives. Combined with 2PC, this gives globally serializable transactions. The new danger is distributed deadlock: transaction T1 holds a lock on A and waits for B, while T2 holds B and waits for A, and no single site sees the whole cycle. Systems detect it with a global wait-for graph or, more simply, abort a transaction that waits longer than a timeout.

Sagas: 2PC holds locks across machines for at least two network round trips, and one slow participant slows everyone. Across many independent services, owned by different teams and sometimes different companies, that coupling is often unacceptable. A saga, described by Garcia-Molina and Salem in 1987, splits a long transaction into a sequence of local transactions T1, T2, ..., Tn, each committing immediately in its own service. For each step there is a compensating transaction C1, C2, ..., which semantically undoes it. If step Tk fails, the saga runs C(k-1), ..., C1 in reverse order. A saga does not lock everything at once; it trades isolation for availability.

Saga worked, booking a ride: A ride-sharing app books a trip in three services. T1: the driver service reserves driver Jamal. T2: the wallet service puts a hold of 250 taka on the rider's wallet. T3: the trip service creates the confirmed trip. Suppose T3 fails because the pickup zone was just closed. The saga runs C2: release the 250 taka hold. Then C1: free Jamal for other riders. The final state is as if nothing happened, though for a short time other code could see Jamal as reserved. That visible middle state is the price of sagas, so designers use statuses like "PENDING" to warn other readers. Compensations must themselves be retryable and idempotent (lesson 05), because they may run twice after a crash.

Orchestration vs choreography: A saga can be orchestrated, with one central saga coordinator that calls each service in order and triggers compensations, which is easy to follow and debug. Or it can be choreographed, where each service listens for events on a message queue (lesson 06) and reacts: "driver reserved" triggers the wallet hold, "hold failed" triggers driver release. Choreography avoids a central point but is harder to see as a whole. A related pattern is the transactional outbox: a service writes its data change and an "event to publish" row in the same local transaction, and a separate relay later sends the event, so the database and the message queue never disagree.

Real-life example 1, a bank transfer through two systems: When you send money from a bank app to a mobile wallet in Bangladesh, the bank and the wallet company run separate systems, so a single 2PC across them is usually not used; that would let one company's outage freeze the other's accounts. Instead, such interbank and bank-to-wallet flows typically rely on messages, unique reference numbers, status checks and reversals, which is saga-style thinking. Inside one company, where the shards share one transaction manager, 2PC or a consensus-replicated commit is more common.

Real-life example 2, an online exam registration: A university portal registers a student for exams. It must mark the fee as paid in the accounts database and create an admit card in the exam database. If these two databases are under one team with a transaction manager, 2PC makes it all or nothing. If accounts is an external payment gateway, the portal uses a saga: record payment, then create the admit card, and if card creation keeps failing, issue a refund as compensation.

Common mistakes: Thinking 2PC tolerates coordinator failure without blocking; it does not. Forgetting that a participant who voted yes cannot change its mind. Saying 3PC is "2PC but better" without the assumption of bounded delays and no partitions. Treating compensation as a rollback; it is a new forward action that undoes the effect, and side effects like a sent SMS cannot be unsent. And assuming sagas give isolation; they do not.

What exams ask: Draw the 2PC message diagram with logs for commit and abort cases. Count messages for N participants. Explain the uncertain state and why 2PC blocks. Describe 3PC phases and when it is non-blocking. Compare 2PC with sagas, and design compensations for a given business flow.

Recap: Distributed transactions need atomic commitment across machines. 2PC uses a prepare/vote phase and a commit/abort phase, with forced log writes, about 4N messages. A participant that voted yes must wait, so a coordinator crash can block it; replicating the coordinator with consensus is the practical fix. 3PC removes blocking only under strong timing assumptions. Sagas chain local transactions with compensations, giving up isolation to stay loosely coupled.
key_points: Atomic commitment: a transaction touching several machines must commit everywhere or abort everywhere.
2PC phase 1: coordinator sends PREPARE, participants log PREPARED and vote YES or NO.
2PC phase 2: all YES means the coordinator logs COMMIT (the real commit point) and tells everyone; any NO or timeout means ABORT.
Normal-case 2PC with N participants costs about 4N messages: prepare, vote, decision, ack (12 for N = 3).
A participant that voted YES cannot decide alone; if the coordinator crashes then, it blocks holding locks.
3PC adds a pre-commit phase and avoids blocking only with crash failures and bounded delays, not under partitions.
Replicating the coordinator with Paxos or Raft is the practical way to reduce 2PC blocking.
Sagas run local transactions with compensating actions in reverse order; they trade isolation for loose coupling.
lessons.tip: Draw 2PC as a two-column timeline (coordinator and one participant) and mark every log write with a small box. Then cover the timeline at different points and ask: if the coordinator crashes here, what does the participant do? Doing this for four points makes the blocking problem obvious.
lessons.task: Design a saga for ordering a book from an online shop in Bangladesh: reserve stock, charge the card or wallet, book the courier. Write T1 to T3 and C1 to C3 in plain words, then write what happens if T3 fails, and which step cannot be fully undone (hint: messages already sent to the customer).

quiz.q: In 2PC, what is the actual moment a distributed transaction becomes committed?
options: When the first participant votes YES
When the coordinator writes COMMIT to its log
When the client receives the reply
quiz.explain: Once the COMMIT record is in the coordinator's stable log the decision is final; sending messages only delivers it.

quiz.q: How many messages does normal-case 2PC need with 3 participants (prepare, vote, decision, ack)?
quiz.explain: 4N messages: 3 prepares, 3 votes, 3 decisions and 3 acks, so 12.

quiz.q: Why can a participant that voted YES not abort on its own when the coordinator goes silent?
options: The coordinator may already have logged COMMIT and others may have committed
quiz.explain: After voting YES it is uncertain: deciding alone might contradict a commit that already happened elsewhere.

quiz.q: Under which assumption is 3PC non-blocking?
options: The network may partition at any time
Messages can be delayed without limit
Only crash failures and bounded message delays
quiz.explain: 3PC relies on timeouts meaning crashes; with partitions or unbounded delays the two sides can decide differently.

quiz.q: In a ride-booking saga, T3 (create trip) fails after T1 (reserve driver) and T2 (hold fare). What runs next?
options: C2 then C1 (release the fare hold, then free the driver)
A 2PC abort message to all services
quiz.explain: Compensations run in reverse order of the completed steps: first undo T2, then T1.

lessons.title: Partitioning, Sharding and Consistent Hashing
lessons.content:
Think of the SSC result day at a big board office. If one clerk had to find the marksheet of every student in the division, the queue would reach the next district. So the office splits the work: roll numbers 100001 to 200000 go to desk 1, 200001 to 300000 to desk 2, and so on. Each clerk handles a slice, all clerks work at once, and a student only needs to know which desk to visit. That is partitioning, also called sharding: splitting one big dataset into pieces so that many machines can each own a piece. It is how a distributed system grows beyond what one machine can store or serve.

Where this fits: Replication (lessons 14 and 15) copies the same data to several machines, mostly for availability and read speed. Partitioning does something different: it gives different data to different machines, mostly for scale. Real systems combine them: the data is split into partitions, and each partition is replicated, say three times. This lesson covers how to split, how to find the right partition, and how to move data when machines are added or removed, with consistent hashing as the star. Deeper database internals such as partitioned query planning belong to Advanced Database Systems & Big Data (deep-cse-7-2).

Why partition at all: First, size: a 50 TB dataset does not fit on one server's disks. Second, throughput: if one machine handles 10,000 requests per second and you need 100,000, you need about ten machines sharing the load. Third, locality: a user's data can live near the user. The goal is to spread data and load evenly. If one partition gets far more traffic than the others, it is called a hot spot, and the system is only as fast as its busiest machine. Uneven spreading is called skew.

Partitioning by key range: Give each partition a continuous range of keys, like the SSC desks. For example, a student database with IDs 1 to 1,000 on 4 nodes: node 1 owns 1 to 250, node 2 owns 251 to 500, node 3 owns 501 to 750, node 4 owns 751 to 1,000. The big advantage is range queries: "give me students 300 to 320" goes to one node, and keys inside a partition can be kept sorted. The danger is hot spots. If the key is a timestamp, all of today's writes land on the partition holding today's range, while the others sit idle. Systems that use range partitioning, such as HBase and Bigtable-style stores, split a range into two when it grows too large. A common fix for timestamp hot spots is to put something else first in the key, such as the sensor id, then the time.

Partitioning by hash: Run the key through a hash function and use the hash to choose the partition. A good hash spreads even very similar keys, such as 01711000001 and 01711000002, to unrelated places, so load is even and hot spots from sequential keys disappear. The price: neighbouring keys are scattered, so a range query must ask every partition. Hashing also cannot fix a single super-hot key, such as one celebrity account; for that, applications sometimes add a small random suffix to the key to spread its writes, at the cost of reading several keys back.

The naive hash: hash mod N: The simplest rule is partition = hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of nodes. It works beautifully until N changes. Worked example with small integer keys standing in for hashes, going from N = 3 to N = 4: key 10 goes from 10 mod 3 = 1 to 10 mod 4 = 2, so it moves. Key 11: 2 to 3, moves. Key 12: 0 to 0, stays. Key 13: 1 to 1, stays. Key 14: 2 to 2, stays. Key 15: 0 to 3, moves. Over all keys, a key stays only when k mod 3 equals k mod 4, which happens for 3 out of every 12 numbers, so 75 percent of all keys move. Going from 4 to 5 nodes, 80 percent move; from 10 to 11, about 91 percent move. Adding one machine forces almost the whole dataset across the network, exactly when you were already overloaded. We need a scheme where adding a node moves only its fair share.

Consistent hashing, the idea: Introduced by Karger and colleagues in 1997 for web caching, consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on the same circle. Imagine the hash space bent into a ring, like a clock face. Each node is hashed (say from its name or IP) to a position on the ring. Each key is hashed to a position too. Rule: a key belongs to the first node you meet walking clockwise from the key's position. Because positions come from a hash, both nodes and keys are spread around the ring.

Consistent hashing worked: To keep numbers small, use a ring of positions 0 to 99 with invented positions. Node A sits at 20, node B at 50, node C at 80. Keys sit at 10, 35, 45, 60 and 90. Key 10: walk clockwise, first node is A at 20, so A. Key 35: first node is B at 50. Key 45: B. Key 60: first node is C at 80. Key 90: nothing until 99, so wrap around to 0 and meet A at 20, so A. Now add node D at position 65. Walk again: key 10 to A, 35 to B, 45 to B, 60 now meets D at 65 before C, so D. Key 90 still A. Only key 60 moved, and it moved from C to the new node D. In general only the keys between D's predecessor (B at 50) and D (65) change owner, and they all go to D. Removing a node is the mirror image: its keys go to the next node clockwise, and nobody else is touched. On average, adding one node to N nodes moves about 1/(N + 1) of the keys, the minimum possible.

Virtual nodes: With just three real positions, the ring arcs are uneven by chance: one node might own 50 percent of the ring and another 15 percent. Also, when a node leaves, all its keys land on one neighbour, which might then overload. The fix is virtual nodes: each physical server takes many positions on the ring, say 100, by hashing "A-1", "A-2", ... "A-100". Now each server owns many small arcs scattered around, the shares even out, and a departing server's load is spread across many others. More powerful machines can get more virtual nodes. In a quick simulation with 3 servers of 100 virtual nodes each, adding a fourth moved about 29 percent of the keys, close to the ideal 25 percent, and every moved key went to the new server. Amazon's Dynamo design and Cassandra use this idea.

Fixed number of partitions: Another popular approach avoids reshuffling keys altogether. Create many more partitions than nodes up front, for example 1,000 partitions on 10 nodes, 100 each. A key's partition is hash(key) mod 1,000, and that never changes. Only the assignment of whole partitions to nodes changes. When an 11th node joins, it steals a few partitions from each existing node until each holds about 1000 / 11, roughly 91; about 9 percent of the data moves, again close to the minimum.
